en: The Kauśikapaddhati composed by Keśava. OM, salutation to the Atharvaveda!
An exposition of the ritual rules for the Saṃhitā of the Atharvaveda is now being composed.
In that regard, there are nine divisions of the Atharvaveda.
Among them, within the four branches beginning with Śaunaka and others, this Kauśika Saṃhitā-vidhi was composed;
having set aside the explanatory passages (arthavāda) and so forth from the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, it was fashioned as a ritual manual (vidhi) by extracting only the prescriptive rules.
In this regard, a commentary is composed according to its utility for the ritual procedure of the *saṃhitā*.
Regarding that, Kauśika states the sūtra: [The Procedure for the New and Full Moon Sacrifices].
Now we shall explain the ritual procedure. (Kauśika Sūtra 1.1.1)
The word "atha" (now/then) signifies immediate succession.
Following the study of the *saṃhitā*, there begins the section on the rules [of recitation].
We shall now explain the rules for the *saṃhitā*.
Rites such as those for pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), malevolent magic (*abhicārika*), and portents (*adbhuta*) are taught in the ritual procedures of the *Saṃhitās*.
These rites are of three kinds:
rites according to rule (*vidhi-karma*), rites contrary to rule (*avidhi-karma*), and rites of elevation (*ucchraya-karma*).
The method [of knowledge] consists of three means of valid cognition:
perception, inference, and verbal testimony.
Furthermore, that is based on the authority of sacred tradition. 1.1.2.
That procedure is based on the Veda;
it has the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa as its authority.
Furthermore, the sacred tradition consists of both the mantras and the brāhmaṇas.
What is meant by the word *āmnāya*? To this he replies: the *mantra* and the *brāhmaṇa* are denoted by the word *āmnāya*.
Just as is the rule for the Brāhmaṇas, so too are the mantras characterized by their ritual application.
Just as the ritual action is prescribed according to the rule of *saṃhitā*, so too do the mantras possess such indicative marks (*liṅga*).
For example, one ties a conch shell [with the mantra] beginning with "born from the wind" (4.10).
Likewise, there are others with different meanings. (KauśS 1.1.5)
Mantras also have other purposes,
as for example: "We speak of Agni" (11.6) and "or he whose life is immortal" (5.1.7).
"May they be auspicious," he says as he gives [the offering] to one who has been falsely accused. (KauśS 46.1)
Likewise, the mantras possess the characteristics of Brahmins.
"Brahman indeed was this in the beginning" (Gobhila Gṛhyasūtra 1.1.1);
such is the preceding Brāhmaṇa passage.
There are also mantras of this same nature.
Just as there are mantras whose purpose is to provide explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), such as "In the beginning, indeed, this was Virāj" (8.10.1).
In its absence, there is the oral tradition. KauśS_1,1.7 //

Whatever is not explicitly mentioned in the rules for the *saṃhitā* must all be performed according to the principles of one's own recension (*sva-śākhā*), through tradition and established practice (*sampradāya*).
Thus it has been said by Bhaṭṭapāda: "The ritualists proceed with their rites according to logic and tradition.
Likewise, in rites for pacification (*śāntika*), the altar (*vedi*) is to be constructed with river sand, and the measurement of the altar is to be made with wood from a tree of a peaceful nature.
Likewise, in the Mīmāṃsā, within the Smṛti-pāda, the authority of traditional texts (smṛti) and established customs (ācāra) has been declared.
Because the Brāhmaṇas are completely liberated.
Regarding the tradition of practice (*ācārasampradāya*), certain *Brāhmaṇa* texts were forgotten;
however, the tradition was preserved by the disciples.
This was stated by the teacher Upavarṣa in the *Mīmāṃsā*, in the section on the *Kalpasūtras* within the *Smṛti-pāda*.
The Nakṣatrakalpa, the Vaitānakalpa as the third, the Saṃhitāvidhi,
the Aṅgirasāṃ Kalpa as the fourth, and the Śāntikalpa as the fifth.
Thus it has been established by the venerable teacher Upavarṣa that "these Kalpas are indeed equal to the Vedas," whereas other Kalpas are equal to the Smṛtis.
We shall explain the sacrifice for the gods and for the ancestors.
The *pākayajña* and the *ājyatantra* are denoted by the term "sacrifice" (*yajña*).
We shall explain that.
The sacrifice of the gods consists of rites for pacification (*śāntika*), nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), and so forth.
For the ancestors, it consists of the Pitṛmedha, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, and so forth.
Facing the east, he performs [the rite] in a low voice.
Facing the east, he performs all rites—
whether obligatory, occasional, or optional—
and also those performed in a whisper.
When a second person hears the sound at a distance of one man's length away, that is called *upāṃśu*.
Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, he belongs to the gods.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), [he performs the rites] for the ancestors.
Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), one should perform the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites.
Having placed it over the right shoulder (apasavya), one should perform the rites for the ancestors, such as the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and others.
Or toward the northeast for the gods. (KauśS 1.1.13)
The sacrificial fee belongs to the ancestors.
One should perform all rites for the gods facing either the east or the north;
one should perform rites for the ancestors facing the south.
Some say that one should perform rites for the ancestors facing the intermediate direction between the south and the east.
For the gods, [the rites] are performed with their completion toward the east or the north.
For the ancestors, [the lines] terminate toward the south and the west.

In rites for the gods, the completion of the ritual action is toward the northeast; in rites for the ancestors, it is toward the south or the southwest. Some maintain that in the case of rites for the gods, the completion is in the intermediate direction between the east and the north.
The rite for the ancestors is performed once; that for the gods is at least three times.
In rites such as sipping water (ācamana) and sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), one should perform the action once for the ancestors (pitṛs).
For the gods (devas), one should perform every action either four times or three times.
This applies to actions such as the offering of oblations (nirvapaṇa), the spreading of sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa), and the taking of clarified butter (ājya-grahaṇa).
Or as previously instructed. (KauśS 1.1.18)
Or one may perform the ritual action exactly as it is recited; for instance,
"With the verse, *yathā paritvāgne puraṃ vayam* (7.71.1), he carries fire around [the object] three times" (KauśS 2.10).
The movement of the gods is from left to right; that of the ancestors is counter-clockwise.
One should perform rites for the gods with circumambulation from left to right;
rites for the ancestors are performed without circumambulation.
The gods are those who receive offerings with the utterances of *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ*.
The ancestors receive the offerings of *svadhā* and salutations.

An oblation is offered to the gods with the utterance of *svāhā* or *vaṣaṭ*. "In all cases, the offerings are made verse by verse with [mantras] ending in *svāhā*" (KauśS 4.11). An offering is given to the ancestors with the utterance of *svadhā* or with a salutation (*namaskāra*).
The sacrificial grass for the ancestors is cut near its base.
On the festival days of the gods. (KauśS 1.1.23)
The sacrificial grass (barhis) of the ancestors is with its roots; the sacrificial grass of the gods is cut [without roots];
the sacrificial grass of the ancestors is cut once.
The bringing forward:
"To the north of the fire, he places the fuel and the northern sacrificial grass" (KauśS 2.13–14).
[Recite: "Give me the rib-bone" (12.3.31)].
Thus he hands over the sickle for the purpose of gathering *darbha* grass,
with the formula beginning with "Hand over the sickle" and ending with "not harming" (ŚGS 12.3.31).

Having cut the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) above the joints with the verse beginning "May the plants bite the joint" (*oṣadhīrdāntu parvan*), he brings it silently and places it to the north of the fire.
Having cut the sacrificial grass with the remainder of the formula beginning "May the plants bite the joint," he brings it silently and places it to the north of the fire.
To the north of the *āvasathya* fire, he places the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Some perform the cutting of the grass after completing the rite of entering the vow (*vratopāyana*),
because the ritual actions span two days.
One should not turn the fire away.
One should not dwell behind the fire; one should not pass it without circumambulating it to the right; nor should one pass between the components of the sacrifice. // KauśS 1.1.27 //
One should not pass between [the fire and the teacher];
one should not create an obstruction between the fire, the sacrificial vessels, and the Brāhmaṇas.
Having extended the right knee, he offers the oblation.
At the time of the fire-offering ritual, one should lower the right knee to the ground; then the offering should be performed.
That which is the earlier full moon is Anumati; that which is the later is Rākā.
That which is the earlier new moon is Sinīvālī; that which is the later is Kuhū.
It is stated in the *Sāṅkhyāyana Brāhmaṇa*: "There are two full-moon days and two new-moon days" (*ŚāṅkhB* 4.4). [Namely:
the first day of the lunar fortnight following the full moon is the full-moon day; the first day of the lunar fortnight following the new moon is the new-moon day.
Having fasted on the previous day, one should perform the sacrifice on the following day.
Some consider the fourteenth day to be the previous day; others hold that the full moon or new moon day is that which is mixed with the fourteenth day.
When there is a division of lunar days, that which is mixed with the fourteenth day should be observed as a fast, while that which is mixed with the first day should be used for sacrifice.
Thinking, "Today is the fast-day," one who is about to fast eats a meal.
When there is a division between lunar days, the primary one is the full moon day; when there is such a division, that which occurs earlier is to be observed,
for one performs the fast on it.
In the Veda, *upavāsa* means abstaining from food;
it is that by which the sacrificer performs the sacrifice—he does not eat that [food].
With the exception of honey, salt, meat, and beans.
On the day of preparation (upavasatha), he should not eat these;
these substances are well known.
Having performed everything up to the formal undertaking of the vow (vratopāyana), he then undertakes the vow (vratagrahaṇa).
One practices celibacy and so forth.
There are three kinds of actions:
ritual actions (*vidhikarma*), non-ritual actions (*avidhikarma*), and elevating actions (*ucchrayakarma*).
The rites beginning with the production of intelligence (*medhājanana*) and ending with the *piṇḸapitṛyajña* (KauśS 10–89) constitute the category of ritual acts (*vidhikarma*),
as does the section on days unfit for study (*anadhyāyakaṇḍikā*, KauśS 141).
The section from the *madhuparka* to the *indramaha* (KauśS 90–140) constitutes the *avidhikarma*.

Where, after assigning a hymn (*sūkta*) for a specific purpose, there is a further assignment of individual verses (*ṛc*), that constitutes the *ucchrayakarma*, as in the case of "ud uttamam" (7.88.3).

In the first chapter, the *paribhāṣās* serve all purposes, whether for the sake of prescriptive acts (*vidhi-karman*) or for the sake of non-prescriptive acts (*avidhi-karman*). The remaining [chapters] constitute the nature of the *paribhāṣās*, while the five *kalpas* constitute the nature of prescriptive acts.
In the *Adbhuta* [Pariśiṣṭa], there is a second definition:
"Whether it be a family, a village, or a district, the king or lord of the land should choose a learned descendant of Bhṛgu or Aṅgiras," and so forth;
therein it is stated that a manual for the performance of the rites taught by Kauśika is being composed for the benefit of the learned.

"And [the rite] without the *avakā* grass" (19.68.1): having performed everything up to the cutting of the *barhis* grass, the preparation of the altar (*vedi*), the *uttaravedi*, and the installation of the fire, he offers fuel-sticks with the mantra "O Agni, may splendor be mine" (5.3.1) and enters upon the vow. (KauśS 1.1.33)
Or [he may do so] with the mantra: "By means of the vow, O Lord of Vows... (RV 7.74.4).
The student observing the vow (brahmacārī) shall sleep on the ground.
Having placed fuel sticks with the mantra "O Agni, my splendor," he offers a portion of food with the verse "By the vow, O Lord of Vows.
Having performed this, he does the same on the second day.

When the fire has been offered in the morning, having washed his hands with the formula, "For your work, for your attire, for your good deed," he spreads darbha grass to the west of the fire; upon that, he spreads a red bull's hide with its neck to the east and its hair upwards, and then prepares two strainers.
Having washed two blades of *darbha* grass whose tips have been cut off, he strokes them in the direction of the hair with the mantra, "Purified by the mind of Viṣṇu, you two are pure.
He washes his hands with the mantra, "For the sake of the ritual, I take you two.
Having spread *darbha* grass to the west of the fire, he spreads upon it a red bull's hide with the neck facing north.
He prepares two purifiers from Darbha grass with uncut tips;
having washed them, he strokes them in the direction of the hair with the mantra: "O you two, purified by the mind of Viṣṇu, you are pure."
The First Section (Kaṇḍikā).
"You shall attain the earth by your power; you sit upon the altar, beautiful at the sacrifice.
The seers, bringing you as a purifier, purify us from our misdeeds. (19.33.3).

Having placed a strainer between, he pours out the oblation with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour you out, acceptable to Agni. (KauśS 1.2.1)
The evening and morning fire-oblations, the Vaiśvadeva, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, and other such rites are to be performed once the fire has been drawn out.
With the verse "Thou art the earth," he places the two strainers upon the hide and pours out four handfuls [of grain] with the formula "Thee for the God.
The fourth handful is poured silently.
"I offer what is pleasing to Agni."
[Thus: "To Agni and Soma...
(KauśS 1.2.2)] The modification is: "I offer what is pleasing to Agni and Soma."
"To Indra and Agni" [is the mantra] on the new moon day. (KauśS 1.2.3)
The Āgneya [offering] is always performed first.

Having poured out [the grain], he sprinkles it with the two purifiers (pavitra) according to the respective deity, saying: "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to such-and-such," as follows: "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Agni," and likewise for Agni and Soma.
The sprinkling applies to both as well.

Having washed the mortar, pestle, and winnowing basket, and having placed them upon a hide, he pours the rice-grains into the mortar; while threshing them, he releases his speech three times with the call to the preparer of the oblation, saying, "O preparer of the oblation, come hither! With the verse, "The enemy... (10.6.1), he fashions the mortar and pestle; with the verse, "What thou, O skillful one... (10.6.3), he washes them; and with the verse, "Whatever the black one... (12.3.13).
Thus he purifies with the Ṛg-verse.
Then, having poured rice grains into the mortar, he threshes them three times with the formula, "O preparer of the oblation, come hither. Thereafter follows the winnowing with a winnowing basket.
Then, there is the thrice-washing of the rice grains.

[Having removed the husks, made them well-purified, and washed the rice grains three times, he places the sacrificial porridge upon the fire with the verse: "O Agni, the sacrificial porridge has ascended thee" (KauśS 1.2.7).
He places the porridge upon the fire with the ṛg-verse beginning, "O Agni, the porridge."
With the verse, "Pure, purified," he pours water;
that is, he pours water with the Ṛgvedic verse, "Pure, purified."
With the verse, "Purified by the Brahman" (ŚB 11.1.1.18), he pours in the rice grains after having placed the two strainers in between.
With the verse, "O Agni, we [place] a rampart around you" (RV 7.71.1),
he performs the circumambulation with fire three times.
The circumambulation with fire is performed three times using the Ṛgvedic verse beginning, "O Agni, we [place] a rampart around you."
With the *nekṣaṇa* spoon, he stirs [the mixture] three times from left to right.
[From this point onward, it is according to one's desire. (KauśS 1.2.12)
To the north of the fire, he places the fuel.
"The sacrificial grass to the north" (KauśS 1.2.14):
he places the fuel on the north side of the fire,
and then the sacrificial grass.
"‘I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni,’ thus [he sprinkles] the fuel.
"‘I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni’—this is the sprinkling of the fuel."
[Regarding the verse "To the Earth...": "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to the Earth," with which the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is sprinkled.
Having sprinkled a handful of *darbha* grass, he places it behind the fire with its tips pointing eastward, using the mantra: "Soft as wool, spread yourself out, providing a good seat for the gods.
Having sprinkled a handful of *darbha* grass, he spreads it behind the fire with the mantra beginning "ūrṇamradam."
Having taken blades of darbha grass, they place the seat of the Brahman priest to the south of the fire with the mantra: "Thou art the sacrificial strew of the seers" (KauśS 16.2.6).
They place the seat of the Brahman priest to the south of the fire with the words: "Thou art the sacrificial strew of the seers."
"O Lord of the Earth"—this is the selection of the Brahman priest.
And so says the Gobhila-Brāhmaṇa:
"One should place either a visible [priest] or one made of Darbha grass, or a seat, or a water-pot, in the position of the Brahman."
Then follows the consecration of the Brahma-seat.
"Having spread [the grass] in front of the fire, covering the roots of some with the tips of others, he creeps around to the south of the fire as far as its western half.
Regarding this, the performer says: "Then the spreading in front of the fire."
"Spread [the grass] around," he issues this command. (KauśS 1.2.20)
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, being impelled by his command, I spread thee around.
Then he spreads [the grass] with the mantra beginning "By the impulse of the god."
[In this way, one should arrange the odd-numbered elements to the north. (KauśS 1.2.22)
Where they meet, he makes that the south and north;
he spreads out the *paribhojanīya* blades of grass.
He sprinkles the strewn grass with the formula: "I sprinkle you, who are acceptable as an oblation. (KauśS 1.2.24)
That which has not been sprinkled with water shall not be fit for use, even if it has been spread out.
The fuel is the placing [of the wood] upon [the fire]. 1.2.26.
The sacrificial oblation must not be unpurified.
No sacrificial implement is [to be used] unless it has been sprinkled with water.
In that [vessel], he places [the items] after they have been washed and aired.
This technical definition applies everywhere.
[The *sruva* ladle and the *ājyadhānī* vessel.
They place the *sruva* ladle and the *ājyadhānī* vessel down.

Having taken the clarified butter that has been melted and purified, having placed it over the fire, having carried a firebrand around it, having removed it from the fire toward the north, and having set it down behind the fire, he purifies it with two strainers whose tips point northward.
[Thou art purified by the mind of Viṣṇu. (KauśS 1.2.32)
May Savitṛ purify you with the divine [purifier]. KauśS_1,2.33.
"By means of an unbroken strainer, with a hundred streams, with a thousand streams, I purify you well"—this is the third [verse]. *Kauśikasūtra* 1.2.34.
The fourth [offering] is made silently with the mantra:
"Thou art purified by the mind of Viṣṇu."
He pours an oblation of boiled milk over it, saying: "Anointing with honey, you shall act as one rich in ghee."
He sprinkles the cooked oblation with clarified butter while reciting, "Anointing with honey."
Having sprinkled [the oblation], he removes it toward the north with the verse: "We have prepared the cooked offering for Agni; sit upon the back, the abode of immortality" (PaippS 5.16.3).
With the words "remove from Agni," he removes it using the Ṛgvedic verse.
[Having placed it behind the clarified butter and having adorned it, he purifies it with an equal amount.
Then, having placed it behind the clarified butter and having adorned it, and having sprinkled the sacrificial pap (caru) with clarified butter, he purifies it with an equal amount.
He gazes at [the child] with the mantra, "adārasṛt" (1.22.1).
"Arise! (7.72.1–3) is for Indra; [it is used] according to the *Kauśika Sūtra* 1.2.40.
He gazes at the sacrificial pap.
He adds fuel with the three verses beginning "Agni on the earth" (12.1.19–21), or with "To him the dominions" (7.78.2) and "This kindling-stick" (10.6.35). (KauśS 1.2.41)
"I unite you with the divine *brahman* so that you may carry this oblation, O Jātavedas.
Kindling you, may we live long with good offspring and brave heroes, offering tribute to you. [KauśS 1.3.1] "Agni is in the earth, in the plants..."
"Agni heats from the sky," "Agni is clothed, the earth has black knees," "O Agni, [to him] who maintains the lordships."
With the words "This fuel" or with these five verses beginning with "I yoke thee," he places the fuel on the fire.
The second section (kaṇḍikā).

Having placed a vessel of water made of bell-metal, belonging to the Jāṅmāyana, to the south of the fire, he consecrates it with the mantra: "Hold that vessel of water just as Brahmaṇaspati held it in the beginning, according to the true law, at the impulse of the god Savitṛ. (KauśS 1.3.2) Having placed the Jāṅmāyana vessel of water to the south of the fire, he consecrates it with the verse beginning, "Hold that vessel of water."
Then he pours water [on the ground], saying: "Come here, O goddesses, clothed in immortality, golden-hued and of blameless form!
May the waters, the ocean, and King Varuṇa enjoy their share of the oblation from the contact."
"Commanded by Indra and impelled by Varuṇa, let the waters carry up from the ocean to heaven;
commanded by Indra and impelled by Varuṇa, let them bring the splendor from heaven and earth.
With these two verses, beginning with "Come hither, O goddesses," he pours water from a vessel in an unbroken stream.

"O Jātavedas, I sprinkle you around with Ṛta through Satya"—having sprinkled water around him together with the sacrificial oblations, having sipped water with the *jīvā* verses, and having stood up, he enters by means of the *vedaprapada* formulas: "Om, I enter; I enter Bhūḥ; I enter Bhuvaḥ; I enter Svaḥ;
I enter Janat. (KauśS 1.3.4)

Having sprinkled water around [the fire] together with the oblations while reciting "ṛtaṃ tvā satyena," and whenever one is about to sacrifice in any ritual involving a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should sacrifice with "ṛtaṃ tvā satyena" and then recite "satyaṃ tvartena" (KauśS 6.20);
this is stated in the traditional text (sampradāyagrantha).
One sips water three times while reciting the hymn "jīvā stha" (19.69–70).
With the nine verses beginning with "satyaṃ bṛhat" (12.1.1–9), the verse "śāntivā" (12.1.59), and the two verses beginning with "udāyuṣā" (3.31.10–11).
Thus he rises with two [verses].
He enters with the Veda-stepping formulas: with the Ṛg-verse beginning "Oṃ, I enter Bhūḥ," [he says] "...I enter."

Having entered and spread out darbha grass upon that which has already been strewn, he gazes at the seat of the Brahman priest, saying: "O son of two wives, depart; sit on the seat of another who is more foolish than we.
He throws away a blade of grass toward the south, saying: "The one with wealth has been cast out along with evil; may he who hates us and whom we hate be cast out. (KauśS 1.3.5–6)
Then, having touched it, he mutters: "Here I sit upon the seat of Arvāgvasu; I sit upon the seat of Truth; I sit upon the seat of the Desired;
I sit upon the seat of the Bestowed. O divine *barhis*, do not harm me; may I sit upon you, who are a good resting place, soft as wool, and free from sorrow."

Having sat down with the verse *vimṛgvarīm* (12.1.29), he mutters the *brahmajapa* for the seat: "Bṛhaspati, as the Brahman priest, shall sit upon the seat of the Brahman; O Bṛhaspati, protect the sacrifice, so that I may be able to ascend from the heights and the depths.
Having spread darbha grass upon the seat, he performs the consecration of the seat with the formula: "O son of a remarried woman, depart and stand aside! *KauśS_1,3.8*
Having wiped the *sruva* spoon with *darbha* grass, he heats it over the fire, saying: "The *rakṣas* is scorched; the enemies are scorched; the *rakṣas* is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away.
Having thus heated the *sruva*, he wipes it with *darbha* grass, saying: "The *rakṣas* is scorched," and so forth, and heats the *sruva* again.
Taking the *sruva* ladle by its base, he recites: "Thou art the hand of Viṣṇu, given by Pūṣan, [and] by Bṛhaspati;
thee, the *sruva*, the bearer of oblations for the gods, I take up.
This *sruva* offers the oblations with the *jagatī* metre consisting of a hundred syllables."
"The Bārhaspatya sacrifice anoints all the stations of the sacrifice with divine protection. Thus [ends the section]. KauśS 1.3.10.
"Oṃ bhūḥ! Śam! I take you for prosperity, for well-being"—with these words he takes the first draught. (KauśS 1.3.11)
"Oṃ bhuvaḥ! For prosperity, I take you for prosperity"—this is the second [formula]. (KauśS 1.3.12)
"Oṃ svaḥ! I take thee for prosperity and for thousandfold nourishment"—thus the third [verse]. (KauśS 1.3.13)
"Oṃ, I take you for the people, for immeasurable prosperity"—thus the fourth [verse]. (KauśS 1.3.14)

In rites for the king or for malevolent magic, he takes the fifth [cup] with the formula: "I take thee for the out-breath of so-and-so, for the in-breath, for the diffused breath, for the level breath, for the up-breath. (KauśS 1.3.15)
He takes portions of clarified butter from the vessel for clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, using the four [mantras] beginning with: "Oṃ bhūḥ! Peace! For prosperity, I take thee."

All actions leading to complete success have been accomplished; there is no distinction among actions in any respect; this means that all desires are fulfilled.

It bestows all forms of prosperity: sons, cattle, wealth, grain, progeny, wives, victory, triumph, the attainment of fortune, horses, elephants, vehicles, gardens, villages, houses, wells, tanks, ponds, the study of the Vedas, the recitation of ritual manuals, knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, knowledge of Mīmāṃsā, knowledge of grammar, knowledge of the Sūtras, the maintenance of the domestic fire (*āvasathya*), the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*), the desire for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the desire for the Sattra sacrifice, and excellence in virtue, wealth, and pleasure.

Regarding others, namely enemies, there are the various accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as: expulsion (*uccāṭana*), subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), the inciting of domestic strife, causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), paralyzing (*stambhana*), alchemy (*rasāyana*), metallurgy (*dhātuvāda*), and so forth; as well as the enjoyment of women, sensual desires, impure objects, bulls, malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), rites for well-being (*svastyayana*), longevity, the nourishment of the fourfold army, and the attainment of divine knowledge.
These are called the manifold accomplishments of desire.
Regarding the phrase "the attainment of unprecedented success":
in all cases, there is no fixed sequence of actions;
in all cases, there is optionality.
For one who seeks results, the accomplishment of action comes through repeated practice—that is, through the repeated performance of the rite.
Because desires are infinite, they have been enumerated as "all prosperities"; in the world, this is called the fulfillment of manifold desires.
Those desiring specific wealth,
those desiring specific sons—
such as sons of a tawny complexion or a fair complexion— thinking that it will be thus.
There is no fixed sequence for the ritual actions; the rite has been taught by way of a compendium. Thus ends the manual of rituals for the Sāmpada.
