He offers husks with the three verses beginning "The destroyer of worms," and he offers husks with the hymn beginning "The divine Pṛśniparṇī, auspicious to us. There is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
For the fumigation of a man,
one who desires the expulsion of a piśāca offers oblations of chaff with the hymn beginning "ā paśyati."
He offers oblations of clarified butter with the two hymns, "tānt satyaujāḥ" and "tvayā pūrvam";
there is an option regarding the ritual procedure (tantra).
One who desires the eradication of *piśācas* everywhere offers roasted barley (*tuṣa*) with the hymn beginning "In front of me" (*purastādyukta*). One who desires the eradication of *piśācas*.
One who desires the eradication of piśācas offers parched grain (*tuṣa*) with the *anuvāka* beginning with "rakṣohaṇam.
One offers chaff (*busa*) with the two hymns (*sūkta*) beginning with "stuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ."
Or [he uses] a tantra;
he fumigates the person with smoke and performs a fire offering (homa) at the place where the piśāca resides.
One should act so that smoke arises and remain in that place;
one offers husks with the hymn beginning "aniḥsālām," and offers husks with the three verses beginning "arāyakṣayaṇam."
He offers husks with the hymn beginning, "The goddess Pṛśniparṇī is auspicious to us";
he offers husks with the hymn beginning, "She beholds";
[and with the hymn] "Tānt satyaujāḥ."
He offers husks with the two hymns beginning with "By you formerly";
he offers husks with [the verse] beginning with "Yoked in front";
and he offers husks with the anuvāka beginning with "The slayer of Rākṣasas."
"In all cases, one restrains the smoke of the fires that are to be kindled" (KauśS 7.28).
With the two hymns "stuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ," he offers pieces of wood;
this is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Everywhere there is the expulsion of piśācas and everywhere fumigation.

With the hymn beginning "Out of the house" (*aniḥsālām*), he offers oblations of wood-shavings. With the three verses beginning "The destroyer of the arāya-demon" (*arāyakṣayaṇam*), he offers oblations of wood-splinters.
He offers wood-shavings with the verse, "May the goddess Pṛśniparṇī be auspicious to us.
He offers wood-shavings with the hymn beginning, "She beholds.
[And he offers them] with the verse, "Those [trees], possessing true power..."
He offers wood-shavings with the two hymns beginning with "By you previously";
he offers wood-shavings with [the verse] beginning with "Yoked in front";
and he offers wood-shavings with the anuvāka beginning with "The Rakṣas-slayer."
In all cases, there is an option regarding the ritual manual because it is a hand-homa;
and in every instance, one produces smoke.
Wherever there is apprehension—whether in a person's place, a city, a village, or a house—there one produces smoke by means of the oblation.
He recites over the man possessed by a Piśāca the two hymns beginning with "stuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ"; he recites over the man the hymn beginning with "niḥsālām";
and he recites over the man the three verses beginning with "arāyakṣayaṇam."
One should cause the person possessed by a piśāca to be addressed with the hymn beginning "śanno devī.
One should cause the man possessed by a piśāca to be addressed with the hymn beginning "ā paśyati.
With the two hymns "tānt satyaujāḥ" and "tvayā pūrvam," one recites over the piśāca.
Having recited the hymn beginning with "purastādyuktaḥ," he recites [the following].
With the section beginning with "rakṣohaṇam," he addresses a man seized by a piśāca.
If this occurs in a village, a city, on a road, or in a field, then having performed the recitation, he should utter the names of the piśācas.
In all cases, there is a distinction among karmas.
He places fuel-sticks of *trapusa*, *musalī*, *khadira*, and *tārṣṭāgha* wood.

With the two hymns beginning with "The one who praises" (*astuvānam*) and "This oblation" (*idaṃ haviḥ*), he places *karkaṭikā* fuel-sticks; there is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
With the hymn "niḥsālām," he offers fuel-sticks of *karkaṭikā* wood, or performs the ritual procedure (*tantra*),
or fumigates one possessed by a *piśāca*.

One who desires the eradication of *piśācas* should offer fuel-sticks of *trapusa* wood with the three verses beginning with "arāyakṣayaṇam. One should offer fuel-sticks of *trapusa* wood with the hymn (*sūkta*) beginning with "śanno devī."

One who desires protection from *piśācas* should offer fuel-sticks of *karkaṭikā* with the hymn beginning "ā paśyati. With the two hymns beginning "tānt satyaujāḥ" and "tvayā pūrvam," he offers fuel-sticks of *trapusa*.
In every case where there is the mention of a *sūkta* and so forth, one should understand it as a *sūkta*; where there is the mention of an *ṛc* and so forth, one should understand it as an *ṛc*;
and within a *sūkta*, one should understand it as an *ṛc*.
He places fuel-sticks of *trapusa* with the formula, "Yoked in front. He places fuel-sticks of *karkaṭikā* with the section beginning, "The slayer of Rakṣas.
There is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
One who desires the eradication of piśācas offers fuel-sticks with a pestle while reciting the two hymns beginning with "astuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ";
this is the remedy for piśācas.
With the hymn beginning "niḥsālām," he places the well-known pestle-wood pieces;
with the three verses beginning "arāyakṣayaṇam," he places the pestle-wood pieces,
or [performs] the ritual procedure (tantra).
With the verse "śanno devī," he places the wooden pestles;
this is a remedy against the Piśācas in all cases.
With the hymn "ā paśyati," he places the fuel-sticks of wooden pestles.
With the two hymns "tāntsatyaujāḥ" and "tvayā pūrvam," he offers oblations of pestles, wooden sticks, and wood chips as a ritual modification.
Or the *tantra* for the eradication of *piśācas*:
with the hymn "He who was mentioned before," he places fuel-sticks of *musala* wood [upon the fire].
In all cases, the oblation is offered at the end of the *ṛc*;
in all cases, the utterance of "svāhā" occurs at the end of the *ṛc*.
In rituals not following a specific manual (*atantra*), there is always the regulation of the smoke.
With the *anuvāka* beginning "rakṣohaṇam," he places fuel-sticks of *musala* wood;
there is no restriction regarding their species.
In all cases of hand-homa, there is an optionality of ritual procedure (*tantra*).
With the two hymns "stuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ," he offers pieces of khadira wood as fuel;
with the hymn "niḥsālām," he offers pieces of khadira wood as fuel; and with the three verses beginning "arāyakṣayaṇam," he offers pieces of khadira wood as fuel.
With the verse "śanno devī," he offers fuel-sticks of Khadira wood; with the hymn "ā paśyati," he offers fuel-sticks of Khadira wood;
[and with] "tānt satyaujāḥ."
With the two hymns beginning with "By you first," he offers fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood; there is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
With [the verse] beginning "That which was joined before," he offers *khadira* fuel-sticks.

One who desires the eradication of *piśācas* offers fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood while reciting the section beginning with "rakṣohaṇam. In all cases, there is an option regarding the ritual framework (*tantra*).
In all cases, there is an option regarding the ritual acts:
one may perform one, two, or many.
With the two hymns "astuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ," he places mustard-wood fuel-sticks into the fire.
With the hymn "niḥsālām," he offers fuel-sticks of mustard seeds; with the three verses beginning "arāyakṣayaṇam," he offers fuel-sticks of mustard seeds;
and with the hymn "śanno devīḥ," he offers tārṣṭāghī fuel-sticks.
With the hymn "ā paśyati," he places fuel-sticks of *tārṣṭāghī* wood;
with the two hymns "tānt satyaujāḥ" and "tvayā pūrvam," he places fuel-sticks of mustard;
and with the hymn "purastādyuktaḥ," he places fuel-sticks of mustard.
With the *anuvāka* beginning with "rakṣohaṇam," he offers fuel-sticks of mustard seeds; there is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
By means of pestles and fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood, the expulsion (*uccāṭana*) of a twice-born man is accomplished.
By the other two [mantras], the eradication of Śūdras and others occurs.
[With the verse, "Pierce the two eyes with odd-numbered stakes made of *khadira* wood" (5.29.4), he drives them into the ground level with the earth behind the fire.
Having consecrated seven or nine *khadira* stakes with the two hymns beginning with "The praising one" and "This oblation," he buries them behind the fire.
With the verse, "Pierce the eyes into the level ground," [he should perform the rite].

The mantra for burying [the stakes] during an affliction by Piśācas: having consecrated seven stakes of Khadira wood with the hymn beginning "Niḥsālam," he buries them behind the fire with the verse beginning "Akṣyau ni vidhya."
In the event of fear of *piśācas*,

having consecrated seven stakes of *khadira* wood with the three verses beginning with "The destroyer of *arāya*," he buries them behind the fire with the verse "Having fixed [the stakes] in the eyes," for the purpose of protecting against *piśācas* and *rakṣas*.
Having consecrated an odd number of stakes made of *khadira* wood with the hymn beginning "śanno devīḥ," he buries them behind the fire with the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya.
Having consecrated seven wooden pins with the hymn beginning "ā paśyati," he buries them behind the fire with the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya.
In every case, he levels the ground.
Having consecrated seven stakes with the two hymns "tāntsatyaujāḥ" and "tvayā pūrvam," he buries them behind the fire with the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya," in the event of fear of Piśācas.
Having consecrated seven stakes made of *khadira* wood with the *anuvāka* beginning "rakṣohaṇam," he buries them behind the fire with the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya" in the event of fear of *piśācas*.
[In this way, for iron nails: Having consecrated five or seven iron pegs with the two hymns "astuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ," he subsequently buries them behind the fire with the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya.
In every case, the burying of the pegs is performed in this manner.
Having consecrated iron pins with the hymn "niḥsālām," he buries them behind the fire with the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya.
Having consecrated the iron pins with the three verses beginning with "arāyakṣayaṇam," he buries them. Having consecrated the iron pins with the hymn "śanno devīḥ," he buries them.
In all cases, there is burial behind the fire.

Having consecrated iron stakes with the hymn beginning "He beholds" (*ā paśyati*), he buries them behind the fire. In all instances, [he uses] the verse beginning "Pierce their two eyes" (*akṣyau ni vidhya*).

With the two hymns "tāntsatyaujāḥ" and "tvayā pūrvam," he consecrates five or seven iron pegs and drives them into the ground with the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya. With the hymn "purastādyuktaḥ," he consecrates iron pegs and drives them into the ground behind the fire with the ṛc "akṣyau ni vidhya."

Having consecrated five or seven iron pegs with the *anuvāka* beginning with "rakṣohaṇam," he buries them behind the fire with the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya. In every case, the act of burying is performed in this manner.
Having consecrated copper pegs with the two hymns "stuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ," he buries them behind the fire with the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya."

With the hymn "sarvatra piśācāya" and the hymn "aniḥsālām," he consecrates copper pegs and drives them into the ground behind the fire. With the three verses beginning "arāyakṣayaṇam," he consecrates copper pegs and drives them into the ground behind the fire.
Having consecrated copper pegs with the hymn beginning "śanno devī pṛśniparṇī," he drives them into the ground.
Having consecrated copper pegs with the verse beginning "ā paśyati," he drives them into the ground behind the fire.
Having consecrated copper pegs with the hymn beginning "tānt satyaujāḥ," he drives them into the ground behind the fire while reciting "akṣyau ni vidhya."
Having consecrated copper pegs with the hymn "By you formerly" (*tvayā pūrvam*), he drives them into the ground with the verse "Pierce their eyes" (*akṣyau ni vidhya*).
Having consecrated copper pegs with the verse "Yoked in front" (*purastādyuktaḥ*), he drives them into the ground.
This is done in all cases when there is fear of *piśācas*.
Having consecrated copper pegs with the *anuvāka* beginning with "rakṣohaṇam," he buries them behind the fire.
With the verse "akṣyau ni vidhya," he performs the burying everywhere;
in every case, he buries them behind the fire.
In all cases of fear of piśācas, medicinal remedies [are prescribed].
[He scatters heated gravel around the bed, the heaps, and the straw mats.

Having consecrated the heated gravel with the two hymns, "Stuvānam" and "Idam haviḥ," he should scatter it around the bed, the interior rooms, the house, or the village, in these places when there is fear of *rakṣas* demons.
When there is fear of *piśāca* spirits, he consecrates the heated gravel with the hymn "Aniḥsālām" and scatters it around the house and other such locations.
With the three verses beginning with "arāyakṣayaṇam," he consecrates heated pebbles and scatters them around the sleeping places and heaps of grain;
he scatters them wherever there is fear of Piśācas.
With the hymn beginning with "śanno devī," he consecrates heated pebbles and scatters them around the sleeping places and heaps of grain.
Saying "He looks on," he scatters heated pebbles;
having consecrated the heated pebbles with the two hymns beginning with "Those [beings] of true power" and "By thee before," he scatters them over the heaps of bedding in case of fear of Piśācas.
Having consecrated heated pebbles with the hymn beginning "Purastādyukto vaha," he scatters them around the sleeping-place and the heaps of grain when there is fear of Piśācas;
having consecrated heated pebbles with the Anuvāka beginning "Rakṣohaṇam," he scatters them around the sleeping-place and the heaps of grain when there is fear of Piśācas.

On the new moon day, having scattered the barley grains taken once, which have not been removed from their husks and have not been ground, after performing the ritual enclosure for malevolent purposes, he throws on the fire the fuel-sticks of Tārṣṭāgha.
If anyone should come, he should say to him: "Wiping his tongue with a cord of hemp, let him leap out of the hall."
Acting thus, while reciting the *anādyehi* verses,
on the new moon day, having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, he spreads sacrificial grass made of *śara* reeds;
there is the addition of fuel consisting of mustard seeds.
With the two hymns "stuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ," he offers barley-flour (saktu) taken once with each verse.
The subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra) begins with the Abhyātāna offerings.
Within this procedure, having taken a single handful from the middle of the heap of barley, it is crushed with a mortar and ground counter-clockwise.
Then, having caused the afflicted person to lie down, he performs the cleansing of the tongue with a hempen cord; thus, the seizure is said to be released.
If he does not perform the cleansing of the tongue with hemp, then one should know that the seizure has not departed.

On the new moon day, having performed the ritual procedure for clarified butter (*ājyatantra*), having placed reeds upon the fire and added fuel of mustard seeds, and having completed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he [offers] barley grains taken once, unthreshed and unobstructed, with the hymn beginning "O houseless one" (*aniḥsālā*).
He offers flour-meal;
he is liberated.
Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
If he cleanses his tongue with a hempen thread, then the seizure has departed. On the new moon day,

having spread sacrificial grass made of *śara* reeds and having performed the ritual procedure distinguished by an oblation of mustard seeds, he offers groats— barley grains that have been seized once, not threshed, and ground without being turned back— with the three verses beginning "The destruction of the *arāya*."
Then follows the supplementary ritual (*uttara-tantra*):
If one cleanses the tongue with a hempen cord, then the seizure has departed.

On the new moon day, having spread sacrificial grass made of *śara* reeds and performed the ritual procedure distinguished by fuel-sticks of mustard seeds, he offers parched barley grains that have been ground into flour and mixed with groats, without interruption, while reciting the three verses beginning with "The destroyer of the *arāya* worm."
Then follows the supplementary ritual (*uttara-tantra*).
If he cleanses his tongue with a hempen cord, then the seizure has departed.

On the new moon day, having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* oblations in the morning, he spreads sacrificial grass made of *śara* reeds and prepares a fuel-offering distinguished by mustard seeds. With the hymn beginning "May the goddess Pṛśniparṇī [be] auspicious for us," he [offers] barley grains that have not been scattered and without interruption.
He offers flour-meal as an oblation; thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure;
the cleaning of the tongue is performed with hemp.

On the morning of the new moon day, having spread sacrificial grass made of *śara* reeds and performed the ritual procedure (*tantra*) distinguished by fuel-sticks of mustard seeds, he offers barley-grains that have not been pounded and have not been carried forward, as well as ground flour-meal, without interruption, while reciting the hymn beginning with "He beholds" (*ā paśyati*).
Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

The cleaning of the tongue is done with hemp (*śaṇa*). On the new moon day, having spread sacrificial grass made of *śara* reeds and performed the ritual procedure distinguished by fuel-sticks of mustard seeds, [he recites] "Those, O one of true power" (*tānt satyaujāḥ*).

Having ground once-grasped barley grains that have not been sprinkled with water, he offers them as flour-meal (*saktu*) without interruption, using the two hymns beginning with "By you [O barley]... This is followed by the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
The cleaning of the tongue is performed with hemp.

On the new moon day, having spread sacrificial grass (*barhis*) made of *śara* reeds in the morning, distinguished by fuel-sticks of mustard seeds, and having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he offers once-grasped barley grains that have not been sprinkled with water without interruption, using the hymn beginning with "Yoked in front..."
He offers flour-grains as an oblation;
thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*);
the cleaning of the tongue is performed with hemp.

On the morning of the new moon day, having spread sacrificial grass made of Śara reeds and distinguished by fuel-sticks of mustard seeds, and having performed the rites up to the Abhyātāna offerings, he offers barley-grains that have been taken once, not yet removed from their husks, and ground into flour without interruption, using the Anuvāka beginning with "rakṣohaṇam.
Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra).
One performs the cleansing of the tongue with a hempen thread;
if one does not do so, then the seizing spirit has not departed—
it is an incurable seizure.
The meaning is that the planet is incurable.
Now, the ritual for subjugating the planets (grahābhicāra) is described. This rite is said to be the means for bringing an uncontrollable planet under one's control.
This ritual is intended for the purpose of subjugating an irresistible planet.
[He offers iṅguda mixed with vīriṇa-tulā in a hollowed leaf-vessel.
Having performed the ritual procedure for clarified butter up to the Abhyātāna offerings,
he offers the iṅguda mixed with vīriṇa-tulā from a full leaf-vessel while reciting the two hymns beginning with "astuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ."
Then follows the subsequent ritual (*uttaratantra*).

With the hymn beginning "niḥsālām," he offers *iṅguda* seeds mixed with *vīriṇa* flowers and clarified butter using a *palāśa* leaf-cup, according to the clarified butter ritual (*ājyatantra*). Then follows the subsequent ritual.

Having performed the ritual procedure (*tantra*), one offers *iṅguda* mixed with the down of *vīriṇa* grass using a leaf-cup of *palāśa*, reciting the three verses beginning with "The destroyer of Rākṣasas" (*arāyakṣayaṇam*).
This is the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

Having performed the ritual procedure, one offers *iṅguda* mixed with the down of *vīriṇa* grass using a leaf-cup, reciting the hymn (*sūkta*) beginning with "May the goddess Pṛśniparṇī be auspicious to us" (*śanno devī pṛśniparṇī*).
This is the Uttaratantra.
This is the sorcery against a planet.
Having prepared the ritual manual (*tantra*), one offers *iṅguda* mixed with the cotton-wool of *vīriṇa* using a pair of hollowed leaves, reciting the hymn beginning with "ā paśyati."

Having performed the *ājyatantra* ritual, he offers the *iṅguda* fruit mixed with *vīriṇa* grass and cotton into the fire using a pair of tongs, while reciting the two hymns beginning with "Atān satyaujāḥ" and "Tvayā pūrvam."
The *Uttaratantra*:
The sorcery ritual (*abhicārakarma*) for a *piśāca*.
Having performed the ritual procedure, one offers an *iṅguda* fruit mixed with the cotton-wool of *vīriṇa* grass from a leaf-cup, using the hymn beginning with "yuktaḥ purastāt" (RV 10.85).
The *Uttaratantra*:
With the *anuvāka* beginning with "rakṣohaṇam," he offers the *iṅguda* mixed with *vīriṇa* cotton in a hollowed leaf-vessel (*prapuṭa*) according to the procedure for clarified butter (*ājyatantre*).
The ritual for the seizure (*grahābhicāra*) is completed.
Now, when there is doubt as to whether or not there is a *piśāca* in this house, this ritual act is prescribed: he hangs the fuel and the sacrificial grass in the hall.
On the following day, [he performs the rite] for Vikṛta with the mantra "piśācato rug" (from the Piśāca comes disease).
The *homa* has been explained.

[KauśS 4.1.33] Having consecrated the fuel-sticks of mustard seeds and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) made of *śara* reeds with the two hymns beginning with "praising" (*astuvānam*) and "this oblation" (*idaṃ haviḥ*), he places them above the hall;
he performs it above the hall.
Then, at dawn, an inspection is performed;
if there is a deformity, there is apprehension of a *piśāca*,
and then the fire-oblation (*homa*) is prescribed.
"Vīriṇatūlam," and so forth.
Having consecrated the fuel of Tārṣṭāgha and the sacrificial grass made of Śara with the hymn "Niḥsālām," he places them above the house.
If that [grass] becomes disfigured, then that house is possessed by a Piśāca.
Then the fire sacrifice (homa) is described:
one offers iṅguda mixed with vīriṇa grass and cotton using a hollowed leaf-cup (prapuṭa), according to the ritual manual (tantra).
Having consecrated the fuel and the sacrificial grass with the three verses beginning with "arāyakṣayaṇam," he places them above the hall;
on the second day, he should inspect them.
If the sacrificial grass is damaged, there is danger from Piśācas.
There, he offers iṅguda mixed with vīraṇa-tulā grass by means of a double-pracchanna oblation.
Having consecrated the fuel and the sacrificial grass with the verse "śanno devī," he hangs them in the hall.
On the following day, there is a disease caused by a piśāca in the deformed one.
Then, he offers *iṅguda* mixed with *vīriṇa* grass-wool by means of a double-pot offering (*prapuṭa*).
According to the ritual manual (*tantra*), he places the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) in the hall while reciting the hymn beginning with "ā paśyati."
On the following day, [the victim] becomes deformed and suffers from the disease called piśācatō.

Then, having taken fuel and sacrificial grass (idhmā-barhis) from the hall, he performs the ritual procedure up to the Abhyātāna offerings with that material, and offers the iṅguda-oblation mixed with the fibers of vīriṇa grass using a hollowed-out vessel, reciting:
"tānt satyaujāḥ."
Having consecrated the fuel and the sacrificial grass with the two hymns beginning with "tvayā pūrvam," he hangs them in the hall.
On the following day, for a deformity caused by a Piśāca,
he offers an iṅguda cake mixed with the down of vīriṇa grass into a hollowed leaf-cup, using that same hymn.
Having consecrated the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) with the hymn beginning "purastādyuktaḥ," he hangs it in the hall.
On the following day, for the modified rite against the Piśācas, [he performs] the *rug* sacrifice;
there, he offers the *iṅguda* fruit mixed with the down of *vīriṇa* grass using a hollowed-out vessel.
With the *anuvāka* beginning with "rakṣohaṇam," he attaches the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhiḥ*) to the hall. On the following day, for the sake of warding off the Piśācas and disease,
having performed the ritual framework (*tantra*), he offers the *iṅguda* fruit mixed with the down of *vīriṇa* grass using a hollowed-out vessel, while reciting that same *anuvāka*.
The malevolent incantations of the Piśāca-grahas.
[Having joined his palms in reverence to Vaiśravaṇa, while reciting, he causes [the guest] to sip water and sprinkles him.
Having paid homage to Vaiśravaṇa with the two hymns beginning with "astuvānam" and "idaṃ haviḥ," he consecrates the water and causes him to sip it and sprinkles him with it.
Having paid homage to Vaiśravaṇa, one consecrates water with the hymn beginning "aniḥsālā" and causes the sick person to sip it and sprinkles them;
this is for one desiring protection from Piśācas and seizing spirits (grahas).
Having paid homage to Vaiśravaṇa, one consecrates water with the three verses beginning "arāyakṣayaṇam" and causes the man possessed by a Piśāca to sip it and sprinkles him.
Having paid homage to Vaiśravaṇa, one consecrates water with the hymn "aśanno devī" and causes the person to sip it and sprinkles them; this is for protection against *piśācas* and *rakṣas*.
Having paid homage to Vaiśravaṇa, one consecrates water with the hymn "ā paśyati" and causes a sick person to sip it and sprinkles them.
Having paid homage to Vaiśravaṇa, one consecrates water with the two hymns "atānt satyaujāḥ" and "tvayā pūrvam," and then makes the sick person sip it and sprinkles him;
[this is done] in the event of fear of piśācas.
Having formed a *añjali* to Vaiśravaṇa and having consecrated water with the hymn beginning "He was placed in front" (*puraḥsadyuktaḥ*), he causes the sick person to sip it and sprinkles him.
This is for one desiring protection from the fear of *piśācas*.
Having formed an *añjali* to Vaiśravaṇa and having consecrated water with the section beginning "The slayer of Rakṣas" (*rakṣohaṇam*), he causes the sick person to sip it and sprinkles him.
One who desires protection from the fear of *piśācas* [should perform the rite];
there is an option regarding the ritual actions in all cases.
When a person possessed by a *piśāca* has been touched, an oblation (*homa*) must be performed in every instance.
And the practice of medicine;
its application in the home.
The nocturnal rites are now described: [At night, he draws together a firebrand. *Kauśika Sūtra* 4.1.35.
He performs the *svasti* (well-being) rite first. At night, while [the fire] is not being praised,
he consecrates two firebrands with the two hymns beginning with "This oblation" (*idaṃ haviḥ*) and rubs them against each other.
Then, at dawn, in the event of fear of Piśācas, he steps forward with his right foot while reciting the hymn beginning with "May those who grant well-being" (RV 1.21).
At night, having consecrated two firebrands with the hymn beginning "Niḥsālām," he rubs them against each other.
Then, at dawn, in the event of fear of Piśācas, he steps forward to the south while reciting the hymn beginning "Svastidāḥ."
At night, having consecrated two firebrands with the mantra "arāyakṣayaṇam," they rub them against each other.
Then, at dawn, he strides forward with the steps while reciting the hymn "svastidāḥ.
At night, having consecrated two firebrands with the mantra "śanno devī," they rub them against each other.
Then at dawn, he places footprints while reciting the words "Svastidāḥ.
At night, after the entire ritual of consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), he rubs together two firebrands (*ulmuka*) while reciting "Ā paśyati.
Then, at dawn, having muttered the hymn (*sūkta*) beginning with "Svastidāḥ," he steps upon the footprints.
At night, having consecrated two firebrands with the two hymns "atāntsatyaujāḥ" and "tvayā pūrvam," he rubs them together.
Then, at dawn, he places footprints with the hymn "svastidāḥ," for the purpose of protection against Piśācas and Rakṣasas.
At night, having consecrated two firebrands with the mantra "purastādyuktaḥ," he rubs them together.
Then, at dawn, having recited the hymn beginning with "svastidāḥ," he strides his steps;
this destroys all malevolent spirits and planetary influences.
Having gone [there], the oblation is performed with the *gaṇavikalpa* [mantra].
There is also pacification for the *brahmarākṣasa*.
At night, having consecrated two firebrands (*ulmuka*) with the *anuvāka* beginning with "rakṣohaṇam," they rub them against each other.
Then, at dawn, having recited the hymn "Asvastidāḥ," he takes his steps;
the rites of the night are completed,
as are the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Apsarases, Pretas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and the seizing spirits (grahas).
Furthermore, all other minor Brahmin classes, as well as the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and so forth, who are [afflicted by] planetary spirits (grahas), are satisfied by these rites.
The section on Rākṣasa-grahas, the Bhūtatantra, is completed.
Now the remedy for dropsy is stated:
[With the twenty-one blades of *darbha* grass, together with the leaf-sheaths, he sprinkles [the patient] over his head while reciting "This [is the power] of the gods" (RV 10.99.1). (KauśS 4.1.37)

Having thrown *darbha*-grass stalks (*piñjulī*) and twenty-one blades of house-grass into a water jar with the hymn "This [is] of the gods" (*ayaṃ devānām*), and having consecrated that jar with mantras, he then sprinkles the sick person with it;
thereafter, the ritual purification (*mārjana*) is performed. Three *darbha* blades tied together are called a *piñjūlī*.
The medicinal treatment for *jalodara* is completed.
Through regular practice, the success of the rite is achieved;
one should perform it day by day for the purpose of destroying *jalodara*.
The first section on medicine is completed. // KKp_25 //

Now, the remedies for wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*) are stated: [Regarding the phrase "born from the womb" (1.12), one causes the patient to drink fat, honey, clarified butter, and oil.
With the hymn "Born from the Womb," having consecrated meat and fat, one causes the patient to drink it in the case of a disorder of wind.

Having consecrated honey with the hymn "jarāyujaḥ," one causes it to be drunk in cases of disorders of phlegm (kapha). Having consecrated clarified butter with the hymn "jarāyujaḥ," one causes it to be drunk in cases of combined disorders of wind (vāta) and bile (pitta). Having consecrated oil with the hymn "jarāyujaḥ," one causes it to be drunk in cases of disorders of wind and phlegm.
The treatment for wind, bile, and phlegm is completed.
The rites for excessive coughing, head congestion, and headache are now described:
[With his head covered by a bundle of muñja grass, holding fried grain in a sieve with his left hand, he walks along scattering it with his right.
Having wrapped his diseased head with muñja grass, he takes a winnowing fan containing fried grain in his left hand.

Holding those parched grains (lāja) with his right hand, he proceeds while scattering the grains with the hymn beginning "ajarāyujaḥ," as far as the region of the disease; at that very spot, there is the casting away of muñja grass, the praśna plant, and the parched grains.
With the left hand he holds the two ends of the strainer, and with the right hand the bowstring-fastener.
In front of the one who has sent [the messenger],
having taken the fan and the muñja-ball with his left hand, and having taken the bowstring and the drughnī with his right hand, he places the sick person in front.
[Wherever the disease seizes him, there he places two *titaupraśna* straws.
Having gone to the place where the disease has arisen and having muttered the hymn beginning with "ajarāyujaḥ," the afflicted person throws in a *mauñjapraśna* straw and a *pavana* straw.
And the bowstring. KauśS 4.2.6.
Regarding the "returning":
in that place, he silently places the bowstring.

[Clarified butter for nasal administration // KauśS_4,2{26}.8 //] It is the remedy for fever caused by wind (vātajvara), pain in the waist, diseases of the head, abdominal tumors caused by wind (vātagulma), disorders of wind, all diseases, bow-like arching of the back (dhanurvāta), trembling of the limbs, wind affecting the body, bodily collapse, and all wind-related disorders.
Having consecrated clarified butter with the hymn "jarāyujaḥ," one administers it as a nasal drop.
In cases of headache or a breaking pain in the head caused by wind (vāta).
[Having propped against his forehead a bamboo staff with five joints, he mutters:
With the hymn beginning "jarāyujaḥ," he prods a bamboo staff with five joints against his forehead and mutters it,
in cases of headache, backache, abdominal tumors caused by wind, or other disorders of wind.
The section on the affliction of the *liṅgin* is concluded.
Now, when blood is flowing within the body or externally due to a wound from a weapon or an impact from stones, clubs, bricks, and so forth, the rites are prescribed:
[With the hymn beginning] "amūryāḥ" (1.17), he scatters it with five-knotted [stalks] and dust and sand.
Having placed a five-knotted bamboo staff at the place where the blood flows, he mutters the hymn "amūryāḥ."
For a flow of blood, [the following is] the remedy:

taking dust from a road and consecrating it with the hymn "amūryāḥ," one scatters it over the wound caused by the blood. Having consecrated sand with the hymn "amūryāḥ," one scatters it upon the site of the disease.
[He ties on a small skull-cup.
Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, he pours water over a small skull-cup while reciting the hymn beginning with "Those who... (*amūryāḥ*), consecrates it, and ties it on.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* offerings.
[He causes her to drink:
Having consecrated a dried clod of earth with the hymn beginning "amūryāḥ," he causes her to drink it. A *armakapālikā* is a dried clod of mud.
The medicine for the excessive flow of a woman's menses and for the discharge of blood.
[With four tips of *dūrvā* grass, one causes [the patient] to drink curd and meat-paste.

// KauśS_4,2{26}.13 //] Having ground four tips of *dūrvā* grass with the hymn "amūryāḥ," and having mixed them together with curd, meat-paste, meat, and so forth, he then consecrates it with mantras and causes [the patient] to drink it.

[This is done] in the case of a flow of blood within the body due to injury by weapons and the like, as well as when blood flows externally from the anus, the mouth, the nose, or from the head, fingers, and other parts.
The medicinal treatments for hemorrhaging are concluded.
Now, the medicinal treatments for heart disease and jaundice are stated:
[With the mantra beginning "anu sūryam" (1.22), he causes [the patient] to rinse with hair-mixed water. *Kauśika Sūtra* 4.2.14.
Having consecrated water mixed with the hair of a red bull while reciting "anu sūryam," he makes [the patient] drink it;
this is the remedy for jaundice and heart disease.
Having brought water on the back of a red bull with the hymn beginning "anu sūryam," he consecrates it and then makes [the sacrificer] sip it.
[He ties the *śaṅkudhāna* to one seated on a hide who has milked; it is accompanied by the pouring-in of remnants.

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, he places the gem—the perforation in the red hide of a cow—into the cow's milk with the hymn beginning "In accordance with the Sun" (*anu sūryam*), and having poured the remnants over it and consecrated it with mantras, he ties it [to the person].
[He] causes [him] to drink; he also causes [him] to drink milk.
The subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra) begins with the Abhyātāna offerings.
In cases of jaundice and heart disease, there is pain in the genital region.

Having given the patient yellow rice to eat, and having combined his leavings and non-leavings together, one anoints [the patient] from the feet upward with that mixture. Then, having tied [the substances] with a green thread upon the left shanks beneath the bed according to the mantra, one causes him to bathe.

Having given the patient yellow rice to eat, and having put his leavings and non-leavings together in one place, and having used them for an ointment, starting from the head down to the feet, one then seats the patient on the bed and [applies it] beneath the bed.
The parrot (*śuka*), the wood-parrot (*kāṣṭhaśuka*), and the *gopītilaka*— these three birds,
having been tied with a green thread on the left leg, he binds beneath the bed. Then,
having consecrated water with the hymn beginning "Then after the sun" (*tato 'nu sūryam*), he causes the sick person to bathe.
In cases of jaundice and heart disease.
[He causes him to drink: Having consecrated the stirred drink (*mantha*) with the hymn beginning "In accordance with the sun" (*anu sūryam*), he causes him to drink and gives it to him.
In every case, having placed the sick person at the front of the house door and having led him inside first, he himself enters; then, having consecrated the food, he gives it to the sick person.
In every instance wherever the word "aprayacchati" occurs, it should be understood in this very manner.
[One should cause it to speak and establish it.
With the hymn beginning "Following the Sun," one should consecrate a parrot that is speaking;
with the hymn beginning "Following the Sun," one should consecrate a wooden parrot that is speaking.
Having seen a bird with a mark on its forehead (gopītilakā) speaking anywhere, the sick person should consecrate it there with the hymn beginning with "anu sūryam";
this is also for the disease of jaundice (kāmalā).

Having smeared the hair from the belly [of a bull] with lac and encased it in gold, and having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, one fashions an amulet (*maṇi*) from the heart-hair of a bull—dyed with lac and wrapped in gold—using the hymn beginning with "In accordance with the Sun" (*anu sūryam*). Having consecrated it with the *sampāta* oblations and empowered it with mantras, one binds it upon the sick person;
the subsequent ritual procedure consists of the *abhyātāna* formulas and the rest.
In all cases where many rites are prescribed, one may perform one, two, or all of them;
in every instance, there is an option regarding the rites.
The medicinal treatments for epilepsy, insanity, heart disease, jaundice, and consumption are completed.
Now, the remedies for white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*) are stated:
[the mantra] *naktañjātā* (1.23) and *suparṇo jātaḥ* (1.24).
Having thus rubbed [the patient's body] with cow dung until blood appears as prescribed by the mantra, he anoints it. For white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*),

having rubbed [the body] with cow dung until blood is seen, he grinds together these five— *bhṛṅgarāja*, *haridrā*, *indravāruṇī*, and *nīlikāpuṣpa*— and having consecrated them with the two hymns beginning with "born at night" (*anaktajātā*) and "the eagle was born" (*suparṇo jātaḥ*), he anoints the leprosy.
The taking of either three or four medicinal herbs.
[Having plucked out the grey hairs // KauśS_4,2{26}.23 //] Regarding the removal of grey hair:
having cut and rubbed the grey hairs, one applies [the ointment].
Now the verses dedicated to the Maruts are stated:
He worships the Maruts with the two hymns beginning "Suparṇo jātaḥ," according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*, as one would for Varuṇa.
[This applies] in cases of white hair, gray hair, and white leprosy.
Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he recites "Naktañjātā."
With two hymns beginning with "Suparṇo jātaḥ," he offers the clarified butter of a black cow.
The subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra) begins with the Abhyātāna offerings.
Having performed the rites up to the end of the Abhyātānas, [he recites] "Naktañjātā."

Having gathered the *kāsa*, *divi-dhruva*, *vaka*, and *vetasa* herbs together in one place, having performed the *sampāta* rite and consecrated them with the two hymns beginning with "suparṇo jātaḥ," he then causes them to enter the midst of the water and pours out the vessel face-down;
thereafter follows the *uttara-tantra*.
Having performed the *tantra*, [he recites] "naktañjātā."

Having placed the *kāsa* and other medicinal herbs into water with the two hymns beginning with "suparṇo jātaḥ," he sprinkles them after performing the *sampāta* consecration and reciting the mantras;
then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
[He also uses] the hymn beginning with "naktañjātā."

Having tied a dog's head and a ram's head, along with human hair and a rope, to the tips of two bamboo poles using the two hymns beginning with "suparṇo jātaḥ," one causes them to fight; that is to say, one makes them hold [the heads] against each other.
These are the remedies for the loss of grey hair and white leprosy.
Having performed the rites up to the end of the Abhyātāna, [one recites] "naktañjātā."
Having poured water over [the vessel] with the two hymns beginning with "suparṇo jātaḥ," and having sprinkled that [water] upon the unbaked earthen vessel, he then places a stone thereon.
Then he places both the unbaked earthen vessel and the stone on a tripod-hanger.
Then he throws them into the water.
Next is the Uttara-tantra.
The rites pertaining to the Maruts are completed.

In all the rites pertaining to the Maruts, there is rice cooked with milk for the Maruts (*mārutakṣīraudana*), boiled for the Maruts (*mārutaśṛta*), strewn around by the Maruts, and performed with the Marut-spoon and Marut-ghee.
The medicinal treatments for leprosy are completed;
this [treatment] destroys white hair and grey hair, and it destroys misfortune.
Now the medicine for fever is described:
[Reciting "yad agniḥ" (1.25), he heats, boils, and sprinkles an axe.

For chronic fever, intermittent fever, continuous fever, quotidian fever, quartan fever, cold-fever, and four-fold fever, one consecrates an iron axe with the hymn "yad agniḥ" and heats it in the fire.
Then, having recited the hymn "yad agniḥ," he boils that axe in hot water;
then, having recited the hymn "yad agniḥ," he sprinkles the sick person with that water.
The rinsing of the mouth and the ritual purification (mārjana) are performed silently.
The treatment for fever is completed.

Now the remedies for the destruction of agitation are stated: [With the verse beginning "upa prāgāt" (1.28), he binds four stalks of white-flowered *vīriṇa* grass, which has been heated on both ends, to the patient who is agitated.

Having performed the rites up to the *Abhyātāna* formulas, he takes four stalks of white *vīriṇa* grass, binds them together at one end after they have been heated on both sides, fashions them into an amulet (*maṇi*), consecrates it with the pouring of water (*sampāta*), recites the mantra over it, and ties it on.
At the conclusion of the auspicious day,
then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*),
which is the medicine for agitation.

[Having prepared a three-fold burnt stalk of white vīraṇa grass as a gem: KauśS 4.2.27] Having performed the *tantra* ritual, having fashioned a gem from a three-fold burnt stalk of white vīraṇa grass with the hymn beginning "He has come near" (*upa prāgāt*), and having consecrated it with the *sampāta* offerings and mantras, he binds it.
Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
The medicine for agitation.
[Regarding the two firebrands, beginning with *svasti*:
KauśS 4.2.28] Having consecrated the two firebrands with the hymn beginning "upa prāgāt," one should rub them together.
This ritual act is performed either at night or at the time of dawn.
Then, at dawn, he steps forward with his right foot while reciting the hymn beginning with "May the Givers of Well-being" (RV 1.89); this is the rite for securing well-being (*svastyayana*).
One should perform this whenever the elderly, children, young men, women, or men experience sudden agitation or delirium.
The medicines for agitation are completed.
Medicines for the Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Apsarases, Bhūtas, Grahas, and so forth are now described:
[Having offered as an after-offering all fragrant powders from the names of the Mothers, one anoints the patient with the remainder.
Having performed the rites up to the Abhyātānas, [one recites] "The divine Gandharva" (2.1).
With this hymn, he offers all medicinal herbs smeared with clarified butter.
He anoints the afflicted person with the remainder of the oblation.
This is the subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra).
Having performed the introductory ritual (*tantra*), he offers all medicinal herbs mixed with clarified butter while reciting the four-verse hymn beginning with "imaṃ me agne" (6.111).
Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual (*uttaratantra*).
In the Tantra, one anoints a sick person with the remainder of the *homa* offering;
this is the remedy for afflictions caused by *gandharva*-spirits and the like.
[At a crossroads, having placed a *darbha*-tuft on the head upon a skull-bowl filled with embers...

Having made a representation of the sick person at a crossroads, having placed a *darbha*-tuft on his head, and having placed a skull-bowl filled with fire and set ablaze upon it, one should offer oblations of clarified butter soaked in ghee into that blazing fire while reciting the hymn beginning with "The divine Gandharva. (*Kauśikasūtra* 4.2.30)
He offers all the medicinal herbs.

At a crossroads, having kindled a fire on a head-shaped mound of earth with two blades of *darbha* grass upon a pan of embers, he offers all the medicinal herbs, anointed with clarified butter, with the four verses beginning "This [oblation] for me, O Agni," verse by verse; there is no ritual framework (*tantra*) required for the offering at the head.
[The one who is plunging against the current sows, while the other pours water from behind.
Having taken a *vallanikā* (a small basket) filled with all medicinal herbs in his hand for the sick person, and having led him into the river facing the water, he causes him to plunge therein.
With the hymn beginning "The Gandharva of the Waters" (*davyo gndharvaḥ*), the performer sows all the medicinal herbs into the midst of the water.
Standing behind [the patient], he sprinkles the diseased person with the hymn beginning, "The divine Gandharva."
[Having placed [the substances] in a raw earthen vessel and poured [them] in, he ties [it] to a three-legged sling made of muñja grass, suspended from a tree where birds dwell.
Then, having placed all the medicinal herbs remaining from the oblation into a raw earthen vessel, he makes a sling with three legs on a tree where birds reside and ties it there;
it is a remedy against *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, and *rākṣasas*.
With the hymn beginning "imaṃ me agne," one offers all medicinal herbs smeared with ghee into a small vessel (*vallanikā*) in the middle of a river, verse by verse.
Then, the performer sprinkles the sick person with water using the four verses beginning "imaṃ me.
Afterwards, having placed [the herbs] in a raw earthen vessel and poured [water] over them, he ties it to a tree that has three roots, is made of muñja grass, and serves as a dwelling for birds.
The medical treatments for the planetary afflictions caused by Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Rajasic spirits, and Tamasic spirits are hereby completed.
Now, the remedy for worldly curses, Vedic curses, the reviling of women, and [the reviling] of men is stated:
[the hymns beginning with] *agha-dviṣṭā* (2.7) and *śaṃ no devī* (2.25).
*varuṇa* (6.85),
*pippalī* (6.109), [and] *vidradha* (6.127).
"Those which are tawny" (8.7). KauśS 4.2.33.
With a four-finger-width [measure] of Palāśa wood taken from near the top, he anoints [the post].
With the first [verse], he binds that which was spoken by the mantra. (KauśS 4.2.35)
With the second [verse], he anoints [the body] with that which has been prepared as prescribed by the mantra.
With the third [verse], he binds that which was spoken by the mantra. KauśS 4.2.37.
With the fourth [verse], he causes [the guest] to eat. KauśS 4.2.38.
With the fifth [verse], he brings the remnants of the oblations onto the head of one seized by Varuṇa.

[With the verse beginning] "uttamena śākalam" (KauśS 4.2.40). In all ritual procedures according to the *Saṃhitā* rules, during the midst of the principal rites, one should place a water-pot to the north; with that water, consecrated by the hymn "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" (1.33), one should cause the patron to be sprinkled at all ceremonies such as those for generating intelligence (*medhājanana*) and others.
Thereafter, one should perform the rites beginning with the binding of the amulet (*maṇibandhana*).
One should not perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) over medicinal substances.

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* oblations, one pours barley-grains into an amulet, consecrates it while reciting the hymn "The god-born ones who hate sin" (*aghadviṣṭā devajātā*), and having again muttered that hymn, binds it [on the patient].

The subsequent ritual procedure beginning with the Abhyātāna hymns is for worldly abuse, Vedic [ritual] abuse, the curse of a Brāhmaṇa, the falling of a cruel gaze, and [protection against] Piśācas, Rākṣasas, and the like; thus ends the medical treatment.
Now, the medicine for the seizure caused by a *rākṣasa* is described:

having performed the *ājya*-tantra, one should consecrate *pṛśniparṇī* with the *sūkta* beginning "May the goddess [grant] us well-being, *pṛśniparṇī*," and after sprinkling it and reciting the mantra over it, one should rub it and then, having again muttered the *sūkta*, smear it upon the afflicted person.
The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttara-tantra*) begins with the *abhyātāna* offerings and so forth.
This concludes the medicinal treatment for those seized by evil spirits, for miscarriages, for women whose children have died, and for those possessed by carnivorous beasts, piśācas, or rākṣasas.
Now, the remedy for consumption (*rājayakṣma*) and other ailments is described:

having performed the *tantra* ritual, one should empower a gem made from the wood of the *varaṇa* tree by sprinkling it with water while reciting the three-verse hymn beginning with "O *varaṇa*, you ward off" (*varaṇo vārayātā*). Then, having again muttered the *sūkta*, one binds it [upon the patient].
The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) begins with the *abhyātāna* offerings and so forth.

The medicinal treatment for severe diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā), the eighteen types of leprosy beginning with śvetodumbara and kuṣṭha, and all diseases beginning with fever is hereby completed.
Now, the medicine for disorders of wind (vāta) is described:

having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, one should pour [the medicinal substance] over long pepper (*pippala*) while reciting the hymn "The long pepper is the scattered medicine" (*pippalī kṣiptabheṣajī*), consecrate it, and then, having recited the hymn again, administer it.
The ritual procedure beginning with the *abhyātāna* formulas and following is the same as the subsequent standard practice (*uttaratantra*).

In all cases— whether it be disorders of wind (vātavikāra), bow-like wind (dhanurvāta), wind-tumor (vātagulma), wind-pain (vātaśūla), the provocation of displaced wind (kṣiptavātapradoṣa), or wind arising from [excessive] physical exertion— in every disorder of wind, this concludes the medicinal treatment.
The medicine for dropsy (jalodara) is now described:

having performed the rites up to the Abhyātāna formulas, one pours down the Sampāta oblations upon the head of the patient with the hymn consisting of the three verses beginning "Of the swelling tumor and the phlegm" (RV 7.50.1–3),
and performs the consecration (abhimantraṇa).
The subsequent ritual manual begins with the Abhyātāna rites.
This is the medicine for dropsy;
it is the medicine for all spreading diseases, for heart disease, or for dropsy. Thus concludes the medicine for these [conditions].

Having ground a four-finger-length splinter of *pālāśa* wood while reciting the hymn beginning with "vidradhasya," and having consecrated it with mantras and again muttered the hymn, one anoints the afflicted person.

This is the remedy for all spreading diseases (*visarpaṇa*), for their provocation, for phlegm (*balāsa*), for the spreading of the intestines and so forth, for spreading of the eyes, for the spreading of ear diseases, for heart ailments, and for unknown consumption (*rājayakṣman*). The treatment for these is complete.

With the three utterances of "svāhā," beginning with "To the sky, svāhā! (dive svāhā), there is one *sampāta*.
With three *svāhākāras*, there are three *sampātas*;
with two [verses] each, there are two *sampātas*.
Thus, there are six.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* offerings.
Having performed the rites up to the end of the *abhyātānas*, one performs oblations with each successive half-verse (*ardharca*) of the hymn "imaṃ yavam.
Having poured the remnants of the oblations into a vessel of water, two portions are placed on the ground.
Having taken those two and cast them into a vessel of water, he then performs the consecration;
thereafter, he causes the patient to be immersed.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* hymns.
The medicine for all diseases.
[He ties a barley-grain with a *yava* stalk to the north.

Having performed the rites up to the end of the *abhyātāna* formulas, he makes six *sampāta* offerings with the hymn beginning "To the sky, svāhā! He pours four *sampāta* portions into a water-pot containing barley;
having placed two *sampāta* portions on the ground and thrown earth into the water-pot, there follows the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) and the immersion (*āplāvana*).
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* offerings.
With the three utterances of "svāhā" beginning with "To the day, svāhā!", there is one pouring together (*sampāta*).
One should perform everything else according to the purpose.
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] six times everywhere.
Having performed the *tantra* ritual, one performs six oblations with the half-verses of the hymn "imaṃ yavam" and pours the remnants (sampāta) into four vessels of water;
two [remnants] are placed on the ground.
Having placed those two [substances] in a vessel of water, one should then perform the consecration with the *sūkta*.
The *sampātas* are poured into the vessel of water containing barley.
Then follows the sprinkling, the purification (*mārjana*), and the sipping of water (*ācamana*).
The subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra) beginning with the *abhyātāna* rites is complete;
this concludes the remedy for all diseases.

Having performed the rites ending with the *abhyātāna*, one prepares a barley amulet (*yavamaṇi*) by scattering [barley] over it while reciting the hymn "imaṃ yavam," and then consecrates and binds it [on the patient].
Then follows the Uttara-tantra [dealing with]:

cold fever, minor fevers, fever born of desire, fever born of phlegm, summer fever, and monsoon fever; [the treatment for] the darkness of intellect regarding the giving and receiving of gifts, the renunciation of wealth, officiating at sacrifices, studying, teaching, and the duty of one who should sacrifice or cause others to sacrifice;
[and the treatment for] the agitation of the eye-lids, [and for] women and men characterized by sin, malice, heart-burning, joy, despondency, and epilepsy.

Regarding the medicine for all diseases: where many rituals are prescribed for a single disease throughout an entire treatise, there is an option (*vikalpa*) among those rituals in every case.
Where sprinkling (*avasecana*) is prescribed, there *ācamana* (sipping water) and *mārjana* (purification) are to be performed everywhere.
The Fourth Section (Kaṇḍikā).
The remedy for snake venom is now described: [Regarding "adadirhi" (5.13), it is said, "to Takṣaka.

Having paid homage to Takṣaka, one consecrates water with the Ṛgvedic verse "dadirhi" and sprinkles it upon one bitten by poison;
this is the medicine for poison.
Having rubbed a splinter of the *kṛmuka* tree with the Ṛgvedic verse "dadirhi," and having added water to it, one then consecrates it and sprinkles it upon one afflicted by poison.
With the Ṛgvedic verse "dadirhi," one consecrates water over a hide ignited by fire and sprinkles it upon the patient.
With the Ṛgvedic verse "dadirhi," one consecrates water over the aged skin of a deer ignited by fire and sprinkles it.
With the Ṛgvedic verse "dadirhi," one consecrates water over grass from a cleansing refuse-pit ignited by fire and sprinkles it.
This is the medicine for moving poison.
Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* oblations, he pours water into a vessel while reciting the verse "dadirhi," and then makes [the patient] drink it.

With the verse "dadirhi," he churns a mixture of barley meal (*saktumantha*) using two upward-pointed fruits smeared with poison; having consecrated it with mantras, he makes one bitten by a snake drink it.
The medicine for moving poison:
having consecrated a madana fruit with the verse beginning "adadirhi," one consumes it for the purpose of inducing vomiting;
this is the medicine for moving poison.
With the verse beginning "dadirhi," he consecrates turmeric and ghee together and makes [the patient] drink them;
this is the remedy for moving poison (*jaṅgamaviṣa*).
With the second [verse], [he treats] the *grahaṇī* disease. [KauśS 4.5.2]
He walks around to the left.
With the verse, "That which of yours is waterless" (5.13.2), he walks around the sick person counter-clockwise.
The medicinal remedy for neutralizing poison:
once the poison has been neutralized, it cannot be removed by anything else except by means of this Vedic mantra.
[He unties the knots of the post with the *śikhāsici* formula.
Having murmured the verse, "That which is waterless for thee," he ties his topknot (*śikhā*). This is a medicinal rite for paralyzing poison.
Having recited the verse, "That which is yours, waterless," he ties a knot with a white cloth;
this is a medicinal remedy for paralyzing poison.
Having recited the single verse, "That which is yours, waterless," he ties a knot on a stalk of hemp.
The poison does not spread;
it remains localized in its place and does not circulate through the body.
The immobilization of poison occurs.
[With the third verse:
"My roar is like a bull" (5.13.3),
he presses the spot where he was bitten by muttering this verse.
Poison moves elsewhere from its location;
there is a medicine for the destruction of poison.
With the fourth verse, "Go away from the right" (7.88.1), having dragged the snake with *daṃśma* grass, he drives it away.
With the mantra, "Your eye by my eye" (5.13.4).
Then the teacher circumambulates [the snake] clockwise while reciting the Ṛgvedic verse;
having muttered the verse "Apehyarirasi" and having set fire to blades of grass, he then throws them toward the snake.
[From where he was bitten:
Having muttered the verse, "Go away, you are an enemy," he throws burning grass from the place where he was bitten onto the bite.
[With the fifth verse, "By the flame of the leaf and the fat" (KauśS 4.5.8),
he consecrates water that has been set ablaze upon a blade of grass with the Ṛgvedic verse, "O Kirāta, O Pṛśni" (5.13.5), and makes the sick person drink it and sprinkles him with it.]
[With the verse beginning with "ṣaṣṭhyārtnījyāpāśena" (KauśS 4.5.9), he binds the noose for the sacrifice of the bowstring.
Having consecrated the noose for the sacrifice of the bowstring with the verse "of the black one" (5.13.6), he ties it during the ritual procedure involving clarified butter (*ājya-tantra*).
This is the medicinal treatment for poison.
[With two [verses], he causes him to drink honey-mixtures. (KauśS 4.5.10)] "Āligī and Viligī" (5.13.7),
"[The hymn] of Urugalā" (5.13.8).

[On the ninth day, the dung of a porcupine.
Regarding the verse, "The porcupine said this to the two ears" (RV 5.13.9), the dung of parrots, mainas, and *kṛśa* birds is referred to as "the dung of a porcupine."
Having consecrated excrement with mantras, he makes one bitten by poison drink it.
[He causes him to eat meat three times with a white [spoon].
Having consecrated the porcupine quill and the meat with the verse, "The earless one has found it; he has spoken," he causes him to eat it.
This is a medicine for the destruction of poison.
[On the tenth day, he causes him to sip water from a gourd.

The medicine for snake venom.
On the eleventh day, he ties a navel-band.
With the verse, "I have praised, I have not praised" (RV 5.13.11),
having sprinkled and consecrated the stalk of a gourd, he ties it during the ritual procedure involving clarified butter.
One bitten by snake venom [should be treated].
In all cases, the application of the rites is optional; there is no requirement for their combination.
One may perform one, two, three, or all of them.
The medicinal treatment for snake venom is completed.
Where many rites are prescribed for a single affliction, one may perform either one, or two, or all of them, because of the statement:
"In every case, there is no requirement for a ritual sequence (tantra) in hand-homa."
Now, the binding of the mouths of evil speakers is described:
[Having crushed *madhulā*, *vṛṣaliṅgā*, *khala*, and *tulaparṇī*, he makes them drink it in honeyed gruel.
"And one for me" (5.15); "If you are a single bull" (5.16).

Having thus combined these three—*kulapallava*, honey-water, and [the aforementioned substance]—into one using the two *sūktas*, and having consecrated them with mantras, he then makes the afflicted person drink it.
This is the medicine for binding the mouths of malicious speakers;
wicked men do not speak [such things] behind one's back.
[With the following verses he partakes: Having consecrated the food with the hymn "If there is one bull" (*yady ekavṛṣaḥ*), he eats it;

"He creates the door" (dvāraṃ sṛjati).

Now the remedy for fever is stated: [With the mantra "Agni [drives away] Takman" (5.22), he causes him to drink parched grain.]
With the hymn beginning "Agnis takmānam," one causes [the patient] to drink parched grain;

Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
In this tantra, the application of the forest fire is taught;

then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*);

[From the village, the dust.

This is the remedy for all types of worms born of parasites—those in the eyes, ears, mouth, head, nose, and teeth—whether they are black, white, or yellow, and whether they are visible or invisible.
The treatment for worms is completed.
Now the medicine for the Rākṣasas is stated. Regarding this, it says:
"With the mantra *ā yam viśanti* (6.2.2), he eats milk-rice boiled with the *vayoniveśana* plant. (KauśS 4.5.27)

Now the remedy for snake venom is stated:
[With the verse, "As if around the sky" (RV 6.12), he makes him drink honeyed water.]

Having consecrated water with the hymn "pari dyāmiva," he sprinkles it;

Having consecrated water that has been heated by burning *dullaka* wood with the hymn "pari dyāmiva," he sprinkles it upon the diseased person.
With the hymn beginning "pari dyāmiva," he consecrates the water that has been poured over the grass used for the under-layer and sprinkles it.
Having performed the ritual framework (tantra), he pours the contents of a water-vessel into it with the hymn "pari dyāmiva," consecrates it, and makes [the child] drink it.
Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra).
With the hymn beginning "pari dyāmiva," having churned a gruel with two upward-pointing fruits smeared with poison, he then consecrates it with the mantra and makes [the patient] drink it.

With the hymn "pari dyāmiva," having consecrated *madana* fruits with the mantra, he has [the patient] eat them for the purpose of inducing vomiting. With the hymn "pari dyāmiva," having consecrated turmeric in clarified butter with the mantra, he makes [the patient] drink it.
The medicinal remedy for snake venom is completed.

This is the medicine for phlegm;
it is not a tantra. This is the fifth section. 29.

The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* offerings.
One performs the primary and subsidiary rites with clarified butter;
then, having anointed the amulet with mustard oil, one binds it on.
This is the remedy for eye disease.

With the verse "Let them go forth," he offers the animal according to the procedure for a barren cow;
