It is called the medicine for all poisons:
"To Indra, the first" (KauśS 10.4)—thus it is said regarding Takṣaka. (KauśS 4.8{32}.20)
Having paid homage to Takṣaka and consecrated water with the *arthasūkta* beginning with "The first of Indra," he causes [the patient] to sip it.
This is the remedy for poison.
Having paid homage to Takṣaka and consecrated water with the *arthasūkta* beginning with "The first of Indra," he sprinkles the diseased person with it.
There shall be cleansing and sipping of water.
This is the remedy against poison.
Having crushed a splinter of the *kṛmuka* tree in water while reciting the *Arthasūkta* beginning with "Of Indra, the first," he consecrates it and makes [the patient] drink it.
With the *arthasūkta* beginning with "Indrasya prathamaḥ," he consecrates water ignited by the dung of a donkey and cow-dung and sprinkles it [upon the victim].
With the *arthasūkta* beginning with "Indrasya prathamaḥ," he consecrates water ignited by a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and sprinkles it upon one bitten by a venomous creature.
With the *arthasūkta* beginning with "Indrasya prathamaḥ," he consecrates water ignited by blades of *mārjanika* grass and makes [the victim] sip it.
Regarding the medicine for poison:

having consecrated a vessel of water by reciting the *Arthasūkta* beginning with "indrasya prathamaḥ," he then makes [the patient] drink it according to the ritual procedure for clarified butter (*ājyatantre*).
The remedy for poison:

having stirred a mash of parched barley with the stalks of *udumbara* fruit while reciting the *Arthasūkta* beginning with "Indrasya prathamaḥ," and then having consecrated it with mantras, he makes [the patient] drink it.
This is the remedy for poison.
Having consecrated madana fruits with the *arthasūkta* beginning with "indrasya prathamaḥ," one consumes them for the purpose of inducing vomiting;
this is an antidote for poison.
Having consecrated turmeric with ghee by means of the *arthasūkta* beginning with "indrasya prathamaḥ," one makes the sick person drink it.
[Having drawn out the *padva* with the right thumb, [he administers it] into the right nostril.

With the hymn "Indrasya prathamaḥ" (The first of Indra), which serves as an explanatory mantra, he grinds the *padva*—known in common parlance as *kīṭaka* or *taliṇī*—and, having consecrated it, administers it into the nose;
specifically, with the right thumb, into the right nostril.
The treatment for poison is completed.
Now, the remedy for the fear of snakes is stated: [In the event of fear of snakes, one sprinkles and submerges [the object].
Having consecrated a *paidva* stone wrapped in a white cloth with the hymn "Indrasya prathamaḥ," one buries it where there is fear of snakes. [The *paidva*...]
A variegated insect resembling the color of gold is called a *paidva*;
it is a medicine against the fear of snakes,
or one may bind it above the house whether a snake is seen there or not.
With the verse beginning "From limb by limb" (*aṅgādaṅgāt*),
ending with "from the tips of the toes" (*ā prapadāt*), he rubs from the head down to the tips of the feet with his hand.
The medicine for the poison of doubt.

[With the verse beginning] "daṃśmottamayā," having heated a firebrand and consecrated it with the mantra ending with "āre abhūt" (10.4.26), he then, upon seeing the wound caused by poison, hurls it toward that [wound]. This is the remedy for snake venom.
[From where he was bitten // KauśS_4,8{32}.25 //] If the snake is not seen, one throws a firebrand from that very spot where he was bitten.
The remedy for snake venom is completed.

Now, regarding the medicinal remedies for all diseases taught by Kauśika—whether they have been explicitly stated or unstated, or whether they have been recited—in all those instances, the medicine is declared;
that is, the mantras among all the medicinal remedies for all diseases.
The unrecited mantras for medicinal herbs and forest plants are not prohibited for use as remedies.
With the verses containing the word *aṃhas*. (KauśS 4.8.27)
These [verses] are to be performed.
The *aṃholiṅga* group is now stated:
"O guardians of the quarters, [protect] the quarters" (1.31.2)—this is one [verse].
There are seven hymns beginning with "agner manve" (4.23–29),
and one [hymn] beginning with "yā oṣadhayaḥ somarājñīḥ" (6.96.1).
"Vaiśvānara has come to us" (6.35.2)—this is one verse;
"Adorning heaven and earth" (7.117.1)—this is one verse;
"That which is nearer" (10.5.22)—this is one verse.
"We speak to Agni" (11.6) is a hymn according to its meaning;
in this hymn [is found] "May he release me" (11.6.7).
"O Bhava and Śarva, this... (11.6.9), "The five goddesses... (11.6.22), "That which Mātali purchased for his chariot... (11.6.23).
Having excluded these four,
there is the *Aṃholiṅga* group;
and those hymns which consist of five verses serve as remedies for all diseases when used for consecration.
They are stated as follows:
"From both eyes, from thee" (2.33),
and "I release thee" (3.11).
"O gods... (4.13), "May they protect you... (5.30), "The headache, the ailment of the head... (9.8).

The *aṃholiṅga-gaṇa* consists of these five mantras. By means of these five mantras, the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of all diseases is performed; the meaning is that one should perform the consecration using any one of these five mantras.
Then, the *aṃholiṅga* group [of mantras] performs the healing of all diseases.
Having poured water into a vessel and consecrated it with the *aṃholiṅga* group, one sprinkles it upon all diseases.
This is the ritual procedure for clarified butter (*ājyatantra*).
Having consecrated water with the group of mantras containing the word *aṃhas*, he sprinkles it upon the sick person.
Having consecrated clay with the group of mantras containing the word *aṃhas*, he makes [the patient] drink it for all diseases.
Having consecrated clay with the group of mantras containing the word *aṃhas*, he smears it upon the sick person.
Likewise, in the case of possible diseases,
one binds the *pramehamaṇi* with the *aṃholiṅga* group for all diseases; thus it is stated in the *Tantra*.
Having consecrated rat-earth with the *aṃholiṅga* group [of mantras], one causes [the patient] to drink it for all diseases and medicinal treatments.
Having ground *pūtīka* plants with the *aṃholiṅga* group [of mantras] and having consecrated them, one causes [the patient] to drink them for all diseases.
Having ground *pramanda* with the *aṃholiṅga* group [of mantras] and having consecrated it, one causes [the patient] to drink it for all diseases.
Having ground the wood-shavings with the *gaṇa* of verses characterized by the word "aṃhas," he sprinkles them with water and gives them to drink.
With the *gaṇa* of verses characterized by the word "aṃhas," he causes these substances to be applied as an enema and gives them to drink.
This is the remedy for all diseases.
Having empowered the vehicle with the *aṃholiṅga* formula and the *gaṇa* mantra, he causes [the patient] to mount it according to the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for all diseases.
In all these cases, the phrase "he discharges the arrow" should be supplied.

Having performed the ritual procedure for the clarified butter (*ājya-tantra*) up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, and having prepared a vessel of water with the remnants of the oblations using the *aṃholiṅga* group of mantras, he wipes the region afflicted by disease with that water.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.
It is the medicine for all diseases.
With the *aṃholiṅga* group [of mantras], one offers fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* and other trees;
it is the medicine for all diseases.
He offers clarified butter with the *aṃholiṅga* group of verses according to the ritual procedure (*tantra*). He offers chaff with the *aṃholiṅga* group of verses according to the ritual procedure.
In the Tantra:
"The remedy for all diseases:
with the *aṃholiṅga* group [of mantras], he offers fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood anointed with *soma* juice."
It is the medicine for all diseases.
Having performed the *abhyātāna* rites up to the end, and having poured water into a vessel while reciting the *aho-liṅga* group of mantras, he sprinkles [the patient] with that water.
Thus, having released the bondage.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* verses and includes all medicinal herbs.
Having performed the *abhyātāna* rites, one pours water into a vessel while reciting the seven verses beginning with *aṃholiṅga*, consecrates it with mantras, and sprinkles it over the sick person.
The *abhyātāna* and subsequent ritual procedures constitute the treatment for all diseases.

Having performed the *abhyātāna* rites to their conclusion, one fills seven *kāmpīla* leaf-cups with water using the *aṃholiṅga* hymn; having poured [the clarified butter] into them and consecrated them with mantras, one sprinkles the patient with the water verse by verse, and finally discards it behind him.
The *puṭas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

Having performed the rites ending with the *abhyātānas*, he brings four portions of the residue (*sampāta*) from the *aṃholiṅga* group into a water-vessel; he pours two onto the earth and, having drawn those back up, he causes them to overflow.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.
Having performed [the rites] ending with the *abhyātāna*, he pours water from a vessel into it while reciting the *gaṇa* of the *aṃholiṅga* verses, consecrates it, and then sprinkles it.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he pours barley grains into a water-vessel with the *gaṇa* of formulas containing the word *aṃhas*, and having poured the remnants of the oblation into it and consecrated it, he causes [the sacrificer] to immerse himself as before.

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he brings four portions of the remnants into the water-vessel containing the barley—two onto the earth—and having drawn those back, he causes him to immerse himself.
This is the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

Having performed the rites ending with the *abhyātāna* formulas, he casts barley-grains into the fire with a verse containing the word "sin" (*aṃhas*), consecrates them with a mantra, and ties them [on the patient].
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.
This is a remedy for all diseases.
With the *Aṃholiṅga* mantra, one causes a person to drink water from a clod of earth that has the form [of a disease];
this is a remedy for all diseases. Having consecrated water extracted from a mound of earth shaped like a disease, as well as parched grain (*lāja*) and so forth, one causes them to be drunk.
It is the medicine for all diseases.
Through the two Vaiśvānara verses, the rites of administering a drink are performed.
Having completed the Abhyātāna rites, one pours water into a vessel while reciting the Aṃholiṅga hymn, consecrates it with mantras, and causes the patient to rinse with it using tufts of grass.
The *Uttaratantra*:

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he pours water from one vessel into another with the *aṃholiṅga* verses and the *gaṇa* hymns, consecrates it, ties it at the joints with cords of *mauñja* grass,
and sprinkles it while dousing it with *piñjūlī* blades.
The *Uttaratantra*:
the medicine for all diseases.
Having performed the *abhyātāna* rites up to the end, he pours water from two vessels together with the *aṃholiṅga* verses, consecrates it with mantras, and sprinkles [the patient].
The *Uttaratantra*:
Having tied a *darbha*-bead with muñja-grass at its joints using a formula containing the word "sin" (*aṃhas*), he sprinkles water over it after consecrating it with water.
He causes [the person] to sip water after consecrating the water with the group of formulas containing the word "sin."
With a verse characterized by the word *aṃhas*, he makes [the patient] drink a decoction of *iḷa* that is still warm;
with a verse characterized by the word *aṃhas*, he places fuel-sticks of *trapusa*, *musala*, *khadira*, and *tārṣṭāgha* [into the fire];
and having consecrated wooden pegs made of *khadira*, iron, and copper with a verse characterized by the word *aṃhas*, he drives them into the ground.
Having scattered barley grains that have been taken once, not yet discarded, and ground by a non-gatekeeper, he performs the oblation with a malevolent rite (*ābhicārika*).
Having consecrated fat, honey, clarified butter, and oil with a mantra containing the word *aṃhas*,
he makes [the patient] drink it in all diseases.
The drinking should be performed as is appropriate.
With a verse containing the word *aṃhas*, he offers an *iṅguda* fruit mixed with the down of *vīriṇa* grass using a hollowed leaf-cup (*prapuṭa*).

With a verse containing the word *aṃhas*, [he performs] the offering of a barley amulet, a *varaṇa* amulet, a *pṛśniparṇī* root, a splinter-amulet from the top-portion, the immersion, and the casting out outside.
One binds on a *kāṇḍamaṇi*, a *yavapalālamaṇi*, a *tilapiñjikāmaṇi*, or a gem wrapped in a lump of clay from the shape of an anthill, or in a sheath made of *jīvaka* fibers, and so forth.
The ritual procedure for clarified butter (*ājyatantra*) is to be applied in all cases,
as well as medicinal remedies as appropriate.
An enumeration of the aforementioned diseases is now made:
[namely] the disease of fever and the disease of diarrhea.
In excessive urine, in painful urine,
in painful feces, and in upward-moving wind (udāvarta).
In the case of the flow of the channels,
in the case of the breaking of the limbs,
and in the case of fever in the limbs.
In the case of the amputation of a limb,
in the case of vomiting Soma,
and in the case of the fever resulting from the emesis of Soma.
Among the fevers of the *apsaras*, *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, and *asuras*; in cases of dropsy;
and in diseases arising from disorders of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*).
In cases of headache,
pain in the limbs,
or epilepsy;
In cases of heart disease, jaundice, and malignant diseases; 20.
In cases of agitation and disease, in fever,
and in intermittent fever.
In the fever of desire,
in the curse of a brahmin,
and in verbal abuse.
And in the case of a disease of the head;
in the case of a wound from verbal abuse;
and in the case of verbal abuse by an enemy.
In the case of sons and daughters who are not born of the same lineage or clan, there is the disease of verbal abuse;
the disease of the falling of the gaze of the eyes; and the disease of ill-omened names.
In the disease of conception and gestation;
in the disease seized by Nirṛti and flesh-eating spirits;
and in pulmonary consumption.
In cases of *dhanurvāta*, *vātagulma*,
and *vātabhaṅga*.
And in fever caused by wind (vāta), in cough, and in asthma. 20. And in hiccough.
And in phlegm,
and in the falling of phlegm,
and in the flow of blood.
In cases of ear disease, in cases of phlegm, and in the spreading of infectious diseases.
In the spreading of foul odor from the armpits; in the spreading of swellings on the limbs;
and in the spreading [infection] of the ears.
In cases of ophthalmia,
heart disease,
and leprosy.
In cases of the eighteen types of hereditary skin diseases (kuṣṭha),
diseases of bodily eruptions,
and disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
When consumption (rājayakṣman) and emaciation of the body are unknown,
when the disease of Rohiṇī occurs,
and when there is the creeping of the limbs [with paralysis].
In cases of hip disease (nitambaroṃga),
injury from sharp horns and the like,
and dropsy (jalodara).
In the case of bulbous poison, in the case of secondary poison, and in the case of snake venom.
In the fever of ritual magic, in the fever of the village,
and in the fever that arises together with villages, cities, and districts.
In the case of a malignant disease, a congenital disease,
white leprosy,
or having white limbs.
When white hairs appear; when cattle, horses, and humans are afflicted by diseases arising simultaneously;
and when cattle suffer from consumption.
In the case of men suffering from consumption,
in the absence of water,
and in the disease of thirsting despite having a relish for food.
In the disease of hunger;
in the disease of *kṣetriya* within one's own body;
and in the disease of abdominal swellings and tumors.
In the case of intestinal worms;
in the case of worms affecting the bodies of men, women, dogs, goats, sheep, elephants, and so forth;
and in the case of non-human diseases such as lice, nits, and the like.
In cases of eye disease, nasal disease, or ear disease.
In diseases of the stomach, diseases of the intestines, and diseases of the anus.
In diseases of the vessels,
in diseases of the abdomen,
and in diseases of the hands.
In the case of heart disease, in the case of dust-like skin diseases,
and in the case of diseases of the fingers.
In the case of nail disease:
[the blood] from both feet,
the forefoot, the heel, the anus, and the hips.
In the case of fever with agitation,
in fever in general, and in intermittent fever.
And in the fever of sensual desire; in the curse of a brahmin;
and in the disease of verbal abuse.
Regarding the wound of verbal abuse:
when an enemy utters abuse,
or when one's son, daughter, or those who are not born of the same lineage or clan utter abuse, it is a disease.
The disease of the falling of the gaze of the eyes;
the disease of foul-smelling sores; the disease of conception in the womb.
In cases of disease seized by Nirṛti or flesh-eating spirits, in pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman),
and in bow-wind (dhanurvāta).
And in cases of abdominal tumors caused by wind (vātagulma), in cases of the breaking of wind (vātabhaṅga),
and in cases of fever caused by wind (vātajvara).
In coughing, in hiccoughing, and in phlegm.
And in cases of phlegm-discharge,
chronic bone-related ailments, elephantiasis, gout,
and hereditary diseases.
In all diseases and ailments; in the disease of evil;
in the diseases of the Gandharvas, Rakṣasas, and seizing spirits.
In the disease of being seized by unwholesome thoughts;
in persons who possess a void intellect regarding virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and who are thus devoid of the three aims of life;
and in the disease of the head.
In cases of long-standing eye disease (20),
in diseases that afflict the body with the pain of illness,
and in diseases resulting from injury to the feet.
In diseases caused by physical trauma,
such as injury from bricks or clods of earth,
or injury from weapons and the like.
When there is a blow from a wooden object;
when there is the disease of childbirth following the first delivery;
or when witnessing a miraculous phenomenon.

In the midst of illness, there is that which is declared by physicians; in the case of fatal illness (*ariṣṭa*), there is that which is declared by astrologers for the purpose of determining the influence of planets and constellations;
and therein, regarding the disease of being struck by a fatal omen, there is also the binding of gold.
In diseases arising from bodily winds, in the disorder of the humors (sannipāta),
and in diseases resulting from the derangement of wind, bile, and phlegm;
In the case of a disease caused by sexual intercourse; when blood flows from the ear;
at the root of the ear.
In cases of erysipelas, consumption, and autumnal diseases. 20.
In cases of cold-fever, minor fever, and fever caused by passion.
In phlegm-fever; in ringworm;
in summer-fever.
In the case of fever lasting for a year;

in giving, in the relinquishing of property, in receiving gifts, in officiating at sacrifices, in studying, in teaching, in sacrificing for those for whom one should not sacrifice, when diseases have arisen, and upon the destruction of the intellect.
In cases of disease of the eye-lid,
in bodily affliction,
and in agitation.
Regarding snake venom, artificial poisons, root poisons, and the like;
regarding men and women characterized by evil;
and regarding a heart devoid of desire.
In cases of burning pain in the heart, consumption (rājayakṣman),
and disorders arising from the desire for women.
In cases of epilepsy (20),
in chest ailments, in swellings,
in disorders related to the fetus, and in the twelve types of birth-constitutions.
In cases of ulcers with or without wounds, on swellings, in consumption, and in leprosy.
When a bull is castrated;
when there is excessive drying up [of the body];
and when worms have appeared on the body.
In the case of being bitten by a scorpion;

or in the case of being struck by any of the following—serpents, cocks, peacocks, ruddy geese, crows, pigeons, hawks, vultures, deer, tigers, leopards, hyenas, bears, buffaloes, cows, horses, cats, or any other wild animals or birds; or when there is a seizure in the abdomen, at the navel, in the throat, or in the neck.
In the sight of a snake, in the fear of a snake, or when bitten by a snake.
In the case of being bitten by a human, or bitten by a dog, or struck by the hand or other such means.
In the flow from the womb,
in the flow of blood,
in all diseases, and in the falling out of hair.
For strengthening the hair;
for glandular swellings (gaṇḍamālā); for cervical lymphadenitis (grīvāmālā).
In scratching the scalp;
in binding the hair; in a stream of a hundred great [waters];
and in having a putrid nose.
O you with the navel-tuft!
O you with the broad belly!
O you with the swollen belly!
In cases of swellings of the navel, neck, nose, feet, ears, teeth, and so forth;

in cases of eruptive boils, malignant diseases, leprosy, consumption, vitiligo, udumbara-type leprosy, and other such skin diseases; and in cases of ringworm, eczema, and women afflicted by *sannipāta* disorders.
For immediate vomiting,
for bodily pain,
and for diseases of wind (vāta).
In cases of wind disorders,
in the obstruction of the channels,
and in attachment to women.
In the case of reviling a brahmin, reviling a woman, or the loss of wealth. 20.
In cases of heart disease;
in diseases involving fruits, roots, leaves, vegetables, fresh meat, oil, ghee, condiments, and the consumption of desired foods; and in cases of indigestion.
In the four types of general indigestion, in abdominal pains,
and in headaches.
In diseases of the male organ,
in diseases of women, and in diseases of children.
The arising of youthful bracelets;
gray hair;
and the cutting off of limbs.
In the cutting of weapons; in boils and tumors; in sin and the practice of unrighteousness.
In the case of worms and diseases; in the activity of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
and in desire, anger, greed, delusion, and so forth.
In the case of a blow from a horn;
in the case of a blow from a tooth;
in the case of a blow from various [objects]. 20.
In the countryside, in cases of thumb-constriction,
in the disease of arbuda,
and among mosquitoes.
In the Tilakas, in the Dubhittakas, and in the Kulikas.
Regarding the outbreaks of diseases:
this concludes the enumeration of all the aforementioned diseases.
Now, the medicinal formulas have been recited; all of these should be applied for all diseases using the *aṃholiṅga* [mantra].
One performs the ritual with a water-pot using the *aṃholiṅga*;
this is the tantra.
Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he pours out the water-vessel with the *gaṇa* mantra beginning with "Oṃ aho," and wipes away the wrinkles with that water;
then he performs the ritual procedure (*tantra*) again.
This is done for all diseases.
Having performed the *tantra* rite with the *aṃholiṅga* [mantra], he binds [the patient] with a rope made from the head-hair of a *muñja* grass.
The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) begins with the *abhyātāna* mantras and so forth;
it consists of all medicinal herbs.
Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, one binds the urinary obstruction with the *aṃholiṅga* hymn;
the subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas. Alternatively, all [the rites] may be performed with those *sūkta*s.
Alternatively, all [rites] are to be performed by means of the Aṃholiṅga Gaṇa.
This includes everything such as "he places the fuel-sticks" and "he offers the clarified butter," which constitutes the entire *bhaiṣajya*.
Whatever rites are recited here, all of them are to be performed with the *aṃholiṅga* [mantra].

Whatever classes of diseases arising from indigestion are taught in medical treatises— namely those recited in the works of Caraka, Bāhaṭa, and Suśruta— all those medicines for those diseases are included in the collection known as the *aṃholiṅga*.
"Since diseases arise from indigestion," such actions should be performed when possible:
he binds [the patient] during the acts of binding, drinking, and rinsing;
fumigation, bathing, anointing, massaging, wholesome eating, ointments, abundant collyrium, sprinkling, lying down, and so forth—these should be prepared with the *aṃholiṅga* mantra.
The meaning is that they are to be prepared after being consecrated with mantras.
The meaning is that the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), which is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), must be performed in every case; as it is said:
"All [items] are to be consecrated" (KauśS 7.16).
Because of this statement,
the ritual procedure (*tantra*) applies to imprisonment;
those [rites] recited in one's own scripture (*svaśāstra*) are to be performed with the *aṃholiṅga* [mantra].
All those [rites] recited in other treatises and those recited in medical works should be performed;
or, in every case, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) should be applied as far as possible.
Thus it has been stated in the *Mūlakauśika* text:
The recitation for the binding of herbs (*oṣadhībandhana*) should be performed by the *gaṇa* known as *aṃholiṅga*.
It is to be tied after having been poured into the clarified butter (*ājya*) and consecrated (*abhimantrya*) within the ritual procedure of the clarified butter.

Regarding this, it is stated in that very [text] concerning the rule for digging and binding: "In all cases, the food, the woman to be bound, the bath, the vehicle, and the things to be eaten are accompanied by the pouring-in (*sampāta*); all are to be consecrated" (KauśS 7.15–16).
Because of this statement;
and so it has been said: "The digging for medicinal herbs is explained" (KauśS 33.16).
The digging for medicinal herbs is indeed according to the prescribed rule.
Even the binding [of the thread] is performed according to the prescribed rule.
Thus it is stated in the Gopatha:
"In medical treatises, astrology, and the Purāṇas, the formula 'aṃho-liṅga' should be employed everywhere in rites such as binding, drinking, and bathing."
It is called "disease" because it arises from unrighteousness (*adharma*).
This very same medicine has been taught in the *Hastivaidyaka* and *Aśvavaidyaka*;
the distinction lies in the specific mantras employed.
If it were performed otherwise, there would be no benefit, whether visible or invisible;
for a Śūdra performing the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is neither visible nor invisible merit.
Diseases are of two kinds: those caused by diet and those caused by unrighteousness (adharma).
Disease arises from food; for that, there is medical treatment.
When disease has arisen through unrighteousness, its pacification occurs through the performance of rites prescribed in the Vedas.

Having sprinkled the hall with a water-pot that has been filled by pouring [from another], he turns it upside down on the other side of the door-panel.

he sprinkles the entire bedchamber.
At the inner door,
he pours out the remaining water with its mouth turned downward;
the subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.
The rite of inducing sleep.

[He consecrates] the mortar at the northern corner and the foot of the southern bed while reciting the *tantu* formulas.

With the hymn beginning "The thousand-horned one," he consecrates the northern corner of the house.
With the hymn beginning "sahasraśṛṅgaḥ," he consecrates the right foot of the woman's bed;
with the hymn beginning "sahasraśṛṅgaḥ," he consecrates the rope of the bed. There is an option between these two rites.
The lulling of women:
desire arises in a man toward a woman;

Now, for a woman who has fled, the act of binding is performed according to the sequence of the ritual; a cord is prepared;

"The heaven has stood firm" (6.77)—this is the binding. (KauśS 4.12.5)
Having bound the top of the bamboo pole with a wrapping, he ties it to the middle [post].
With the second hymn, "The sky has stood firm," he consecrates the rope-wrapping, fastens it to the top of the bamboo pole, and ties it to the middle pillar.
And the foot of the bed is an utpala lotus.
And when [the victim] has been drawn forth. KauśS 4.12.8.
With the *ākarṣaṇa* [rite], he offers sesame seeds as an oblation.
With the hymn "The sky has stood firm" (*asthād dyauḥ*), he consecrates the foot of the bed and ties on blue lotuses.
With the hymn "The sky has stood firm," he offers sesame seeds with a hook.
For a woman who has fled, the acts of binding and the means of restraint have been completed.
The method for ensuring that husband and wife remain free from anger is stated:
[With the verse, "This which is dear" (6.89), he consecrates the head and ears. *Kauśikasūtra* 4.12.10.

and likewise those of a man.
[He holds his hair.
With the hymn beginning "This is that head which is to be cherished," he holds his hair.
The procedure for preventing anger in women and men is completed.
The means for bringing about good fortune is stated: "With the vulva, with pride, this I dig."
Having thus applied the *sauvarcala* salt and the white-flowered medicinal herb (*śuklaprasūna*) to his head, he enters the village.

Having performed the rites up to the end of the *abhyātāna* formulas, he digs up the root of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* plant like a medicinal herb with the hymn "May I [be blessed] by the auspicious one made of *śiṃśapā* wood," pours clarified butter over it, consecrates it with mantras, and binds it [on the head].
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.
Having consecrated *sauvacala* flowers with the hymn beginning with "bhagena mā," one binds them upon the head of the person for whom one desires good fortune; he then engages in sexual union.
This concludes the procedure for producing good fortune.

The "Enchantment for Good Fortune" (*saubhāgyasaṃvanana*) is described as follows: having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* oblations, one takes the root of *sauvarcala* salt, pours water over it while reciting the hymn beginning with "Thou hast mounted upon the pillow" (*anyastikā rurohitha*), consecrates it with mantras, and ties it [on the arm]; then one places a flower on the head.
Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, one pours [the powder] over the root of *sauvarcala* while reciting the hymn "I dig this" (*idaṃ khanāmi*), consecrates it with mantras, and binds it [on the patient].
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.
*Sauvarcala* is commonly known as *sūryaveli*.
Having consecrated the root of *sauvarcala* with the hymn "idaṃ khanāmi," he binds it; according to the ritual manual (*tantra*),
this is done on the head of a woman.
The section on making [the food] pleasing to the husband is completed.
The subjugation of a wicked woman is now described:
[With the verses beginning "rathajitām" (6.130–132), he sows *māṣa-smarā* beans. *KauśS* 4.12.13.

either at the place of the bedstead, in the house, or at the sleeping place.
[He hurls flaming arrow-heads in every direction with the *āvalekhani* formula.

Among these, having made an image of the husband, he pierces the heart with a splinter of *dāru* wood and a splinter of *bhāṅga* wood while reciting the three hymns beginning with "arathajitām."
The rites for subjugating wicked women are completed.

Having combined a woman's flower garland, her faded mouth-cleanser, and her hair,

then he places [the mixture] in the mortar.
One desiring misfortune [should take] a garland, a withered tooth-stick, and a lock of hair from a woman; having combined these, he should consecrate them with the hymn "abhagam asyāḥ.
A cow killed by fire is called an *anustaraṇī*.

Having wrapped her in her hide, he then buries her in a three-edged hole at the base of the mortar;

"I dig this up along with progeny and wealth"—

Whatever has been done by means of this hymn, "Bhagam asyāḥ," is destroyed by this [next one].
This brings about good fortune for her whose misfortune has come to an end.

Thus, having mixed *bāṇāparṇī* with the curd-water from a red goat and the *drapsa* [milk-drop], he scatters it around the bed.
With the hymn beginning "I dig this," he mixes the *bāṇāparṇī* with curd-water from a red-colored goat, consecrates it with mantras, and scatters it upon the bed of his rival wife;
this brings about enmity between the rival wife and her husband.
With the verse "abhi te'dhām" (3.18.6), he places a *palāśa* leaf beneath;

One who desires victory should [sleep] on the bed of a rival wife.
[With the verse "I have placed [the fire] near you" (3.18.6), he places it upon her.
With the line "I have placed [the fire] near you," having consecrated the leaves of the *bāṇāparṇī* plant, he throws them onto the bed of his rival wife.
The *bāṇāparṇī* is well known in the world as the *māsikā* plant.
The rites for conquering a rival wife are completed;
the meaning is that enmity arises with her husband.

Having consecrated countless pebbles with this hymn,

Whether it be a woman or a man.

Desire perishes.
Up to the desire for women;

Having touched one who is envious, he mutters the verse beginning with "From the person, from the one belonging to all people.
Having touched one who is envious, he mutters the verse beginning with "By the [power] of Tvaṣṭṛ, I..."

With the hymn beginning "ava jyāmiva," he consecrates a bow in the shadow of an angry man and makes it strung; that is to say, he causes it to snap.

Having performed the preliminary ritual (tantra) with the hymn "This is the Darbha," one digs up the root of the Darbha grass like a medicinal herb, pours [the water] over it, consecrates it with mantras, and binds it upon the personification of Wrath (Manyu).
Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual (uttaratantra).
This results in the destruction of Wrath.
The destruction of anger toward women occurs;
the methods for destroying anger toward women are complete.
"Begetting no hero" means begetting no son— [as in the mantra] "O Agni, those born [of you]... (7.34), [one should not think] "...may he beget another hero" (7.35).
Thus, one should not know [this]. Having rubbed together the urine of a mule and a stone disk, [one should apply it] to food and ornaments.

[He] looks at the parting of the hair [of the pregnant woman]. With the verse "O Agni, those born," having ground a stone with the urine of a mule and having consecrated it with that, he gives it along with food to a rival wife.
With the verse "O Agni, those born," having rubbed mule urine with two pebbles and having consecrated it, he applies it as an ornament to a rival wife who is his enemy.
With the verse "O Agni, those born," the husband gazes at the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*) of his wife,
or of a daughter, or of a man;
or else a dark child is born.
The chapters on the birth of other heroes are completed.
Now, the method for causing barrenness is stated:
with the three-verse hymn beginning "The other rivals," one grinds the urine of a mule against two stones, consecrates it with the mantra, and gives it to food.
That food is given to the rival wife of another man, who is the object of hatred, for her to eat.
With the three-verse hymn beginning "prānyāntsapatnān," having rubbed the urine of a mule against two stone disks and consecrated it with the mantra, he smears her ornaments with it.
With the three-verse hymn beginning "prānyān," he gazes at the parting of the hair of a woman who is his enemy.
The methods for making another's wife barren are completed.

The eradication of a paramour is now described: one recites the hymn beginning with "api vṛśca" (KauśS 4.12.35) after seeing the paramour of one's wife. One mutters this three-verse hymn upon seeing the paramour.
With the hymn beginning "api vṛśca," he cuts down the obstructing bow at the place where the word *jāra* (paramour) occurs.
[He hurls a stone at the seat of the paramour.
Having consecrated a stone with the hymn consisting of the three verses beginning with "api vṛśca," he throws it into the place where the paramour has sexual intercourse for the purpose of expulsion.
The expulsion of the paramour is complete.
The means for causing mutual enmity between a man and a woman are now described:
with the two-verse hymn beginning "tṛṣṭikaḥ" (7.133), one takes the *bāṇāparṇī* plant, mixes it with the juice of a red goat, consecrates it with the mantra, and scatters it around the bed.
And [this applies] to the beds of men and women.
Thus concludes the procedure for causing enmity, which effects the destruction of the mutual affection between a woman and a man.
Now, the rite for causing misfortune is described:
he touches the items mentioned in the mantra "ā te dade" (RV 7.114.1).
Moreover, he recites [the verses] in succession;
"ā te dade" is one verse.
He consecrates the heart or the mouth of another's wife.
Having muttered the single verse, "I have taken from thee," he recites the subsequent [verses].
These [verses] cause misfortune for either a woman or a man.
The rites pertaining to women are now concluded.
In that regard, Bhadraśloka says:
"The medicinal rites have been proclaimed for the pacification of all diseases;
thereafter, the rites concerning women [are taught] in the fourth section of the Saṃhitā."
The twelfth section (kaṇḍikā).
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Kauśika Saṃhitā-vidhi.
The fourth chapter is completed.
Now begins the fifth chapter:
[The Rites of Knowledge]. Now we shall explain the procedure for the rites of knowledge.

Whether there will be gain or loss, victory or defeat, pleasure or pain, excellence or inferiority, abundance or famine, security or insecurity, fear or fearlessness, illness or health; whether there is terror or not;
whether there will be wealth or poverty, merit or demerit, life or death, and whether there will be grain or not;
and whether it will happen in the field or not.
Will there be residence in one's home, or not?
Will there be grain, sons, cattle, gold, jewels, and clothing?
Will there be the acquisition of knowledge, scriptures, and so forth, or not?
Regarding life and death, going and coming, strength and weakness, and existence and non-existence;
for one who is ill, it is by way of life and death;
and regarding birth, it is by way of connection with a son.
When a son is born, due to his connection with dharma,
and due to his connection with friends and enemies,
one wonders whether a village exists or not.
Whether a man has married or not;
whether it will happen within a year or a month;
or whether she will be fortunate or unfortunate.
Having reflected with mind or speech on such matters as whether a house, a village, and so forth will come to be, or whether one's studies will succeed, or not— one should perform that action.
Now the procedure for the rites of discernment is stated:
with the verse "The mothers go" (1.4), there are the discernments of milk-rice, a swelling breast, and a split bamboo-stalk.
Having consecrated the milk-rice being prepared with the hymn "The mothers come" (*ambayo yanti*), one should then pour it out.
One should contemplate it with the mind; one should contemplate the winds.

Having consecrated the cloth with the twenty ṛg-verses beginning with "vaiśvānaro raśmibhiḥ" and "udehi vājin," he gives it away;
this is for one desiring pacification regarding [the horse's] running away and so forth.
Thus, the rites for the pacification of obstacles are completed.
Now, regarding the aversion and hostility toward the calf, conciliation is prescribed:
"As meat... (6.70), thus [the] recitation. (KauśS 5.5.18)
Having chased the calf away, having sprinkled it with cow-urine, and having led it around three times, he performs the *upacṛtati* rite.

With the hymn beginning "Just as meat," he causes the calf to bathe, sprinkles it with cow-urine, then leads the calf around three times, then consecrates it with mantras, and finally releases it for the purpose of drinking. [He consecrates its head and ears. (KauśS 5.5.20)

With the hymn beginning "yathā māṃsam," he consecrates the head and the ear of the cow. When there is a conflict among cows along with their calves, this rite of reconciliation is performed for the discord between calves and cows.
The reconciliation regarding the calf's dispute is concluded;
if it is not performed, the elder cow perishes.
The method for the destruction of a horse is stated.
Now we shall explain the ritual for the pacification of a horse: [With the verse beginning "vātaraṃhā" (6.92), one pours the remnants of the oblation over the bathed horse. *Kauśika Sūtra* 5.5.21.

Having performed the rites up to the end of the *abhyātāna* formulas, having bathed the horses and placed them at the front with his own horse, he pours water into a vessel and consecrates it by reciting the hymn beginning with "Become one who has the speed of the wind."
[Regarding the *palāśa* leaves and the powders, the subsequent ones.
Then, having placed all the medicinal herbs upon a *palāśa* leaf, he pours the remnants of the subsequent oblations over those herbs.
[He causes [the sacrificer] to sip water. (KauśS 5.5.23)
He causes [the water] to flow over;
with a vessel of water, he causes [the person] to sip and he causes [the water] to flow over.
[He] strews [it] with powders.
And with the verse "tri-rekayā" (VS 7.4.1), he sprinkles it three times with the powder of all medicinal herbs. "With one and with ten. (7.4.1)
With this verse, he sprinkles water on the heads of those who have bathed.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.
This is the *aśvaśānti*.
The horses become peaceful, radiant, free from affliction, swift, and healthy.
The ritual for the peace of horses is completed.
The fifth section (kaṇḍikā) of the fifth chapter.
Now, the raising of wealth through travel is described:
"With [the verse] 'From Bhadra' (7.8), one who is about to go on a journey should place [the fire] down. (KauśS 5.6.1)

He offers clarified butter with the verse, "From good fortune," according to the procedure for clarified butter. He places the fuel sticks with the verse, "From good fortune, may there be better fortune," while they are being pacified.
One who desires the pacification of obstacles offers a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with the verse, "From good, may there be better. There is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
One offers milk with the verse "From the auspicious" (*bhadrādadhi*) according to the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
One should perform the placing of the oblations, such as cooked rice and so forth, with the verse "From the auspicious, [may] what is better" (*bhadrādadhi śreyaḥ*).
In all cases, there is freedom from doubt regarding the tantra.
Having gone abroad, there shall be no obstacle to one’s journey, such as fear of thieves or fear of water.
This concludes the pacification of obstacles for those traveling abroad.
[He mutters:
"From the auspicious... (RV 10.151.1). He mutters this verse; for those traveling on a road, no obstacle shall arise.
Thus ends the pacification of obstacles.
[Having sprinkled the vehicle, he releases it.

With the verse beginning "From the auspicious one" (*bhadrād adhi*), having consecrated the vehicle by sprinkling it with clarified butter according to the ritual procedure, he goes to the village; then, he sprinkles it with water and releases it, desiring the pacification of obstacles.
And the raising up of the substance.
[It raises the substance like a shower of sparks.
(KauśS 5.6.4) If one travels by vehicle, then this rite is performed:
in the ritual procedure involving clarified butter (*ājya-tantra*), having consecrated it with the *sampāta* oblation, one should mount [the vehicle].
[Having bathed, he bestows [the gifts].

Having performed the rites up to the end of the *abhyātāna* offerings, he pours [milk] over the merchant's goods—clothes, bracelets, horses, and so forth—all such articles—and consecrates them with the verse beginning "From misfortune" (*abhadrād adhi*). The mantra is to be repeated for each individual article.
Horses, clothing, bracelets, and so forth;
from that arises the subsequent tantra.
One brings goods such as clothing for the purpose of sale.
When he takes the substance, this is the ritual act:
having consecrated it with the verse beginning "From the auspicious," he takes it.
The ritual for obtaining profit from trade is completed.
Whether on the road, at home, or elsewhere, no harm shall come to the merchant.
Then, harmony is established among the guests who have arrived. When a distinguished person comes to the house, this act of friendliness is performed.
As for their friend, when he comes to the house upon arriving at the sight [of them], then one should do this.
"Both of you have conquered" (RV 7.83.4)— with these words, while standing on wet feet, he effects concord.

Having performed the ritual procedure for clarified butter (*ājyatantra*), he consecrates the vehicle— such as an elephant or other conveyance— with the verse "Both of you have conquered," sprinkling it with drops of butter, and thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
In that vehicle, for whomsoever a consensus is made,
they all sit upon the vehicle;
they all climb onto the vehicle.
[Having caused the two [carts] to drive back to the villages by means of a vehicle, he gives them away.
Then, having gone toward the western direction and returned home again,
he consecrates the rice-gruel with the Ṛgvedic verse, "Both of you have conquered," and gives it for the purpose of eating.
Or they eat the stirred drink together with everyone; thus,
their harmony is complete.
The meaning is that while a single battle is being waged, the action belongs to one who has gone as an ally;
it is common to another as well.
This action belongs to him who provides assistance in the battle.
First, having washed the feet, then the ritual action;
some consider this ritual to be for the two Kṣatriyas.
Thus concludes the act of concord, the instigation of the matter, the pacification of obstacles, and [the rites concerning] war and so forth.
Now, when there is discord in the household, conciliation is prescribed:
[Having returned with fuel-sticks, bringing strength, without forming a formal resolve, he approaches and lays them on the fire once. *Kauśika Sūtra* 5.6.8.

The performer, having gone to the forest and taken sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), returns home silently; then, with the hymn beginning "ūrjaṃ bibhrat," he places all those sticks at once at the conclusion of the hymn. There shall be harmony among the household members, and there is the warding off of quarrels.
The meaning is that no quarrel occurs.
This concludes the section on domestic harmony and the pacification of obstacles.
For one who desires the substance of both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, this rite beginning with the acceptance [of the gift] is prescribed:
"He offers the oblation for the Anupravacanīya [rite] with the words, 'The Ṛc and the Sāman... (KauśS 5.6).
The third [offering] with the two joined [fingers]. KauśS 5.6.10.
[Regarding] the fourth [offering], the *ānumatī*:
having performed the rites up to the end of the *abhyātāna* [hymns], he offers clarified butter with the verse beginning "ṛcaṃ sāma";
he offers clarified butter with the verse beginning "ṛcaṃ sāma yadaprākṣam."
With the two verses beginning "ṛcaṃ sāma," he offers the third oblation;
with "anumataye svāhā," he offers the fourth oblation.
The subsequent ritual procedure follows the Abhyātāna rites.
Desiring to bring forth the meaning through the recitation of the Vedas and the recitation of the Śāstras, one performs this;
thus, when the Veda and the Śāstra have been completed, the pacification of obstacles regarding the bringing forth of the meaning is accomplished.
Now we shall describe the ritual procedure for the final bath of release (*parimokṣa-samāvartana*):
this same sacrifice is to be performed for both the one who is about to return home (*samāvartanīya*) and the one who has completed his studies (*samāpanīya*).
With the verse, "The divine waters" (7.89), one who has completed his vow consecrates the water for pacification at the edge of a body of water.
When the sun has set, having approached with fuel in his hand, he places the fuel-sticks on the fire, omitting the third one.
With the mantra "idāvatsarāya" (KauśS 42.17), one should offer clarified butter as a libation for the release from the vow.
One should place the fuel-sticks upon the fire.
To the Idāvatsara, the Parivatsara, and the Saṃvatsara, we announce this:
whatever evil we have committed against the sacred observances, by that sin and that impurity we are stained.
O Lord of Vows, whatever vow of mine you have caused to falter, may Day and Night restore it for me. May the Moon, rising in the east, be my healer; may the Sun, with his rays, heal this for me.
The vow which he has undertaken with thought, mind, and heart—
may the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle that within me.
"I offer the vows to Agni, the Lord of Vows;
may he grant me great splendor, glory, and long life. With these words, he performs the rites for the completion of the vow.
Having performed the ritual procedure for the Godāna ceremony up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he then prepares the *śāntyudaka* (water for pacification) and consecrates it with mantras.

With the four verses beginning with "apo divyāḥ," and having performed the rites from the Abhyātānas up to the Paridhāpana— some say up to the Paridāna— then, having offered the Abhyātānas, one should offer clarified butter with the four Ṛg-verses produced by the Kalpa-sūtra beginning with "idāvatsarāya.
Furthermore, one should place four fuel-sticks (samidhs) while reciting the four verses beginning with "idāvatsarāya."
Thus ends the dismissal of the vow,
the proclamation of the vow,
and the formal release of the vow.
Then he offers the Abhyātāna oblations.
Having offered the first clarified-butter oblation with the verse "The Ṛc, the Sāman," he offers the second with "The Ṛc and the Sāman which I asked about.
With the two [verses] beginning with "yuktā," he offers the third; and the fourth is the Ānumatī offering.
[For three nights, he eats no food and performs the vow of bathing.
Then he offers the *abhyātāna* oblations.
With the hymn beginning "Doṣo gāya" (6.1), he sprinkles cooked food with water, consecrates it with mantras, and eats it.
The *abhyātāna* and subsequent rites constitute the *uttaratantra*.

Thus ends the *parimokṣa*. Having performed everything up to the *abhyātāna* in the case of the *vedavrata*, *kalpavrata*, *mṛgāravrata*, *viṣāsahivrata*, *yamavrata*, *śirovrata*, *aṅgirovrata*, and so forth, the dismissal of the vow (*vratavisarjana*) is performed with the mantra: "For the coming year... (*idāvatsarāya*).
And he performs the proclamation of the vow (*vrata-śrāvaṇa*).
Because it is a hand-homa, there is a variation in the ritual procedure (*tantra-vikalpa*).
Wherever there is a vow—whether Vedic or worldly—in all such cases, the undertaking of the vow and the dismissal of the vow must be performed according to the prescribed rule.
The *śirovrata* and others are obligatory;
the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and others are prescribed by the *smṛtis*;
and the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and others are optional, being prescribed by the *smṛtis*, *purāṇas*, *śāstras*, and the *Vedas*.
Therefore, all those things denoted by the term *vrata* must be performed according to the prescribed rules. In every case where there is shaving (*vapana*), one should perform the *godānika* rite.
Immediately after the release, he should observe the vow of bathing for three nights.
When the sun has set, he offers fuel-sticks with the three verses beginning "The celestial waters," omitting the third.
Others perform the offering of fuel-sticks for one night.
Thus ends the section on liberation.

Now, the pacification for a woman possessing evil characteristics is described: [Regarding the verse *nirlakṣmyam* (1.18), he sprinkles the face of the woman with evil characteristics with water from each verse, beginning from a tuft of hair on the right side.]
With the hymn beginning "nirlakṣmyam," that woman washes her face verse by verse.

Regarding her face, the *Sāmudrika* [treatise on physiognomy] explains the female characteristics of ill omen, such as the presence of moles, *śigru*-spots, or *vāraka*-spots, as well as the presence of *tilakas* and short hair.
Having consecrated a water-pot with the hymn "nirlakṣmyam," she [should then act toward] the woman...
One sprinkles [the water] upon the "mark of evil," beginning from the hair on the right side up to the left side;
thereupon, the mark of evil perishes.
Having offered the husks with palāśa leaves, he brings back the remainder.
He places the husks, chaff, and bran upon his left heel.
Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, he offers parched grains (*kukusa*) with a leaf of the *pālāśa* tree while reciting the hymn beginning with "anirlakṣmyam.
He places the remaining parched grains from the oblation upon his left heel.
Then follows the supplementary ritual (*uttaratantra*):
with the hymn "anirlakṣmyam," he offers oblations of husks;
because this is a hand-oblation (*hastahoma*), there is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantravikalpa*).
With the hymn beginning "nirlakṣmyam," he offers husks of rice.
He places the remaining husks of rice from the oblation under the heel of his left foot.
With the hymn beginning "nirlakṣmyam," he offers chaff.
He places [the wood] upon the left heel with the hymn "nirlakṣmyam"; he offers the pieces of wood as they are being carved;
he places [the wood] upon the left heel.
By this, the characteristic of sin does not arise.
Thus ends the *Śānti* for the pacification of the fault of the characteristics of sin.
Now, the pacification for the sight of evil is prescribed: [One recites the counter-spells while observing the removal and the driving away:
"Āre 'sáu" (1.26) and "Apa naḥ śośucad agham" (4.33).
Having thus examined with these two hymns and having seen [the deity], one should recite [them];
no defect of vision occurs.
Whether once, or three, five, seven, or nine times.
When it is a man's time of fortune, even deer move clockwise around him.
This recitation is performed for deer that do not circumambulate clockwise,
as well as for birds;
even in a village or outside, when an ill-omened animal is seen, one performs this.
This [remedy] applies when there is the howling of dogs, the cawing of crows, or the howling of jackals;

as well as upon witnessing the mating of crows, the mating of humans, or the mating of hawks; upon seeing a naked woman, a naked man, or a eunuch; and upon seeing a promiscuous woman, the lunar disc, or something dark-colored—these are declared to be ill omens occurring under the asterisms of Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī.
Wherever ill omens are mentioned, in all such cases this recitation is prescribed.
Whether mentioned in the Śruti or the Smṛti, those [omens] should not be regarded as [ordinary]; upon seeing any of them, or upon seeing portents, this recitation must be performed.
Whatever is contrary [to the norm] in the world [is an omen].
This recitation for those whose misfortune is well-known and yet unseen is concluded;
thus ends the *apaśakunajapa*.
Now, whether it be a man or a woman, the ritual act for accomplishing tasks and pacifying obstacles is stated:
one ties [the amulet] as prescribed by the mantra beginning with "For long life" (2.4).

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, he ties a *jaṅgiḍa* amulet with a hempen cord using the hymn beginning with "For long life" (*adīrghāyutvāya*), consecrates it by pouring oblations over it while reciting mantras, and fastens it on.
Thereafter follows the *uttaratantra*.
This is for the purpose of neutralizing malevolent sorcery (*kṛtyā*).
He causes nourishment;
he is the performer of protection for the pacification of obstacles;
the obstacle is to be cast away.
The pacification of obstacles is complete.
The sixth section (kaṇḍikā) of the fifth chapter.
Furthermore, the pacification of obstacles is stated:
[Regarding *karśaphasya* (3.9): it is the yellow thread, the *araḷu* staff, and whatever weapon [is used]. *KauśS_5,7{43}.1*

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, he ties on an *aralu* gem upon a reddish-brown thread, having consecrated it by pouring [the oblation] over it with the hymn beginning "Of *akarśapha*.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* offerings.
This gem is a pacifier of the *viskanda* obstacle.
The meaning is that the destruction of rivalry occurs;
the meaning is that for one who is competing, the rivalry perishes.
The *maṇiśānti* for the pacification of obstacles is concluded.

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, one consecrates bamboo staffs and other such items with the hymn beginning "Of Karśapha"; then, having wiped them with that same hymn, one holds them.
Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

Whoever holds a variegated staff, a banner-staff, a insignia-staff, a sacrificial post, or a staff such as a club, after having consecrated it all in this manner, will not encounter obstacles such as snakes, horned animals, or fanged creatures.
Whether unknown or known, there is an increase in splendor.
Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, he consecrates the weapon with the hymn beginning "Of Akarṣapha," wipes it, and holds it.
Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
When all weapons have been brought down, the magical arts and so forth serve as a defense in the battle of the net of illusion; in the conflict, there is the warding off of sorcery,
and no obstacle arises in the fight.
He wards off the assault of the enemy;
the enemies depart;
he conquers the rivaling enemy.
It destroys forceful exertion.
[He fumigates with husks.
Having cast the husks into the fire with the hymn beginning "Of Karśapha," he fumigates the person seized by an obstacle;
the pacification of the obstacle occurs.
This rite is for one whose undertakings do not succeed;
thus ends the pacification of obstacles.
Now, regarding the purification of the ground:
one who intends to build a house performs this—
[“O you who are exceedingly arid” (7.41)].

[The rites for] settling the foundation, following [the site], pouring out [water], and sacrifice: with the two verses beginning "Over the desert wastes," he consecrates a vessel of water and pours it there on the ground where he intends to build the house;
thereby the pacification of obstacles occurs.

Having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings according to the procedure for a *pākayajña* for the deity Śyena, he offers the *caru* oblation with the two verses beginning "ati dhanvāni. The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) is the same as that of the *Pārvaṇa* and other sacrifices.
Having performed the Śyena sacrifice at the site where the house is to be built—where the earth is situated—one should then construct the house.

Alternatively, the Śyena sacrifice should be performed in a new house; the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that there is an option [regarding when it should be performed]. Or rather, the Śyena sacrifice is to be performed first in a new house.
Now the entry into the house is described. Regarding the consecration of the site:
with the mantras dedicated to Vāstoṣpati, after the ground has been ploughed by a pair of oxen, he brings the ritual materials to the south of the fire.
He pours out the Vāstoṣpatya and other [oblations] for the great pacification.
With the group of verses beginning with "Right here, the firm one," he plows the ground with a plow.
Then, from the south, he brings together the ritual materials for the fire.
Then he performs the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*).
Having performed [the rites] excluding Mātali, the fourfold great pacification (*mahāśānti*) beginning with Vāstoṣpati is carried out;
he pours [the substances] into the water for pacification.
Then, having performed the *mātali* rite, the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*) is completed;
with that, one should sprinkle the ground. Then...
In the middle pit, upon the *darbha* grass, he scatters rice and barley.
He casts it down.
In other cases, [the ritual is performed] with water for pacification, young grass, and sugar.
He pours the water of pacification, along with young grass and sugar, into the other pillar-pits situated at the sides.
With the hymn beginning "ihaiva dhruvām" (3.12), he consecrates the hall while it is being measured and erected.
Specifically, he consecrates the hall being measured with the hymn "ihaiva dhruvām."
When the sacrificial post is being erected, he consecrates it with the hymn beginning, "Right here, the firm one."
Having silently anointed the pillar and the beam with ghee, as prescribed by the mantra "Having anointed with the *ṛta*... (3.12.6).
Then, with the verse "With truth, the pillar," he erects the bamboo beams.
[“Full is the woman” (3.12.8): taking a water-pot and fire, they enter.

Then, having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* (declaration of an auspicious day), and having consecrated the wife together with the water-pot by means of the Ṛgvedic verse “Full is the woman,” they cause her to enter the house from the outside.
The patron of the sacrifice, taking hold of the fire, enters;
the others enter after him.
[He makes it firm with two verses.
With the two ṛcs beginning "Right here, the *dhruvā*... (3.12.1–2), he causes the floor of the hall to be made firm.
[He causes it to flow with the two verses addressed to Śambhu and Mayobhū.
Having consecrated a water-pot with the two verses, "For you are waters" (1.5) and "The goddesses be auspicious to us" (1.6), he sprinkles the ground of the house with it.
O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us; be easy of access and free from disease for us.
Whatever we implore of you, accept that from us, and cause the four-footed and two-footed creatures to settle here.
"O Vāstoṣpati, free from disease, entering all forms, be a most gracious friend to us"—with this verse he offers an oblation of milk-rice (kṣīraudana) to Vāstoṣpati.
Then, according to the procedure for the *pākayajña*, the pouring out of the grain is performed with the formula: "I pour out what is pleasing to Vāstoṣpati."
The sprinkling [of water] is performed with the formula: "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Vāstoṣpati.
For the oblation of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he says: "May the oblation go to Vāstoṣpati, svāhā!

Having prepared milk-rice (*caru*) dedicated to the deity Vāstoṣpati and having completed the rites up to the portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he offers the *caru* with the two verses beginning, "O Vāstoṣpati, recognize us."

Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttara-tantra*) beginning with the *pārvaṇa* offerings; some, however, having performed the oblations in this ritual up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, [recite] "The *yajus*-verses at the sacrifice" (5.26).
With this hymn of twelve verses, they offer one oblation at a time, mixed with clarified butter and honey, in the nine-chambered hall.
With the verse "The evening has come" (6.1), he offers the second oblation.
With the two [verses] beginning with "yuktā," he offers the third oblation.
The fourth [offering] is with the *ānumatī* verse.

Having taken water from the jar, the preceptor sprinkles the hall with his two fingers; then, having sat down in the midst of the houses occupied by the sacrificer and his wife, he pours the jar-water onto the ground.
At the beginning, the preceptor and the others observe silence.
The release of speech is performed with the ṛc verse, "Stay right here" (7.62.7).
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the Abhyātāna offerings.
He feeds all kinds of food to the Brahmins.
The meaning is "sweet foods."
[The Auspicious Rites // KauśS_5,7{43}.15 //] Elderly women perform songs and auspicious rites,
and Brahmins recite the "Days of Merit" (puṇyāha).
Some perform the *śrāddha* ceremony afterwards, while others perform it beforehand;
in all cases, however, there is the prescribed procedure for purifying the ground and the prescribed procedure for constructing the house.
Wherever one constructs a house, a pavilion, a hut, a picture gallery, a monastic cell, a rampart with watchtowers, a temple, or any other structure— whether made of grass, wood, brick, or stone—
the Vāstuyāga must be performed there according to this procedure.
The ritual for entering the house is completed.
By this rite, the dwelling has been made peaceful;
the householders are free from calamities, happy, possessed of sons, and enriched with cattle, wealth, and grain.
The hall becomes fit for enjoyment;
thus there is happiness in the dwelling.
Now, the pacification rite for a house, a field, or elsewhere, such as a cow-pen, wherever it may be that has been struck by a flesh-eating demon (*kravyāda*), is described:
[With the verse] "The fires which... (3.21), [one recites] "unstruck by the flesh-eater" and binds an amulet from *pālāśa* wood.

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, one consecrates and binds an amulet made of *pālāśa* wood after having poured oblations over it with the seven-verse hymn beginning, "The fires which are within the waters."
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* hymns.
[He offers oblations. With the seven-verse hymn beginning "ye agnayaḥ," he offers clarified butter according to the ritual procedure for clarified butter.
[He places them:
with the seven-verse hymn beginning "The fires which... (ye agnayaḥ), he places fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood; there is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).

When a carnivorous beast has entered a house, boys die, or calves, colts, or other young animals perish; or wherever there occurs injury, family strife, loss, or the destruction of wealth—one should know that such a house, village, or city is afflicted by a carnivorous beast.
Having poured barley grains with water from a wooden trough (udañcana) into a water-vessel (udapātrī),
he offers the water into the fire while reciting the hymn consisting of seven verses beginning with "ye agnayaḥ. This is an alternative ritual procedure (tantra-vikalpa).

With the seven-verse hymn beginning with "ye agnayaḥ," he pours that water from the *udadhānī* vessel into a water-vessel made of *palāśa* wood, places barley grains therein, and then offers oblations into the fire verse by verse.
In the case of a hand-oblation (*hastahoma*), there is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).

[The following are] the signs of raw-flesh eaters (*kravyāda*): quarrels in the family, the death of a boy, the death of cattle, the destruction of wealth and grain, anxiety over contemplated matters, and so forth.
The *Kravyādopahataśānti* is completed.
Now the procedure for the pacification of the flesh-eating fire (*kravyād*) is stated:
"With the verse *ye agnayaḥ* (3.21), having churned the mash with a ladle made of *pālāśa* wood and two churning-sticks made of *kāmpīla* wood...

With the ten-verse hymn beginning *ye agnayaḥ*, one stirs the mash of parched grain flour and water using two fuel-sticks of *kāmpīla* wood; then, one offers oblations verse by verse with a ladle made of *pālāśa* wood.
The ritual procedure is optional because it is a *darvihoma*.
The pacification of the flesh-eating [spirits] is completed.

One should perform this either in a common fire, or in the domestic *āvasathya* fire for the sake of rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), or in the churning fire, or wherever the affliction by a flesh-eater is observed; one should do it in all such cases.
Now, the ritual procedure for pacifying the barren cow (*vaśā*) is stated:
having consecrated the barren cow with the ten-verse hymn beginning with "Those fires" (*ye agnayaḥ*), he then gives her to a Brāhmaṇa.
One should know that the house in which a barren cow (*vaśā*) resides is struck by fate;
thus ends the pacification rite according to the procedure for the barren cow.
The seventh section (kaṇḍikā) in the fifth chapter.
Now, the ritual procedure for pacifying the barren cow is stated:
"He who gives himself" (KauśS 4.2)—this is the pacification of the barren cow. (KauśS 5.8.1)
In front of the fire, they hold [the vessel] facing westward.
Having sat down to the west of the fire facing east while [the wife] holds on to him, he performs the *śāntyudaka* (water for pacification) for her who is holding on to the barren cow (*vaśā*).

Having performed the standard ritual procedure up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, and having caused the cow to stand facing west in front of the fire, the performer, sitting to the west of the fire facing east, performs the *śāntyudaka* for her who is holding on to the barren cow.
[In this regard, one applies this hymn:
One should apply the hymn beginning with "He who, with wood or with grass... (RV 10.87) to the water for pacification.
With that [water],
ending with the verse addressed to Mātali, he causes her to sip water and sprinkles the barren cow with the *śānti*-water.
Standing while [the officiant] stands, he loudly recites the *Mahāśānti*. Standing above the performer,
he loudly recites the *Mahāśānti* consisting of the four groups beginning with Vāstoṣpati.
The practitioner stands facing the cow.
Having offered oblations with the hymn "He who rules as Paśupati of animals" (2.34), he anoints the barren cow on the head, the hump, the shoulder, and the hindquarters.
Having offered clarified butter with the hymn "He who rules as Paśupati," he then anoints the barren cow on the head, the hump, the shoulder, and the hindquarters.
[He anoints one or the other edge of the axe.
He anoints it on the back of the knife.
With the verse beginning with "aktayā," he digs out the omentum.
On the right side, he scatters two blades of darbha grass with the formula, "For such-and-such [deity], thee, acceptable," according to the respective deity.
With the verse "niḥsālām" (2.14), he carries a firebrand three times from left to right, not carrying it around himself.
On the right side, he throws two blades of darbha grass [upon the animal] with the mantra, "I cast thee up for Prajāpati.
Having caused the animal to stand in the middle and having whirled the firebrand three times clockwise with the hymn "niḥsālām," he does not carry it around himself.
[He takes hold with two *darbha* blades.
Having taken hold of the barren cow (*vaśā*) with two *darbha* blades.
Thereafter, to the north of the fire, he drives in [the stake] with its head toward the west and its feet toward the north.
He places one blade of *darbha* grass with the mantra, "Be united with her body.

Having led the cow behind and to the north of the fire, he then places one blade of *darbha* on the ground with the mantra, "Be united with her," and causes the cow to fall upon it; he pins her down with her head toward the west and her feet toward the north.
Then he establishes her vital breaths with the verse, "Knowing [the way]... (RV 2.34.5).
Then the Adhvaryu priest, having placed fuel on the fire, obstructs the mouth of the cow, renders her breathless, and kills her with the verse beginning "A-prajānantaḥ."
Standing to the south, he mutters the *rakṣohaṇam* section (8.3.4).
Standing to the south, he mutters the *rakṣohaṇam* anuvāka.

When the cow has been slaughtered, he offers the clarified butter with the two ritual formulas prescribed in the Kalpa-sūtra, using the verse: "If the cow, while being slaughtered, has uttered a cry, or if she has struck with her feet—may Agni release me from that sin, and from all distress.
He offers the oblation with the verse beginning, "If the cow, while being slaughtered... when the animal has been slain.
Then the wife, taking a vessel of water, goes near the sacrificial animal.
[With a water-pot, the wife goes forward and washes her face and other limbs.

"Be purified for the sacrifice to the gods. (KauśS 5.8.19)
"Prāṇān" refers to the two nostrils.
"Cakṣuḥ" means the two eyes. KauśS_5,8{44}.21.
"Ear" refers to the two ears.
"Whatever is cruel, whatever is fixed"—with these words, he sprinkles water all around the cord-line.
Having gathered the verses beginning with "caritrāṇi," [he performs the rite]. KauśS 5.8.24.
"Nābhim" means "the navel. KauśS_5,8{44}.25.
"Meḍhram" means the penis. KauśS_5,8{44}.26.

Regarding "the anus," [the performer] should recite the mantra: "Be purified for the sacrifice to the gods" over the anus. He should recite "Be purified for the sacrifice to the gods" over the vital breaths.
"Be purified, O nose," he says over the two nostrils; "Be purified, O eyes," he says over the two eyes;
"Be purified, O ear," he says over the ear.
With the words, "Purify the two ears," he purifies the ears; with the words, "That which is cruel in you, that which is fixed," he purifies the entire area where the cord was tied;
and with the mantra, "The footprints," he gathers the feet together.
With the mantra, "Purify the navel for the sacrifice to the gods," he purifies the navel;
with "Purify the penis," the penis;
and with "Purify the anus," the anus—thus, for each mantra, there is the washing of the body parts.

"Whatever in you is cruel, whatever is settled, cleanse that"—having sprinkled the remaining water on the side, she proceeds according to her purpose. Having poured the residual water on the side with the mantra "Whatever in you is cruel, whatever is settled, cleanse that," the wife then proceeds according to her purpose.

Having taken the two omentum-spits, the clarified butter, the dipping-spoon, the knife, and the *darbha* grass, he proceeds forward; then, having spread the *darbha* grass with its tips pointing upward and following the direction of the path, he strews it upon the region of the navel.
Thus, having taken the two omentum-spits, the clarified butter, the dipping-spoon, the knife, and the *darbha* grass, he goes to the place where the animal was;
then, following the direction of the path, he strews the *darbha* grass upon the region of the navel.
"O herb, protect him! O axe, do not harm him!"—with these words, he hands over the weapon.
With the words, "O herb, protect him," he hands over the knife.

Having cut [the umbilical cord] with the formula, "Here I cut off the out-breath and in-breath of the son of such-and-such a man and such-and-such a woman," he cuts the region of the navel together with a blade of *darbha* grass using the mantra: "Here I [cut] the son of Mahumada, Bhūtikarṇa."
Having struck away the blood by biting off the lower lip.
With the mantra, "Here I bury the out-breath and in-breath of the son of such-and-such a lineage, the son of such-and-such a mother," he buries [the blade] in the mouth;
that is, he removes the piece of Darbha grass smeared with blood from the location of the mouth by means of this mantra.
This is the meaning of "he buries."
"O Heaven and Earth, cover yourselves with the omentum," he says, having covered the two omentum-spits with the omentum.
Having cut it off with a sharp knife after having first prepared it.

Having sprinkled clarified butter over the wound, one covers the two omentum-spits with the omentum while reciting the mantra, "With the omentum, [I cover] heaven and earth. Then, having prepared them with the sharp knife and cut [the omentum], one sprinkles the site of the incision with clarified butter.
The two [spits] are made from *śānta* wood; one has a single prong, and the second has two prongs.
With the words, "To Vāyu, of the drops," he throws in a tip of darbha grass; that is, he casts it.
With the mantra "The demon is burnt away," he places the cooked rice (caru) on the embers behind the fire.
"May Savitṛ cook you," [saying this] he cooks it. (KauśS 5.8.39)
He makes it well-boiled. He cooks it with the mantra "May the god [cook] you," and thereby he makes it well-boiled.
The eighth section (kaṇḍikā) in the fifth chapter.

If there should be an eight-padded footprint in the hollow of the womb, he offers once into the fire of three cubits within the pit— either gold or barley placed in the hollow of the womb— with the hymn beginning "He who gives himself" (*ya ātmadā*).
If there should be an eight-padded footprint in the hollow of the womb, he offers once into the fire of three cubits within the pit with the hymn "He who gives himself."
Having dissected it, one should cut off the portions for the equal-share offerings.
The heart, the tongue, the hawk, the two shoulders, and the two sides—these are six;
the liver, the kidneys, the rectum, and the hips—these eleven are the deities.
The right forehead, the left hip,
and the anus— these three parts constitute the portion for Sviṣṭakṛt alone.
One should cook those portions that have been cut off.
[KauśS 5.9] One takes eleven portions from the animal: the heart, ... [and so forth].
The tongue, the chest, and the left arm.
There are two sides;
the liver is called *kāleya*;
there are two backs.
The anus and the lower right arm—
having grasped these eleven.
Then he takes the portions for the Sviṣṭakṛt;
there are three of them:
the right arm.
The left calf and the division of the intestines—
having taken these three.
He places the pieces of meat in the middle of the sacrificial cake and performs the rites beginning with "O Agni, around thee," and so forth.
When about to offer, one should cut portions for the deities twice each.
[Once each for the portions belonging to Sviṣṭakṛt.
Then, a caru-oblation must be cooked for whichever deity the animal sacrifice is dedicated.
He offers oblations with the verses "Enkindled for the omentum" (5.12) and "Upright are his" (5.27).
Then he cuts the omentum into four pieces.
He offers one piece with the hymn beginning "Kindled today" (*samiddho adya*).
He offers the second piece with the hymn beginning "Upward [is] his" (*ūrdhvā asya*).
[With the two appropriate ones, the third:
KauśS 5.9.9] He offers the third section with the two hymns, "Enkindled today" and "Upright is his."
[The fourth [offering] is for Anumati.
He offers the fourth portion with the words, "To Anumati, svāhā!"
"O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum; for you have become the first Hotṛ.
O Agni, unite with the body of clarified butter; may the desires of the sacrificer come true—svāhā! (KauśS 5.9.11).
Then, he offers the clarified butter with the mantra: "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum."
"Go upward to the wind in the sky," with these words he throws the two omentum-spits after [the oblation].
With the mantra,
"Go upwards to the sky, to the wind," he offers the two omentum-spits together,
having placed the one-horned spit facing eastward and the two-horned spit facing westward.
"O Jātavedas, carry the omentum to the fathers where you know them to be placed in the distance;
