Then he offers the portions with the hymn beginning "He who gives himself" (*ya ātmadā*),
offering with each verse.

[Regarding the placing upon the fire of the *sthālīpāka* for the *samrāj*: "May I overcome all the quarters through my friends.
You are desire; I offer you, who are desire, for the sake of one possessing all heroes, all men, all groups, and all desires."]
"May Anumati, Pūṣan, and the great Sarasvatī favor us today;
may that which I do prosper. To Anumati, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the oblation.
With the mantra "Thou art the sovereign ruler," he offers clarified butter.
He offers four oblations: "To all heroes, svāhā! To all men, svāhā! To all hosts, svāhā! To all desires, svāhā! He offers [the fifth]:
"May Anumati favor us today; may Pūṣan, Sarasvatī, and Mahī prosper that which I do. To Anumati, svāhā! He offers.
Having offered to Prajāpati in the Pārvaṇa and other rites, and having then once cut portions of the meat and the caru, he performs the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
"Svāhā to the beloved ones," and so forth, constitutes the subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra).
Thus concludes the rule for the pacification of the barren cow (vaśāśamana).
The house of one in whose home a barren cow is born is struck by fate;
for him, there shall be the destruction of wealth and other possessions.
Therefore, a propitiatory rite (śānti) must be performed.
There are two ways of dealing with a barren cow:
one may either give it away after consecrating it with mantras, or one should perform its pacification according to the prescribed rite.
By this same procedure, the treatment of other sacrificial animals is explained.
The sacrificial animals have been explained in relation to the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya) rites.
"One should sacrifice with an animal to Agni for twelve nights" refers to the obligatory rite; as for the occasional and optional rites, five animals are offered to Dhūmaketu.
The *Dhātṛ* sacrifice with an animal victim is recited in the *Purohita-pariśiṣṭa*;
such are the occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
The optional (*kāmya*) rites have been recited by Paiṭhīnasi.

The animal sacrifice is recited among the *puṣṭikarmāṇi* (rites for prosperity) in the passage beginning with "thirteen months by means of a goat offered as a self-oblation" (*chāgena svahutena trayodaśamāsān*). Therefore, the deities mentioned in the mantras are the objects of these optional animal sacrifices.
Likewise, in the Vaitānasūtra, there are optional animal sacrifices (kāmyāḥ paśavaḥ) such as "the animal for Indra and Agni for one desiring long life, progeny, and cattle," and so forth.
Their procedure is stated as follows:

having performed the domestic sacrifice (pākayajña) up to the portioning of the clarified butter (ājyabhāga), and having performed [the rites] up to the sprinkling of the water of peace (śāntyudaka) and the formal salutation, the mantra beginning with "He who rules over cattle, the Lord of cattle" (aya īśe paśupatiḥ paśūnām) and so forth is employed.
It is the same for a permanent animal sacrifice.
The offering of the omentum (*vapā*) is performed with the verses "Enkindled today... and "Upright is his...", and likewise in the occasional (*naimittika*) sacrifice.
Likewise, in the case of two [offerings], the primary oblation (*homa*) is performed with the primary *sūkta* alone; and the same applies to those rites intended for specific desires (*kāmya*).
Now, regarding the specific rule for optional ancestral rites (*pitrya-kāmya*), there is a triple repetition of the verse beginning with "vaha vapām."
He offers the omentum three times;
likewise the portions;
likewise the sacrificial porridge; he offers it three times with the formula, "Carry the omentum."
The rest is the same.
Now, when an improper acceptance of gifts has been made, or when officiating at a sacrifice or receiving a priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been performed, that rite by which sin is destroyed is stated:
"Who gave this to whom? (3.29.7–8);
"Desire was there in the beginning" (19.52).
He accepts [the food] with the mantra: "Whatever food... (6.71) and "...the faculty of mind" (7.68). KauśS 5.9.17.
The *uttamā* [mantra] is for all rites. KauśS_5,9{45}.18.
The *pākayajña* sacrifices have been explained by means of the *vaśā*.
Having consecrated the acceptance [of a gift] with the two verses beginning with "Who is this?", he accepts it;
thus no fault arises from the acceptance of the gift.
The specific procedure for receiving land is performed with the triplet beginning with "yad annam" and the verse "bhūmis tvā" (3.29.8).
Having consecrated the act of acceptance with the hymn "kāmas tad agre," he receives it.
Having consecrated the vessel for receiving with the hymn consisting of the three verses beginning with "yad annam," he takes [the gift].
Having consecrated the vessel for receiving with the verse beginning with "punar maitv indriyam," he takes [the gift].
Thus concludes the rite for destroying the defect of receiving gifts.
Having performed all the ritual acts and completed the rite with the verse, "May my senses return to me," he then consecrates himself.
This self-consecration (*ātmaśānti*) occurs in all rites.

In the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*), in the *ājya-tantra*, in this *pākayajña*-tantra, and in all obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites, he consecrates his own heart with the verse, "May my senses return to me."
The ninth section (kaṇḍikā) of the fifth chapter.
Now, when a sinful reputation arises in the world regarding one who has committed no sin, the following pacification is prescribed:
*utāmṛtāsuḥ* (5.1.7) and *śivāste* (8.2.15).

[Thus, for one who has been falsely accused: Having first placed the falsely accused person before him while reciting the verse "utāmṛtāsuḥ," he enters the house silently; then, having consecrated the barley-meal mash (saktumantha), he gives it to the falsely accused.
His sin is destroyed.
Having first placed the one who has been slandered at the front and having had him enter the house, the performer enters afterwards.
Having consecrated the barley-meal mash with the verse, "May the plants be auspicious for you," he then gives it to the slandered person;
thus, censure arises in the world.
Having consecrated the food with the verse, "And may he be one whose life is immortal," he gives it;
having consecrated the food with the verse, "May the plants be auspicious for you," he gives it.
In this world, his censure perishes.
[He binds the head of the wooden mallet with a cord.

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he ties on the *drughaṇa*-gem after having sprinkled it with water and consecrated it with the verse, "And the immortal life... (*uta amṛtāsuḥ*).
Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

In the case of one who is accused, this rite is performed: having prepared the ritual procedure with clarified butter (*ājya*), he casts [the materials] into the wooden mallet (*drughaṇa*) with the verse "May these herbs be unpropitious to you," consecrates it with mantras, and binds it [to the accused].
O accused one!
Then follows the Uttaratantra.
[It is appropriate for wood-apple, iron, copper, and gold.

Having performed the ritual procedure (*tantra*), and having fashioned a wood-apple amulet (*pālāśamaṇi*) shaped like a wooden mallet (*drughaṇa*) with the verse "O immortal one, come hither," he then sprinkles it with the *sampāta* water, consecrates it with mantras, and binds it on one who has been accused.
In the *Uttaratantra*:

having performed the ritual (*tantra*) with the verse "May the inauspicious ones depart from you," one fashions a wooden amulet of *pālāśa* wood in the likeness of a mallet (*drughaṇa*), pours [the sacrificial remains] over it, consecrates it with mantras, and binds it on for one who has been accused.
Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttara-tantra*).

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, one fashions an iron amulet (*lohamaṇi*) resembling a wooden mallet (*drughaṇa*) with the verse "utāmṛtāsuḥ"; having then poured clarified butter over it and consecrated it with mantras, one ties it on the person who has been accused.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins again from the *abhyātāna* offerings.

Having performed the preliminary ritual (*tantra*), one fashions a black iron amulet shaped like a mallet using the verse "aśivās te," heats it over the fire, consecrates it with mantras, and binds it on.
Thereafter follows the subsequent ritual (*uttaratantra*).
Upon hearing of a sin, the destruction of that sin occurs.

Having performed the ritual procedure (*tantra*), he fashions a copper amulet shaped like a wooden mallet (*drughaṇa*) with the verse "utāmṛtāsuḥ," and having consecrated it by pouring oblations (*sampāta*) and reciting mantras, he ties it on.
Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

Having performed the ritual procedure, he fashions a copper amulet resembling a wooden mallet with the verse "śivāste," and having consecrated it by pouring oblations and reciting mantras, he ties it on.
Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, he fashions a golden amulet in the form of a wooden mallet (*drughaṇa*) with the verse "utāmṛtāsuḥ," pours [the sacrificial remains] over it, consecrates it with mantras, and ties it on.
Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure.

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, one fashions a jewel made of gold in the likeness of a wooden mallet (*drughaṇa*), consecrates it by pouring oblations over it while reciting the verse "May they not be inauspicious for you," and binds it [to the patient].
Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
This rite is for one who is reviled despite having committed no sin.
Or, if an expiation has been performed,
this rite is to be done if there is the hearing of evil reports;
thus ends in the world the rite for destroying censure.
In all cases, Kauśika, there is an option regarding ritual actions.
When many rituals are prescribed for a single object, one may perform one, two, or all of them.

Now, while the sacrifice is being performed, that rite by which the pacification of obstacles occurs is stated: "With the verse beginning 'By whom, O Soma' (6.7), one who is about to officiate as a priest eats the *sārūpavatsa*.

Having performed the rites up to the end of the *abhyātāna* formulas, he pours milk over the *sārūpavatsa*—a dish of milk-rice (*pāyasa*)—and, having consecrated it with the hymn "By whom, O Soma," he causes the officiating priests and the sacrificer to eat it.
The success of the sacrifice occurs without obstacles;
hence follows the *Uttaratantra*.
The pacification of obstacles in the sacrifice is completed.
The pacification of obstacles at the conclusion of the sacrifice is stated: [At the end, he sacrifices.

Having performed the *caru* dedicated to Soma according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*, up to the point of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers the *caru* with the three verses beginning "By whom, O Soma... (*yena soma*).
The ritual procedure for the Pārvaṇa and subsequent rites follows.
This concludes the expiation for the fault of officiating at a Soma sacrifice and the pacification of obstacles;
by this rite, one is liberated from the fault of officiating for those for whom one should not officiate.
Furthermore, if one desires to receive wealth, grain, and so forth, or wishes to solicit them, by performing this rite one solicits them and no obstacle arises.
[Thinking,] "That which I entreat" (5.7.5) and "That which I hope for" (7.57.1–2), he is about to make his request.

Having performed the rites up to the end of the *abhyātāna* formulas, he cooks milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with a calf of the same color as the offering; having poured the oblation-remnants over it and consecrated it with mantras, he eats it while reciting the verse "That which I entreat."
Then follows the *uttaratantra*.
He does not refuse what is requested.
Having performed the *ājyatantra*, he pours milk-rice (*pāyasa*) into a vessel containing a calf of the same color, consecrates it with the two verses beginning with "yadāśasā," and eats it.
The *Uttaratantra*.
The prohibition against begging and the rite for pacification are completed.
Now, if a dove or an owl enters a house— or even if it enters elsewhere in a desired location— the pacification for that is stated:
[the mantras] "O gods, the dove has fallen among those who have fallen" (6.27) and "With a verse, [one should appease] the dove" (6.28).
With the mantra "amūn hetiḥ" (6.29),
he pours out the Mahāśānti;
having prepared the water for pacification according to the prescribed rule, he does not thereafter perform the Mātali rite.

The three hymns beginning with "devāḥ kapotaḥ," "ṛcā kapotam," and "amūn hetiḥ," the Vāstoṣpatya hymn, the Cātana hymn, and the Mātṛnāman hymns—these four groups constitute the collection for peace (śāntigaṇa).
One pours these into the water for pacification (śāntyudaka).
Then, having performed the Mātali rite, one should conclude the water for pacification.
At night, he sprinkles that place with the water of pacification using these mantras beginning with "yatāyai," extending as far as the location of the pigeons and owls.
The performer of the rite must perform the ritual sprinkling and the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana).
He sprinkles the location of the house and other such places.
With the verse, "Parīme 'gnim" (6.28.2),
having taken the cow and the fire, he leads them three times around the hall while performing the rite at night.
With the ṛc "Parīme 'gnim," having grasped both the cow and the fire, he leads them three times around the hall.
Or one may cause [the vessel] to revolve in the "pigeon-position" (kapotasthāna).
The mantra is recited once;
the performer should do everything.
When a forest-dwelling bird has entered [the house], one should perform this rite;
likewise when a dove or an owl has entered.
It is heard in the Veda that there is destruction of bipeds and quadrupeds [in such cases]; this is the pacification of that fault.
The pacification of pigeons and owls is complete;
the great pacification is finished.
One performs the offering of ghee, woolen blankets, and so forth.
He makes it either immortal or tenfold.
Now, regarding the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) prescribed for the vision of a terrible dream mentioned in the *Svapnādhyāya*:
the "bad dream" (*duḥsvapna*) referred to in the *Svapnādhyāya* should be understood according to the opinion of the commentator on the *Rudra*.

Having seen cooked meat, the subduing of a *preta*, an embrace, a monkey-cart, an oil massage, the sight of a naked man, or the sight of a naked woman, [one faces] the *Kālasūtra* hell and so forth; these are read many times in the *Svapnādhyāya*.
Thus, when such evil dreams are seen, the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) is described:
Having seen a dream [with the words] "Go away" (6.45) and "He who is not a living being" (6.46), he wipes his face. KauśS 5.10.9.
Having seen a most terrible dream, he places a *maiśradhānya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) upon another seat.
Having seen a contemptible dream, he washes his face while reciting the two hymns beginning with "Go away" (*paro 'pehi*) and "He who is not living" (*yo na jīvaḥ*).
Having cooked a *maiśradhānya* sacrificial cake with the two hymns beginning with "Go away" and "He who is not living," he offers it into the fire.
The ritual procedure for the *tantra-vikalpa*:

having cooked the second sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with the two hymns "O Supreme One, go away" (*paro 'pehi*) and "He who is not the living soul" (*yo na jīvaḥ*), and having consecrated it with mantras, he deposits it in the field of his enemy.
This concludes the rite for the destruction of bad dreams.
Regarding the phrase "paryāvartaḥ" (7.100),
he turns around after muttering the verse beginning with "paryāvartaḥ."
Having eaten, he looks [at the food] with the verse beginning "yatsvapne" (7.101).
He mutters the ṛc "yatsvapne";
whatever food he has consumed in a dream, he now makes that [present].
Now, furthermore, the rite for destroying terrible bad dreams is stated:
"We know you, O Dream" (*vidma te svapna*)—this is the conclusion for all [such rites]. (KauśS 5.10.13)

Having seen a bad dream, one wipes one's face with the single verse, "We know you, O Sleep. Having seen a dream, one lies down on one's side with the hymn, "We know you, O Sleep," using the second [verse].
Having seen food in a dream, one gazes at it with the hymn, "We know you, O Sleep."
With the hymn beginning "vidma te svapna," he offers a cake of mixed grains (*maiśradhānya-puroḍāśa*). There is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra-vikalpa*).
Thus concludes the rite for the destruction of bad dreams.
Now, when the teacher has died, a student desiring spiritual merit performs this rite:
having placed fuel upon the teacher's funeral pyre with the verse, "Not indeed, O Agni, of thy bodies" (6.49), the student circumambulates it three times and offers a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
He should sleep for three nights without turning over.
"One should not sleep [there]," says Kauśika.

When cremating the teacher, having offered the five *sāmidhenī* oblations beginning with "The fire on the earth" (*agnir bhūmyām*), he then circumambulates the cremation site three times; thereafter, he offers the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) into that cremation fire with the hymn ending in "For these, O Agni, are thy bodies" (*na hi te agne tanvaḥ*).
For three nights he sleeps near the cremation fire, remaining facing it;
the owl does not consider sleeping there because of the fear of hungry ghosts and other such beings.
The pacification of its obstruction.
One should bathe with bathing-powders. *Kauśika Sūtra* 5.10.17.
One who has not yet completed his vows should return [to his teacher].
Having bathed with the four ṛg-verses beginning with "apo divyāḥ" (7.94), he should return home for three nights and then sleep; this is the opinion of Kauśika.
This ritual is performed when the teacher has died.
The meaning is that, having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should then perform the *samāvartana* ceremony;
one should attend upon another teacher.
This concludes the section on the expiation for a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
Now, when a religious student (*brahmacārī*) engages in sexual intercourse with a woman, he is called an *avakīrṇin*.
For him, this rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed:
having tied a cord of *darbha* grass to the *avakīrṇin*, [he recites] "That which, O Goddess... (6.63).
Thus he pours [the seed]. KauśS_5,10{46}.19.
Having thus sprinkled [the water] from a vessel that has been filled by means of a ladle.
Having sprinkled [the student] with water for pacification as prescribed by the mantras,
he ties a cord of *darbha* grass around the neck of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) and offers sesame seeds with the hymn beginning "That which the goddess Nirṛti...
Having tied a cord of *darbha* grass around the neck of the religious student, he then offers rice with the hymn beginning "That which the goddess Nirṛti...".

Having tied a darbha rope around the neck of the *avakīrṇin* (the one who has broken his vow of chastity), having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* offerings, and having poured water from a vessel over him while reciting the hymn "That which is yours, O Goddess," he then sprinkles him with that darbha rope; thereafter, he releases him with the words "That which is yours, O Goddess. Then follows the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).

Having tied a *darbha* cord around the neck of the *avakīrṇin*, he then prepares the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*). Then, having sprinkled [the person] with the hymn "ayatte devī," he releases the *darbha* cord with that same hymn.
The expiation for the *avakīrṇin* is completed.
In all cases, there is an option regarding the ritual acts.
There is no sequence anywhere either.
Now, the expiation for when the fire ignites by itself is stated:
"With the verse *saṃ samid* (RV 6.63.4), one offers barley into the fire that has ignited by itself.
One offers the barley with the ṛc verse beginning *saṃ samid*.
With the verse "saṃ samid," he offers sesame seeds.
If the fire ignites by itself, then this rite is performed;
when it has ignited by itself, there is peace.
Now, the pacification regarding the utterance of the word "Agni" is stated: [He drives away the *rakṣas* from the fire;
thus, he is "driving away" (*sedhantam*). *KauśS* 5.10.23.
With the verse "Agni, the Rakṣases," he worships Agni; this is the pacification for the extinguishing of the fire.
[Regarding the phrase "yadasmṛti" (7.111), which means "if the message has not been delivered"]: now, if the message is forgotten, one worships the fire with the verse beginning "yadasmṛti.
If one does not deliver the message either in the village or at home, then this is the expiation.
Now, the pacification for one—whether a woman or a man—who is born under an inauspicious lunar mansion (*pāpanakṣatra*) is described:
[With the hymn *pratno hi* (RV 6.110), for one born under an inauspicious mansion, using the *mūla* constellation].

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, having bound muñja-grass ropes around his neck and his feet, he then pours water into a jar while reciting the hymn *pratno hi*, consecrates it, and places a blade of *darbha*-grass into the jar.
Having thrown [the items] into it, he then consecrates [the sacrificer].
Then follows the *abhyātāna* rites and the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
He places the noose around the neck upon the river-foams, with the mantra: "The foams of the rivers" (6.113.2).
With the second half-verse, he throws the waist-knot into the middle of the water.
It is heard that there is fault regarding one's mother, father, and brothers; therefore, a propitiatory rite (śānti) must be performed during an inauspicious lunar mansion (pāpanakṣatra).
Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Citrā, Svāti, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Śatabhiṣaj, and Bharaṇī—these are the inauspicious lunar mansions.
This rite is for one who is born under these [asterisms], specifically at the junction of the cheek and the joint;
this rite is performed under the asterism Mūla.
That which is to be done according to the ritual manual (kalpa) of the asterism is now described.

Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he pours [the offerings] over the rice cooked with milk and honey while reciting the hymn beginning with "For he is ancient" (*apratno hi*), consecrates it, and eats it.
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.
In this ritual procedure, the specific distinction is that he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with its roots and places the fuel-stick (*idhma*) together with its roots.
Everything stated in the *Nakṣatrakalpa* is to be applied at the appropriate time;
this is what is taught in the *Nakṣatrakalpa*.
These [rites] are completed for one born under an inauspicious asterism (*pāpanakṣatra*).
This is the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) declared in the *Nakṣatrakalpa*:
namely, these three—the ritual bathing (*āplāvana*), the sprinkling (*avasecana*), and the consumption of milk-rice (*kṣīraudanaprāśana*).
Alternatively, having consecrated water with the hymn beginning "For he is ancient" (*apratno hi*), one sprinkles it upon the head of one born under an inauspicious asterism.
These are the three rites.
The pacification for those born under inauspicious asterisms is complete.
Now, if one performs a marriage, the establishment of the sacred fires, or an initiation while his elder brother is still living, the expiation for that is stated:
[mā jyeṣṭham (6.112), trite devāḥ (6.113)].

Thus, having tied the elder brother who has married before his younger brother and the younger brother who has married before his elder brother at the edge of water with Muñja grass on the joints [of the wood], he causes them to be submerged with tufts of Piñjūla grass.
He sprinkles [it]. KauśS 5.10.27.
Having tied the northern nooses to the froth of the rivers with the verse, "The froths of the rivers" (6.113.2), he causes them to float away.

Having performed the *tantra* ritual, having poured water into a jar while reciting the two hymns "O Jyeṣṭha" and "The gods in Trita," and having consecrated it with mantras, he then binds it with nooses made of *muñja* grass and causes it to float away using that jar together with *darbha* grass.
Then follows the *uttaratantra*.
With the half-verse beginning "The froth of rivers," he places the *uttarapāśa* upon river-froth.
Having taken the *adharapāśas*, he enters into the middle of the river and casts them in silently.
[And with all the hymns addressed to the waters (apām sūkta):
Having consecrated the water with the two hymns "Mā jyeṣṭham" and "Trite devāḥ," he then binds [the victim], and thereafter sprinkles [it].
The releasing of the noose is as before.

Having performed the ritual procedure (*tantra*) up to the *abhyātāna* hymns, he pours water from all the *apām sūkta* hymns beginning with "The mothers go" (*ambayo yanti*) into the jar, consecrates it with mantras, and causes [the person] to be immersed.
This is the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratatra*).
[This concludes] the expiation for the elder brother whose younger brother marries before him and for the younger brother who so marries.
Having consecrated water with all the hymns dedicated to the waters, beginning with "The mothers come" (*ambayo yanti*), he sprinkles [it].
The expiation for the elder brother whose younger brother marries first and the younger brother who so marries is concluded;
it applies separately to each of the two.
Now, when the teacher has died, this rite is performed: [the mantra recited at the *devaheḍana* sacrifice]. (KauśS 5.10)
To the teacher. KauśS 5.10.31.
He should place [the bricks].
With the *anuvāka* "devaheḍana" (6.114–124), he offers clarified butter with the *sruva*-ladle.
When the teacher who maintained the sacred fires has died, this rite is performed.

Now, regarding that food which is intended for one whose disposition is like a pit (khadāśaya), excluding the gods and the ancestors, and which is prepared through a sacrificial rite—that is described as follows:
"He pours it into the pit-dispositioned one. (KauśS 5.10.33)
He sacrifices to Vaivasvata.

He gives four handfuls of rice. With the section beginning "O gods, whatever offense against the gods," having taken out food from the pit for the sword, he offers one spoonful; there is an option regarding the ritual framework (*tantra*).
There is an oblation of barley for each verse.
Having performed the *pākayajña* dedicated to Vaivasvata up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers the *caru* with the section beginning, "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods...
This is the expiation for one who has dug his own pit.
The subsequent ritual procedure (uttara-tantra) begins with the Pārvaṇa [Śrāddha] and other rites.
Having consecrated the food placed in the skull-bowl (khadānna), measured in four bowls, with the Anuvāka beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam," he then gives it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the rite for the pacification of the impurity resulting from the preparation of food in a skull-bowl.

Now, the pacification of the debt for a debtor whose creditor has died is stated: "When the creditor has died, he gives it to his offspring" (KauśS 5.10). [Regarding this, the *Mantra-brāhmaṇa* says: "'A loan that has not been repaid' (6.117–119)."
Having consecrated the substance with these three hymns, he gives it to his son;
thus he becomes free from debt.
[To one of the same lineage:
Having consecrated the object with the three hymns beginning with "That which was borrowed and not returned," he gives it to a kinsman;
thus he becomes free from debt.
[In the cremation ground, he pours it out.
Having consecrated the object with the three hymns beginning with "What was borrowed and not returned," he deposits it in the cremation ground of the creditor;
thus he becomes free from debt.
[And at a crossroads:
Having consecrated the object with the three hymns beginning with "That which was borrowed and not returned," he should cast it down at a village crossroads;
thus he becomes free from debt.

[He kindles the armpits. Having consecrated the object with the three hymns beginning with "That which was borrowed and not returned," and having thrown it into the blazing fire, he then becomes free from debt.
The rite for the pacification of debt-payment is complete.

If there is the fault of the body being drenched by rainwater from the sky, its pacification is stated as follows: "With [the hymn] *divo nu mām* (6.124), he washes himself with distinct drops of water. (KauśS 5.10.41)
He touches [the body] with the mantras as prescribed.
Having consecrated water with the hymn beginning "divo nu māṃ bṛhataḥ," he washes the body;
thus, the fault of droplets falling from the sky does not occur.
Having consecrated oil, all medicinal herbs, perfume, gold, or clothing with the hymn beginning "divo nu māṃ bṛhataḥ," one should rub them upon the body;
thereby peace is attained.
The pacification of the defects caused by drops from the sky is completed.
Now, if the first two upper teeth of a boy or a girl have grown out, there arises for the parents a fear of death; in that case, the following pacification rite is prescribed:
"Into whose mouth the two upper teeth grow first, like two tigers... (KauśS 5.10.43).
Into this [verse], one pours [the water].
With the hymn "The two tigers," he offers rice;
with the hymn "The two tigers," he offers barley;
with the hymn "The two tigers," he offers sesame seeds.
The conceptualization of tantra;
in all cases, there is no sequence.
[He causes it to bite with the mantra recited.

With the hymn "The two tigers" (*yau vyāghrau*), having combined rice, barley, sesame, and beans, he consecrates them with the mantra and causes it to bite with the teeth of a person born with the uppermost set of teeth.
He causes those who have been instructed to consume the water consecrated for pacification.
And [the verse for] the two parents.

Having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, having combined rice, barley, sesame, and beans, and having then prepared the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*), he should cook the *sthālīpāka*.
Then, having offered the *abhyātāna* oblations, he should pour [the remaining substances] into the *sthālīpāka* and consecrate it with the hymn beginning, "The two tigers (*ayau vyāghrau*)."
Then he feeds [the child] when the upper teeth have appeared,
or his parents feed him.
The cooking of the *sthālīpāka* is performed with water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*).
At the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the rite of the *śāntyudaka* (water of pacification) must be performed everywhere.
The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) begins with the *abhyātāna* hymns.
The pacification of the defect arising from the eruption of the last teeth is complete.
Now, if it is heard that a crow has settled upon one's head or body, the expiation for that defect is stated:
one washes away what was defiled by the black bird with the mantra, "This which Kṛṣṇa... (TS 7.64).
Having consecrated water with the two verses beginning "idaṃ yatkṛṣṇaḥ," he washes his body; thus, the fault incurred by sitting upon a crow does not occur,
or he performs a ritual bath.
[Having wiped him, he carries fire around him.
Having consecrated a firebrand with the two verses beginning "That which is black," he carries fire around the man who has been wiped by the mouth of a crow;
having whirled it above, he casts it far away.
The pacification of the fault of sitting like a crow is complete.

Now, the pacification of the defect of contact is stated: [With the verse beginning "pratīcīnaphalaḥ" (7.65), he offers fuel-sticks of *apāmārga* while using *apāmārga* as the sacrificial fuel. (KauśS 5.10.49)

In the ritual procedure for the clarified butter (*ājyatantra*), beginning with the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), one places an *apāmārga* fuel-stick (*idhma*) in the position of the usual fuel. Then, having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, one offers *apāmārga* fuel-sticks while reciting the three verses beginning with "pratīcīnaphalaḥ.
In all cases, the fuel-sticks are to be a span (*prādeśa*) in length. The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *abhyātāna* formulas.

Alternatively, when fire is kindled with Apāmārga wood, he offers Apāmārga fuel-sticks with the three verses beginning "pratīcīnaphalaḥ. Because this is a hand-homa (an offering made directly from the hand), there is no requirement for the ritual framework (tantra). In all diseases—whether caused by black teeth, deformed nails, impotence, or fever—and in all contagions and afflictions, one is liberated from all defects through the use of Apāmārga and other such substances.
The section on the pacification of defects in association is concluded.
Regarding the passage "yadarvācīnam" (KauśS 5.10),
he consecrates the water with the Ṛgvedic verse "yadarvācīnam" and causes [the person] to sip it.
Having spoken a falsehood, he performs the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having engaged in falsehood for the sake of trade, one performs the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
thus, the fault of falsehood does not occur.
The rite for pacifying the fault of speaking untruth is completed.
[With the verse,] "That which is thine, O Earth" (KauśS 12.1.35),
he digs. Wherever he digs— in a house-treasure, in a post-hole, or for the purpose of taking earth for bathing— he digs everywhere with this verse.
The digging of the earth according to the prescribed rite.
[Regarding the rule *yatta ūnam* (ŚŚS 12.1.61), one pours [the grain] together.
With the verse *yatta ūnam*, one fills the house and so forth; everywhere, filling is performed according to this procedure.
In digging, no fault of digging occurs.
In filling [the pit], no fault of filling occurs.
Thus concludes the rite for pacifying through digging and filling.
Now the pacification of ill omens is described: "Prehi pra hara" (Go forth, strike!)—these verses from the *kāpiñjala* hymn serve as propitiatory rites for well-being.
Go forth, strike out, or burn away from our houses for our well-being; O Kapiñjala, speak auspiciously to us with your hundred feathers.
Speak auspiciously from the south; speak auspiciously from the north; speak auspiciously to us from the east; speak auspiciously from the west, O Kapiñjala.
Speak auspiciously from the south; speak auspiciously from the north; speak auspiciously to us from the front; speak auspiciously from behind, O Kapiñjala!
Speak auspiciously regarding our sons; speak auspiciously regarding our homes;
speak what is auspicious for us; speak what is auspicious and fearlessness for us.
O Śakuni, as you speak, utter auspicious words; sitting silently, be mindful of our well-being.
When you fly up and cry out like a karkari-bird, may we, blessed with brave sons, speak loudly at the assembly.
"You celebrate the youth of those who have conquered, like the drum of the victors;
O Kapiñjala, speak auspiciously for us with your hundred feathers"—thus there are the *kāpiñjala* benedictions.
With the six-verse hymn beginning "Go forward, strike down the forest fires," one mutters [this] upon hearing an ill-omened sound, after the cry of a Kapiñjala bird has been heard.

Whether hearing the cries of birds in a village or a forest, or speaking angrily oneself, or hearing improper words from another, or dwelling with cattle, or in the habitation of owls or pigeons— whether in the east or the north— he becomes censured by the world.
Whatever is contrary to worldly norms, whether seen or heard, if one recites [this mantra] everywhere, it becomes a source of well-being.
One who desires well-being constantly mutters the hymn beginning with "prehi pra hara. This concludes the section on constant recitation for the sake of well-being.
The ritual for pacifying the ill omen of a bird's cry is completed.

"O iron one, you who swallow the brown man as he sleeps, lying down, having come to him—Varuṇa has placed us around with a spell of iron and armor of stone. With this verse, he lies down in the open air; he lies down in the open air.
For when he sleeps in the open space—whether in the forest, in a house, in an empty house, or on a mountain—he sleeps after muttering the verse beginning, "O iron one, you who swallow the brown one."

If the royal army sleeps in the sky [or] in the forest, one should perform this rite; the occasional rites must necessarily be performed. If they are not performed, there will be the destruction of wealth, grain, cattle, and so forth.

Therefore, the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites must be performed— such as those beginning with "A cloud-born one, O you who bring the rainy season" (*KauśS* 38.1). Furthermore, regarding portents (*adbhuta*), such as those concerning rain and yakṣas, these occasional rites must certainly be performed.
If [the rite] is not performed, a fault arises in the house, the village, the town, or the district.

The engagement in sacrifice (*ijyā*) is for the sake of generating intelligence, the prosperity of the village, all forms of prosperity, concord, eloquence, victory, royal affairs, rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), rites for women, auspiciousness (*svastyayana*), longevity, and other desired objects;
if there is a desire for such desired objects, then at that time there is engagement [in sacrifice].
Alternatively, if there is no desire [to perform it], one should not employ it;

however, rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) are obligatory (*nitya*). For there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in the non-performance of obligatory and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
And so it has been said:
"One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to destroy transgressions.
The occasional rites have been described according to the sequence of mantras in the Saṃhitā injunction."
O Kauśika, the ritual application of mantras is concluded because it has been recited by a Brāhmaṇa; thus the occasional rites are finished.
For the sake of awakening all knowledge, the Ṛṣi has proclaimed this higher cognition (vijñāna).
In the fifth [chapter], there are incidental teachings for the destruction of wicked faults.
The Tenth Section (Kaṇḍikā) // KKp_46 //
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Kauśikapaddhati.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
[Rites of Sorcery]. Now, the sorcery (abhicāra) prescribed in the Atharvaveda, which follows in due order, is described.
In the Mīmāṃsā, the practice of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is prohibited;
for it is stated that "Dharma is a purpose characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*, Jaiminisūtra 1.1.2).
Thus, the practice of violence (*hiṃsā*) is forbidden.
Furthermore, the practice of *abhicāra* (malevolent magic) has been established regarding rebirth;
and in the *Manusmṛti*, *abhicāra* is prescribed by such passages as, "A Brāhmaṇa shall never be a performer of [such rites].
Therefore, the Śruti of the Atharvāṅgirasa states that one should perform *abhicāra*.
Furthermore, a fault is heard [in the scriptures]:
"One who practices [forbidden acts] toward the six [classes of people] falls," says Manu.
And it has been stated in the Mīmāṃsā that "Smṛti is authoritative."
Therefore, the prescribed rite of exorcism (abhicāra) must be performed.
In rites of sorcery, one should use sacrificial grass made of reeds that is cut off at both ends.
From the south, he brings the ritual materials belonging to the Aṅgirases.
The ritual requisites as described in the *Āṅgirasakalpa* are to be understood [here].
One should construct a pavilion in the southern direction.
The performance should take place under the asterism Kṛttikā, or during the dark fortnight, at night, or when the moon is eclipsed.
There, the preceptor should have a pavilion constructed according to the prescribed rule;
it should be provided with banners and arches, and its entrance is traditionally said to be on the south.
[The iṅgiḍa-oil.
The iṅgiḍa-oil is mixed with poison.
savyāniṃ // KauśS_6,1{47}.4 //
They end toward the south. // KauśS_6,1{47}.5 //
On a saline wasteland sloping toward the south, he performs [the rite] facing the south.
Those accompanied by fires. KauśS 6.1.7.
The oblations preceded by "O Agni, that heat of thine" (2.19–23) [are performed]. KauśS 6.1.8.
"O Agni Jātavedas, act thus for us" (5.29.2, 3)—with these verses, the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāgau*) are offered. *Kauśika Sūtra* 6.1.9.
The concluding oblations (*saṃsthita-homa*) are performed with the mantra *niramuṃ nude* (6.75). KauśS_6,1{47}.10.

[In the case of] the *kṛttikās*, the *rohiṇīs*, the *ārdrās*, and the *āpyas* [nakṣatras], one should everywhere recollect the formula beginning with "So be it, O Agni" (*tathā tad agne*). Having performed the rites up to the *abhyātānas*, one recites: "Dūṣyā, you are Dūṣi" (*dūṣyā dūṣir asi*).
Having consecrated the *tilakamaṇi* with this hymn (*sūkta*) by pouring oblations over it, he ties it on;
the patron, the performer, and all the members of the assembly tie it on for the sake of self-protection.
Now the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is described:
[Bharadvāja Pravraska cuts the staff for Aṅgiras.

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, in the forenoon, having performed the rites up to the *abhyātāna* formulas, he recites the hymn beginning with "Heaven and Earth, the wide mid-air" (2.12).
The statement "gold and silver" is well-said;
by means of these two, the artisan cuts—that is, fells—the bamboo pole.
With the verse "From death am I... (6.133.3), he places the obstructing fuel-sticks.
He places the obstructing fuel-sticks with the ṛc, "From death am I...".

Having performed the *ājya*-tantra, he takes a gem made of gold, silver, iron, and a pair of black *kṛṣṇala* seeds, strings it with a triple cord, heats it over the fire, consecrates it with the hymn beginning "Nine vital breaths" (*anava prāṇān*), and ties it on.

[The Ritual of the Godāna: Now follows the godāna.
One should perform the godāna ceremony at one year of age, or according to the family custom.
Now we shall describe the ritual for the Godāna:
intending to perform the Godāna with the verse "Bestower of Life" (Āyurdā), he prepares the necessary materials.

Having placed to the west a fire made of *amṛtā*, *oja*, *mānī*, *dūrvā*, *akarṇa*, and *aśmamaṇḍala* wood, along with a lump of bull-dung, six tips of *darbha* grass, a bronze vessel, two large garments, pure clarified butter, pacifying herbs, and a new water-pot; and having added fuel from a pacifying tree to the east of the fire—*KauśS_7,4*.3.

A king who desires power must always [be vigilant].
[Regarding the rite for one desiring trade success, beginning with "indramaham" (3.15):

Then follows the *Uttara-tantra*:
there is the acquisition of wealth, gems, grain, and sons through trade and so forth; everything pertaining to commerce becomes exceedingly successful, therefore one should perform [this rite].
One worships Indra with the hymn (*sūkta*) beginning, "Indra, I [praise] the merchant."
Desirous of trade;
desirous of goods such as horses and so forth.
Lead us across with your protection;

With the two hymns, "Lead him upward" and "He who [is hostile] to us, O Brahmanaspati," he offers a *caru* oblation to Indra according to the *pākayajña* ritual procedure.
The *Uttaratantra*:
one who desires a village;

He who desires a village.

In the Pākayajña ritual, one desiring a village offers a pap-oblation (caru) dedicated to Indra with the verse "Indraḥ sutrāmā. One desiring a village also worships Indra with the verse "Indraḥ sutrāmā."
One who desires a village.
[The conclusion of the prosperity of the village.
With the two hymns beginning "Lead him upward" (*ud enam uttaraṃ naya*), he offers fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood; there is an option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
One who desires a village offers fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood with the two hymns beginning with "Lead him upward" (*ud enam uttaraṃ naya*).
One who desires a village.

With the same two hymns, "Lead him upward" and "He who [is] for us, O Brahmaṇaspati," he offers coverings for the assembly halls.

[For one desiring fame, with the hymn beginning "May Indra not leave us without fame" (6.58):

Alternatively, one who desires glory worships Indra with the hymn consisting of the three verses beginning "ayaśasaṃ mendraḥ"; the meaning is that he becomes glorious, shining forth like the sun.
"May the waters be for me"— with this [verse], he desires to expand.

With the two hymns, "I have brought thee hither" and "Firm is the sky," he worships Indra,

The meaning is stability.
One who desires well-being should recite the hymns beginning with "tyamū ṣu" (7.85), "trātāram" (7.86), and "ā mandraiḥ" (7.117).
One who desires well-being worships Indra with the two *ṛc* verses, "atyamū ṣu" and "trātāram," according to the *pākatantreṇa* ritual procedure. "Svasti" is a name for non-destruction.

With the hymn consisting of three verses beginning with "Fearlessness, O Heaven and Earth," he worships or pays homage to the Seven Sages in each direction,

With the three-verse hymn beginning "Thou art a hawk," he worships or pays homage to the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) facing each direction,

Or, staying in one place,

[To the north, there is the handing over of the staff to one who has been initiated or to a religious student (brahmacārin).
With the hymn consisting of three verses beginning with "Thou art a hawk," he hands over the staff to the religious student.

In all cases, the sacrifice is performed according to the procedure for the Darśapūrṇamāsa. In rites for pacification, prosperity, and malevolent magic, one should not wear a turban during any ritual action.
In all rites, one should place the *śāntikalaśa* (peace-pitcher) on the northern side of the pavilion.

In the forenoon, having placed fuel facing eastward outside the peaceful tree, he should kindle it.

Having offered the daily *purastāddhoma* oblations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions, he then places the primary water-vessel (*udapātra*)—which is made of *jāmbūnada* gold—on the altar outside the *brahman* priest's position; one is to the south and the other is further inside, whichever side he intends to perform his duties from.

Having bent his right knee, facing the Aparājita direction, and being either stooping, or using a fist, or an open palm, or a hollowed cupped hand, he should offer a fourth portion with whichever [hand] he intends to cook [the oblation].

With a single *śarāva* measure, he pours out four *śarāva* measures [of grain], saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I pour thee out, acceptable, for the seers, for the descendants of seers, for the one seer.

Then he pours it out, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable, for the seers, for the descendants of seers, for the one seer."
"May the Vasus offer you with the Gāyatrī metre;

With the verse beginning "upaśvase," he scatters [the earth] while lifting it up;

[He anoints the cooking-pot with the mantra: "Thee, the earth, upon the earth" (KauśS 8.2.30); [he recites:

With the verse "Commanded by the ṛṣis" (Ṛgveda 10.97.15), he draws water away from the water-jar; that is, with this foot of a verse, he consecrates the wife as she is being drawn away from the water-jar.
Having placed the two strainers between [the vessel and the water], according to the rules: "Pure, purified" (11.1.17) and "Purified by means of purifiers" (12.3.25).
He pours water. KauśS 8.2.34–35.
The *tantra* for the Svarga and Brahmaudana [offerings] is as follows.
In the case of a combination of all three humors, one should sprinkle water measured by a *brahmaudana* into two parts.
As many grains of rice as there may be, one should neither pour water over them nor sprinkle it against them.
"If you should pour splendor upon me, as well as glory," with these words the Brahman makes the sacrificer recite.
Then he should sprinkle [the water].
One should sprinkle [the water] with the two verses, "Swell up" (ā pyāyasva) and "May thy milks" (saṃ te payāṃsi).
Swell up; let virile power come to you from every side, O Soma;
be present at the gathering of strength.
"May thy milks come together, and likewise thy strengths, and thy virile powers that overcome the enemy.
Swelling for the sake of immortality, O Soma, place in heaven the highest glories.
[KauśS 8.9.4–10] While pouring water into the jar after having placed a strainer within it, one should recite these three lines beginning with "Pure and purified."
With the verse "Of the cooked rice," he consecrates the giver;
he should pour out a measured amount of water in portions.
He should not pour too little, nor should he pour too much, according to the quantity of rice grains there may be.
If he sprinkles [the water] upon [the sacrificer], the Brahman priest should cause the sacrificer to recite: "May splendor and glory be in me.
Then, if he sprinkles [the water] back [upon the vessel], he should sprinkle it back with the two verses: "Swell up" (ā pyāyasva) and "May thy milks unite" (saṃ te payāṃsi).
Having washed them in those waters with the formulas "Purified by Brahmā" (ĀpŚS 11.1.18) and "The drops have been counted" (ĀpŚS 12.3.28),
he pours the rice grains into them. (KauśS 8.2.36)
Having washed the grains in those waters with the verse, "Purified by Brahmā," the donor pours the rice into the cooking pot.
With the formulas "Spread wide" (11.1.19) and "They lift up" (12.3.29),
he cooks it. *Kauśika Sūtra* 8.2.37.
With the half-verse, "uruḥ prathasva," he consecrates the sacrificer as he cooks the offering;
with the half-verse, "pitāmahāḥ pitaraḥ," he causes the giver to recite.
With the words, "Hand over the sickle" (12.3.31), he hands over a sickle for the purpose of gathering *darbha* grass.
He hands over a sickle for the purpose of gathering *darbha* grass.
With the mantra, "May the plants protect the joints" (ŚB 12.3.31), he cuts above the joints.
With the words, "Fresh is the sacrificial grass" (KauśS 12.3.32), he spreads the *barhis*;
having cut it above the joints and brought it silently, he places it to the north of the fire.
Then, the performer silently spreads [the grass] over that which was spread at the beginning, behind the fire.
With the words, "Arise, O altar" (11.1.21) and "O supporter,
support yourself" (12.3.35), he causes [the fire] to be lifted up. *Kauśika Sūtra* 8.2.41.
With the verse, "Arise, O altar," he consecrates the water-pot (kumbhī) as it is being lifted up by the wife.
With the mantra, "May you increase her with progeny," he consecrates the wife. With [the mantra], "Drive away the Rakṣas," he consecrates the water-pot.
With the words, "Grant her prosperity," he addresses the wife;
with the half-verse, "Equal in glory," he causes the giver to recite.
With the words, "Turn back," he causes the cooking pot to turn clockwise.
With the mantra "O tree, [upon thee] strewn... (12.3.33), he places the vessel upon the sacrificial grass (barhis).
With "Established by Truth" (11.1.23)...

With the words, "Spread [the underlayer] (upa stṛṇīhi)," he spreads an underlayer of clarified butter.

Having caused her to be milked with the formula "The first has approached her," he pours water over it as previously described.
The first one has come forward, about to be milked, she who bears all sacrifices and belongs to the All-Gods.
Let her loose toward her calf; the lowing cow bellows. Having been released, she is well-disposed and utters the sound *hiṅ*.
Bind the calf; address him as she enjoys him. Having cleansed yourself, sit down as the milker of the cow and milk her.

"O Irā, swelling for us with rice-porridge, with sweet drink, ghee, exhilaration, and a portion of food—may she, together with her calf, the good milker, run along the first path here, given by Yama, the King.
Given not too hastily, she has come here first; unite the cow of all forms with her calf. [KauśS 8.3.18–21]
With the half-verse, "She has come near, about to be milked," he consecrates the cow as she approaches.

He causes the cow to be milked with the half-verse beginning with "milk," accompanied by the appropriate words. With the half-verse, "Let her run," he consecrates the cow as she is being released.

Having thus caused her to be milked, he pours rice into the milk.

In that case, if one does not apply salt to the mere surface with the fingernail, by that very act his food becomes wasted.
An unwashed garment lies to the south.

[Recite] the *tantra* and the *sūkta* verse by feet during the bath: "O you two wings, that which you stood upon..."

Those two wings of yours, O Bird, which are ageless and with which you strike down the *rakṣas*— with those may we go upon the path to the world of the well-done, where the ancient *ṛṣis*, first-born of old, abide.
When you stood upon the back of heaven in the midst of the sky, O Odana.

"Spread wide with great majesty" (11.1.19);

Now the ritual for the hands is described: the donor, having washed his hands with the mantra "For the sake of action, O left hand," and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the *jīvā* verses, sits facing north with the mantra beginning "O son of a remarried woman" (*ahe daidhiṣavya*) and ending with "the seeker of prey" (*vimṛgvarīm*, ŚB 12.1.29).

O Agni, be our closest relative, our protector, and our gracious guardian.
As such, O most radiant and shining one, we now entreat you for the welfare of our friends.

"This woman" (*iyaṃ nārī*), another person causes the wife to lie down with the deceased for the purpose of *sahagamana* (following in death).
Thus it is stated in the Purāṇa.
By dying together with her husband, she shall attain infinite worlds;
for sixty thousand years, she is honored in the heavenly realm.
[With the words] "Arise" (udīrṣva), he causes him to stand up.
Now, if he stands up, then he causes him to rise while consecrating him with the verse beginning with "Arise."

Taking the gold that he wears in his right hand, having sprinkled it with clarified butter and consecrated it with the mantra "This is gold" (KauśS 18.4.56), he causes the eldest son to take it up using the half-verse beginning with "This is gold."
With the half-verse beginning "svargaṃ yataḥ" (18.4.56), he wipes his right hand;
with the half-verse "svargaṃ yataḥ," the son wipes the hand of the deceased.
[With the mantra "The staff from the hand" (18.2.59), he causes the Brāhmaṇa to take it.
With the ṛc verse "The staff from the hand," the son takes the bamboo staff from the hand of the deceased.
The agent [is established] everywhere by means of the mantra.
Regarding the rule *dhanurhastāt* (Pāṇini 18.2.60), which pertains to a Kṣatriya: with the verse beginning "dhanurhastāt," he takes the bow from the hand of the Kṣatriya.
[Regarding "aṣṭrām" for a Vaiśya: KauśS 11.50.
Having modified the mantra to "āṣṭraṃ hastāt," the son of a Vaiśya takes the staff from the hand of the deceased together with the Vaiśya's splendor, luster, and strength.
With the half-verse, "This for the ancestors" (*idaṃ pitṛbhyaḥ*), he spreads bundles of *darbha* grass upon the funeral pyre.
"In that case, one should place him upon his back with [the verses]: 'The sacrificer has ascended the thought, Agni... (KauśS 11.1).
There, one places the deceased upon his back on the funeral pile;
the performer, standing at a distance, consecrates him with these two ṛg-verses.
With the mantra "In the eastern direction" (KauśS 18.3.30), he should perform this for each direction;
he should place the head of the deceased toward the southeast.
With these Ṛg-verses beginning with "In the eastern direction, thee," he consecrates the deceased while he is still lying in his place.
"Not so," says Uparibabhru. Some make the head face each of the cardinal directions; that is not so, says the teacher Uparibabhru.
[He recites the mantra:
"He should perform the consecration with a mantra"; this is the meaning.
Then he places seven pieces of gold upon his seven vital breaths with the formula: "Thou art immortality; for the sake of immortality, place [me] in immortality."
The mantra is to be repeated seven times;
this should be applied even to a single fire as far as possible.
The first section (kaṇḍikā) of the eleventh chapter.
[Now, for one who has established the sacred fires, having spread a black antelope skin with the hair on the inside upon darbha grass...
KauśS 11.2.1] This refers to one who has established the sacred fires.
The eyes, the ears, the nostrils, and the mouth are the seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
For one who has maintained the sacred fires, having spread a black antelope skin with the hair on the inside upon darbha grass;
[There, having laid him down on his back... Having laid the deceased there on his back.
Then, having filled his sacrificial vessels with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), he places them down in their proper order.
Taking four [portions], they place them upon the limbs of the deceased.
The arrangement of the sacrificial vessels is stated:
one places the *juhū* ladle in the right hand. *Kauśika Sūtra* 11.2.4.
The *upabhṛt* [ladle] on the left.
[He places] the *dhruvā* ladle on the neck, the *agnihotrahavaṇī* in the mouth,
and the *sruva* ladle for the *agnihotra* in the two nostrils; having filled them with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), he deposits them.
He consecrates them with the mantra: "The *juhū* supported the sky;
the *dhruvā*, ascend" (*KauśS* 11.2.7).
"The *juhū* supported the sky" is one verse.
"Ascend, O firm one"— with this single verse,
he consecrates the vessels;
the mantra is recited once.
The *prāśitraharaṇa* [ladle] is placed on the forehead.
But two [should do so] silently.
[With the verses] "This cup, O Agni... (RV 18.3.53–54), he places the *iḍā*-cup upon the head;
having placed the *iḍā*-vessel on the head, he consecrates it with the two verses beginning, "This cup, O Agni... (RV 18.3.53–54).
[With the verse] "The gods [accept] the sacrifice" (18.4.2–4), he places the sacrificial cake on his chest.
With the three verses beginning "The gods [accept] the sacrifice," he consecrates the sacrificial cake on the heart, provided that there is a sacrificial cake.
On the right side [he places] the wooden sword (sphya), on the left the fire-stirring stick (upaveṣa).
[In the belly, the flour-vessel.
In the belly, the vessel for the flour.
[Regarding "the two kneecaps, the mortar, and the pestle" (KauśS 11.2.13):
The knee is well known as the *aṣṭhīvat*; there, one places the mortar and the pestle.
[The cart on the two hips // KauśS_11,2{81}.14 //] A cart in the region of the hips.
[The other sacrificial vessels between the thighs.

Between the thighs, he should place the other sacrificial vessels— namely, the *praṇītā* cup, the *hotṛ* cup, the *brahman* cup, the *yajamāna* cup, the *antardhānakaṭa*, the *pūrṇapātra*, the *ṣaḍavatta*, and so forth— having filled them with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), silently.
A winnowing basket at the two feet.
[They bring earthen vessels.
One should place the earthen vessels in the middle of the water.
They place iron [objects] down;
he silently buries those made of copper in the ground.
"Amā putrā ca dṛṣat.
One should place upon the ground the stone-made items, such as the axe, the sickle, the rib-bone, and so forth, as well as the lower and upper grinding stones (*dṛṣad-upalaka*).
This applies to both those who maintain a single fire and those who have established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).

Then, while both [the bridegroom and the groom] look on, he recites over the hindmost cow as it is being led around counter-clockwise: "Behold the young woman, O inviolable one, who knows [her place]" (RV 10.183.3–4). KauśS 11.2.20.
With the two verses beginning with "I saw a young woman," he consecrates the cow as it is led around the side of the altar in a counter-clockwise direction.
[They cause her to sit down while striking her with the southwest (the direction of Nirṛti) at the region of the hips.
Having caused a cow to be struck with a club in the southwest region—that is, at the region of the hips—they kill her;
it should be done in such a way that the cow, while being struck, sits down.
This rite belongs to the son born of a Śūdra woman;
no one else may perform the killing.
Having extracted the two kidneys from behind it, they place them in her hands with the mantra: "Run past the two dogs" (ŚB 18.2.11–13).

Having extracted the two kidneys from the region of the cow-pen, he places the right one in the right hand of the deceased and the left one in the left hand— the right in the right, the left in the left.
Standing at a distance, the performer consecrates them with the three verses beginning with "ati drava."
[In the heart, the heart.
He places the cow's heart into the heart of the deceased.
[With the verse "Agni’s armor" (18.2.58), they cover the mouth with a seven-holed omentum.
With the ṛg-verse "Agni’s armor," he covers the face of the deceased with a seven-holed omentum.
According to the body, [he places] the limbs. KauśS 11.2.26.
With the right [hands] the right [objects], and with the left [hands] the left.
Having covered the cow-stall with a hide whose head and feet are attached,
and having covered the deceased with a hide whose head and feet are attached.
With the verses "The goat is the portion" (18.2.8–9) and "Let them carry thee up" (18.2.22), he binds the goat on the right side.
Then, with these three verses— two beginning with "The goat is the portion" and one beginning with "Let them carry thee up"— he binds the goat animal on the southern side of the fire-altar.
Just as it is burned, so it is bound.
Regarding this, it is said:
"In that manner, O Māhakī, the unborn is slain and burned."

"From this indeed you were born; from you may he be born, for such-and-such, svāhā!"—with this mantra, the performer, remaining untouching, offers clarified butter while grasping the chest of the deceased who has been placed upon the single fire, or else the kinsmen offer it. Likewise, he offers into the fires with the mantras: "To Agni, svāhā! To Kāma, svāhā! To the World, svāhā!"* *KauśS 11.2.30–31.31*
Then he offers oblations in the Āhavanīya and other fires with the formula: "To Agni, svāhā! To Kāma, svāhā! To Loka, svāhā!
With the three utterances of "svāhā" beginning with "To Agni, svāhā," he offers clarified butter;
thus there are three oblations for each fire.
Some say [it should be performed] in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. KauśS 11.2.32.
They consider this to be a Khaṇḍakalpa;
the deceased is placed in the middle of the altar, and the fires are situated according to the cardinal directions.
"Do not burn him, O Agni" (18.2.4–7);
"Heat him for our welfare" (18.2.36);
Reciting "prajānantaḥ" (2.34.5), the youngest brother kindles the fire;
then the son offers the oblation into the fire.

Having offered the rice-ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased and having circled a stream of water counter-clockwise, he makes a sound three times over the deceased with water-jars and pours it upon the ground; then he offers fire.
Having recited these mantras himself, the performer [proceeds] with the four verses beginning with "mainam agne."

With the ṛc, "O heat, do not overheat," with the three verses beginning, "Take hold, O Jātavedas," and with the one verse, "Knowing [the way], may they receive [it]," the youngest son, or a member of the same lineage, or someone else, kindles the fire. Then, he offers clarified butter with the dipping-spoon (sruva) while reciting the Anuvāka beginning with "devaheḍanena."
While the ladle is aflame, he offers the Yāma oblations with the *sruva* spoon, [reciting]: "He who has gone forth upon the great slopes... (RV 10.14.1). KauśS 11.2.34.
"Yama was the first to find the path for us"—these two [verses] are the first ones. *Kauśika-sūtra* 11.2.35.
"Aṅgiraso naḥ pitaraḥ navagvāḥ"—these are the seven *saṃhitās*. 36. KauśS_11,2{81}.36.
"Whoever died first among mortals" (18.3.13);
"Those who are our father's fathers, those who are our grandfathers" (18.2.49)—these are the eleven [verses]. [KauśS 11.2.37]
When the funeral pyre has been set ablaze and is fully ignited, the performer offers the oblations to Yama with a ladle made of *khadira* wood while the fires have become unified;
this applies even if there was only a single fire.
The first position is that there are two verses, namely "pareyivāṃsam" and "yamo no gātum.
The second position is that there are seven verses taken together, beginning with "aṅgiraso naḥ pitaro navagvāḥ."

The two verses beginning with "pareyivāṃsam," the seven beginning with "aṅgiraso naḥ pitaraḥ," and the two beginning with "ye naḥ pituḥ pitaro ye pitāmahāḥ"— these eleven taken together constitute the third option.
He offers clarified butter with these combined,
according to one of the options.
Then seven, nine, eleven, or more Brahmins, seated facing the east, recite the entire section beginning with "o cit sakhāyam" (18.1–4),
just as in the case of the marriage ceremony.
[Now follow] the Sārasvata [offerings]. (KauśS 11.2.38)
Those seeking the gods invoke Sarasvatī; the ancestors invoke Sarasvatī; O Sarasvatī, you who have come on the same chariot [with them] (18.1.41–43).
"O Sarasvatī, in your sacred observances; this oblation, rich in ghee, is for you, O Sarasvatī" (7.68.1–2);
"May Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, [protect me]" (18.3.25). Thus [ends] KauśS 11.2.39.
To the south, on another [spot], the performer offers oblations.
Then the performer performs the *sārasvata* oblations with the verse:
"Those seeking the gods invoke Sarasvatī. This is one [verse].
"Sarasvatīm pitaraḥ havante" is one verse; "Sarasvati yā saratham" is one verse;
"Sarasvati vrateṣu te" is one verse.

With the verse "This is your oblation" (idaṃ te havyam), he offers one oblation; with the five verses beginning "Indra accompanied by the Maruts" (indro mā marutvān), he offers clarified butter into the fire-pile.
These belong to Sarasvatī.
To the south, the youngest son performs the Yāma-Sārasvata oblations;
then the performer [of the rite].
All oblations must be performed by one wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (pitryupavītī).
Or the Sārasvata rite must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī).
[All approach him, or three or more.
Then all the kinsmen approach with the section beginning, "O, even a friend" (RV 18.1–4).
Alternatively, [the verses] beginning with "The poets have a thousand paths" (18.2.18) and "Three steps" (18.3.40) follow.
Thus, when [the body] is being cremated, the kinsmen stand by in attendance.
Or rather, by those who perform the rites.
Having performed these [rites], one who is desirous [of success]... KauśS_11,2{81}.43.
From "Do not burn him, O Agni" (18.2.4) onwards, excluding "Release [him]" (18.2.10), up to "He who has a thousand paths" (18.2.18).
Thus [ends the section] from *ityātaḥ* (KauśS 11.2).

Alternatively, one may recite the verses beginning with "Do not burn him, O Agni" (*mā enam agne vi daha*) up to "He who has a thousand paths" (*sahasranīthāḥ*), omitting the single verse "Release him" (*ava sṛja*).
These are the verses to be performed.
With these [verses], they perform the ritual worship.
"With the fifteen verses beginning, 'Ascend, O Jātavedas, to the mother,' they worship the one who has established the sacred fires upon the altar.
With these fifteen Ṛgvedic verses beginning, "Ascend, O Jātavedas, to the mother," they pay homage to the one who has established the sacred fires at the fire-altar.
Alternatively, this rite is performed in a single fire for one who has maintained the sacred fires;
now, the rite for both cases is being described.
With the verse, "May Mitra and Varuṇa encompass me" (RV 18.3.12), he washes his hands; with this same verse, everyone washes their hands.
[With the verse, "May [the waters] refresh me with luster" (18.3.10), he sips water.
With the verse beginning "May [the waters] refresh me with luster," everyone causes him to sip water.
[With the verses beginning "vivasvān naḥ" (18.3.61–62),
the other performer offers an oblation to the north.
Thereupon, the performer offers with the two verses beginning "vivasvān naḥ," while the other performer offers to the north.
The rite of cremation is completed.
The second section (kaṇḍikā). // KKp_81 //

Now, the rite for peace (śānti) for those of the son’s lineage on the first day is described: [The younger ones perform the initial rites facing east, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin), and moving clockwise.
Having offered a handful of water to the deceased and having performed a bath, one should then carry out the ritual.
Whether they are of the same lineage or the younger sons,
all of them face eastward with their sacred threads over the left shoulder.
[Then he places seven pebbles each into their hands.
He places seven pebbles each into their hands.
[They walk away without looking back, scattering one of those [grains] with their left hand held downwards.
Whether it be women or a man, they scatter one of those [grains] starting from the youngest, using either the left or the right hand held downwards;
then they walk away without looking back.
He consecrates it with the *apāgha* verse. *KauśS 11.3* (82.4)
All walk in front of the Brahman priest.
Reciting "mā pra gāma" (13.1.59), they mutter the *vyāghāpāgha* formulas at the edge of the water.
Afterwards, he sprinkles [it]. // KauśS_11,3{82}.7 //
The eldest [son] is designated by the rule *uduttamam* (18.4.69).
The performer consecrates him with the hymn *apa naḥ śośucadagham* (4.33).
All the kinsmen walk in front, muttering the verse "mā pragāma" (may we not go astray).
The performer [of the rite] follows behind the kinsmen.
Purity is attained on the fourth day.
The officiant, standing at a distance, shall recite the mantra.
At the edge of the water, they mutter the *vyāhṛtis* and the *āghamarṣaṇa*.
As they go toward the water, [they recite]: "O gods... (3.31).
The Brahman priest mutters the two hymns beginning with "apa naḥ śośucat.
He [the sacrificer] recites the two hymns for the removal of misfortune and sin.
All the Brāhmaṇas themselves pour water over him with the hymn beginning with "uduttamam" and perform the ritual bath.
[With the words "payasvatīḥ" (KauśS 18.3.56), he scatters the *piñjūlī* blades as prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa.
All the Brāhmaṇas perform their bath with the verse beginning, "payasvatīroṣadhayaḥ."
Then the Brahman priest throws twenty-one blades of Darbha grass into a river or a lake.

Having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*) with *śāntyudaka* and having sprinkled it [over himself], he causes [the sacrificer] to cross the river with the verse, "The horse-possessing one" (*aśvāvatīm*).
Therein, he prepares the *śāntyudaka*.
He gives water for sipping to all of them.
Having sprinkled [them], he consecrates those crossing a river with the verse beginning, "aśvāvatīm."

"Having seen a constellation, he worships it with the mantra: 'May the appearance and the likeness of the constellations protect me. Standing outside and having seen a constellation, he worships it with the mantra: "Of those that are not constellations, may their appearance... and so forth.
Having placed śamyāka fuel-sticks on the fire, the Brahman priest mutters the prayers in front.

"May the god Manas speak for us, upon whom the three—gods, humans, and all cattle—depend. May he lead us with good guidance; may we not be delivered over to our enemy. Having sipped water for purification and sprinkled it [over themselves], they take *śāmyākī* fuel-sticks, and then everyone comes together.
Then, having become Brahmā, he mutters the mantra "yasya trayaṃ gatam" in front [of the fire].
Then, everyone performs the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the water of peace near the house.
"Free from dust" (nissālām): having sprinkled the dwelling of the hall with water. (KauśS 11.3.14)
With the verse "Bearing strength" (7.60.1–6), he causes [the bride] to step forward.
Having sprinkled the house with the mantra "Out from the house," the performer causes the kinsmen to enter the house with the six verses beginning with "Bearing strength."
He causes [the sacrificer] to touch the river, the cow, the fire, and the stone.
He causes him to touch those stalks of grass,
the cow, [the fire, and the stone].
The fire is either the common worldly fire or the single sacred fire;
and there is also a stone.
He causes these to be immolated.
[With the mantra: "Thou art barley; bar away from us hatred, bar away the enemy," they all touch the barley grains.
With the mantra "khalvakāsya," they touch the khalvakas and the kulattha beans.
With the two hymns "vi devāḥ" (3.31) and "apa naḥ śośucadagham" (4.33),
the performer places fuel-sticks of *śāmyākī* wood either in a common fire or in a single sacred fire.
For those belonging to the same lineage, the state of impurity lasts for four days.
[They consume their smoke.
Their kinsmen consume their smoke;
if it is the fire of the son, then [they consume it] in that same fire or in a common (laukika) fire.
This rite is performed on the first day;
this rite is completed.
Now, the ritual procedure for the second day is stated: "Whatever the flesh-eater may seize, if the flesh-eaters do not reach the end on the following day,
[may you] milk the bright milk from the sky's cloud, swelling with nourishment and strength."
"O waters, the womb of the waters; those which you have made for life, may they be sweet-flowing for you. With this verse, he pours the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice) into the fire.
Having kindled the fire with the verse "Homage to heaven," he offers the entire *sthālīpāka* as a single oblation near the burning fire;
there is no ritual sequence (*tantra*) required.
Or, at the time of cremation, he performs the offering of the entire pot-cooked oblation (sthālīpāka) all at once.

Or alternatively, having caused a cow suckling another's calf to be milked, he offers on her back with the single verse: "In Vaiśvānara I offer this oblation" (ŚŚ 18.4.35). Or rather, having caused a cow suckling another's calf to be milked, he offers on her back with the single verse beginning, "In Vaiśvānara the oblation."
In its milk. KauśS 11.3.23.
Some say it is a *sthālīpāka* (cooked offering in a pot). *KauśS* 11.3.24.
Some teachers maintain that [the rice] should be cooked;
thus the ritual on the second day is completed,
and on the third day there is no ritual.
The ritual for the fourth day is stated:
[With the verse beginning "ye agnayaḥ" (3.21), having stirred the mash with a ladle made of *pālāśa* wood, he offers the bones over the fire using two stirring-sticks made of *kāmpīla* wood.

With the ten-verse hymn beginning "ye agnayaḥ," having stirred the mash—that is, the barley-flour mash—with a ladle made of *pālāśa* wood, he should perform the offering over the bones verse by verse, using two stirring-sticks made of *kāmpīla* wood.
Having cut off portions as prescribed by the mantras beginning with "upa dyām" (18.3.5–6) and "śaṃ te nīhāraḥ" (18.3.60). KauśS_11,3{82}.26.

He sprinkles the bones of a Brāhmaṇa with milk mixed [with water], those of a Kṣatriya with honey mixed [with water], and those of a Vaiśya with water alone. With the two verses beginning "upa dyāmuṣa vetasam" and the one verse beginning "śaṃ te nīhāraḥ," he combines the water and milk for the medicinal herbs mentioned in the mantras, consecrates them, and sprinkles them over the bones of the Brāhmaṇa.
The medicinal herbs mentioned in the mantra are stated to be the cane (vetasa) and the karṇa.
And river-foam,
and *avakā*, and *agaruherukā*,
and great *dūrvā* grass.
And ākāśaphena,
and maṇḍūkaparṇī,
and śuktikā.
These are the herbs mentioned in the mantra; for a Kṣatriya, [the rite is performed] with honey and water using that same mantra, and those herbs mentioned in the mantra [are used];
for a Vaiśya, [it is performed] with water together with the herbs using that same mantra.

He consecrates with the mantra "Release [him]" (ava sṛja). The cremation of both one who maintains a single sacred fire (*ekāgni*) and one who maintains the established fires (*āhitāgni*) is consecrated with the verse beginning "Release [him]."
[With the verses] "May thy mind... (18.2.24) and "That limb of thine...
(18.2.26), he piles [the bones] line by line.
Then, having performed the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍapradāna*), the *sañcayaṇa-śrāddha*, and the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, he subsequently performs the *sañcayaṇa*.
Having consecrated the bones with these two verses, "May thy mind [not be disturbed]" and "Whatever limb of thine," he places them in the water-jar;
or, holding them with a leaf of the *pālāśa* tree, he does so verse by verse, foot by foot.
First, the skull-bones. KauśS_11,3{82}.30.
[Afterwards, having placed it in a jar, having scattered all fragrant powders over it, and having raised it with the *utthāpanī* verses, they should carry it away with the *hariṇī* verses.
Afterwards, he places it in the jar;
afterwards, he places the powders of all medicinal herbs in the jar; having raised the jar with the *utthāpanī* verses, they should carry it away with the *hariṇī* verses.
and "The watery one" (18.2.48–49).
"ita ete" (Pāṇini 18.1.61), "agnīṣomā" (Pāṇini 18.2.53),
and "idaṃ pūrvam" (Pāṇini 18.4.44).
Thus are the *utthāpanī* verses;
[they are recited] with the eight *hariṇī* verses beginning with "ati drava" (18.2.11–18).
With the verse "Mā tvā vṛkṣaḥ" (18.2.25), he places [the vessel] at the root of a tree;
with the verse "Mā tvā vṛkṣaḥ," he buries the jar containing the bones at the root.
With the verse, "Be soft for him" (RV 10.18.10), those who do not consume food for three nights perform their rites upon the ground;
or else, having consecrated [the object] with the verse "Be soft for him," if one buries it in the ground, then it is by means of this [verse].
The piling of the fire-altar is completed on the fourth day;
some perform the rites beginning with "The youngest first" (KauśS 82.1) and so forth on the fourth day.
In all cases, the ritual action belongs to both.
Thus says Māhaki: "For the one who maintains the domestic fire and the one who maintains the *agnihotra*, all the ritual actions are the same.
On the fourth day, some [perform] the "younger-first" rituals (*yavīyaḥprathamāni karmāṇi*).
They perform [these rites] here in both cases; and so says Yājñavalkya:
"Having sat at the door with neem leaves," and so forth; having become pure, one then gains the qualification for the ritual. Some perform everything exactly as the Sūtra is recited.
From that time onward, they perform auspicious rites for the members of the lineage.
Or according to the custom of his family:

having maintained the remainder of the *āvasathya* fire in the house, or having deposited the two kindling sticks (*araṇi*), the son—if he is one who has established the sacred fires—should perform the rite for pacifying the flesh-eating spirits (*kravyācchamana*) on the new moon day.
Then the kinsmen, abstaining from food for three nights, perform their obligatory, occasional, and optional rites.
"Some say it is ten nights. [KauśS 11.3.34]
Or according to the family custom.
Some say it is ten nights;
or according to the family custom.
