[After the third day, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* for Vaivasvata, he offers it with the mantra: "Vivasvān naḥ... (KauśS 18.3.61–62).

On the fourth day, having performed the collection of the bones (*asthisañcayana*) and returned home, the performer then cooks a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to the deity Vaivasvata; having completed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers [it] with the mantra "Vivasvān naḥ."
With two [verses], he offers two oblations, verse by verse.
With the two joined [mantras], he offers the third oblation.
[The fourth [offering] is for Anumati:
"To Anumati, svāhā!"—this is the fourth.
[Having sprinkled the remainder with the water of pacification and consecrated it, he causes him to consume it.

Having prepared the water of pacification, having sprinkled the remnants of the oblation and the *sthālīpāka* with the water of pacification, and having consecrated them with the two verses beginning "avivāsvān naḥ," he causes him to consume them.
Those who share the same *udaka* (libation) are those of the same lineage (*gotra*) within ten generations or seven generations; such are they who share the same *udaka*.
With the words, "Come forth,
O two cows" (RV 18.4.49), he yokes the two oxen;
then he gives the sacrificial fee.
With the verse, "Come forth, both of you," the performer consecrates and takes hold of the two bulls that carry the deceased.
The sacrificial fee consists of ten cows,
or an unlimited number, or twenty-two, according to one's ability.
"According to [the rule] *eyamagan* (ŚŚS 18.4.50), the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of at least ten cows.
With the verse beginning *eyamagan*, he consecrates and receives the sacrificial fee;
this rite takes place on the fourth day."
Or on the eleventh day.
The ritual procedure for the four-day period is completed.
Now, the *yamavrata* of the performer is described:
"The performer shall observe the *yamavrata* for twelve nights.
The performer shall observe the *yamavrata* for a period of twelve nights.
He should wear either a single garment or three garments.
He shall subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
"He should perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) in the evening and in the morning";
that is, he should bathe in the evening and in the morning.
The student observing the vow should sleep on the ground.
One should employ the *svastyayana* (auspicious) rites.
Having become invested with the sacred thread (*yajñopavītī*) in the evening and the morning, one should perform the ritual acts.
The *svastyayana* rites are now described.
The two verses beginning with "vivasvān naḥ" (18.3.61–62), the one verse beginning with "indra kratuṃ naḥ" (18.3.67), and [the verse] "prāsmat pāśān" (18.4.70).
This is one [verse]: "atyamū ṣu" (7.85),
"trātāram" (7.86),
and "ā mandraiḥ" (7.117).
Thus, with the verse "He who is in the fire" (7.87), with the verse "Salutation to Prāṇa" (11.4.1),
and [with the verse] "O Prāṇa, do not abandon me" (11.4.26).
One verse is "namaste ghoṣiṇībhyaḥ" (11.2.31), one verse is "svasti no astvabhayaṃ naḥ" (19.8.7), and [one] half-verse is "svasti no astvabhayaṃ naḥ."
One should recite these auspicious formulas (*svastyayana*), such as "The earth is peace" (19.9.14),
at the end of the recitation of the Yamaka section, during the performance of the final rites (*anteṣṭi*) and the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛmedha*), and throughout this entire section.
The collection of the bones is completed, as well as the funeral rites at the end and the piling of the vessels.
And the Yamavrata.
The third section (kaṇḍikā) of the eleventh [chapter].
Now the Pitṛmedha is described.
There is a Vedic injunction stating, "One should perform the Pitṛmedha after a year," or alternatively, "One should perform it within the year."
The times, beginning with the month of Māgha, will now be described: "Intending to establish the ancestors, he prepares the necessary materials" (KauśS 11.4).
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (pitryupavītī), he should perform the funeral rites and the ancestral ceremonies.
He causes eleven *caru* offerings to be prepared in vessels made of *cakra*-wood.
The *śatātṛṇṇa* and *sahasrātṛṇṇa*, the *pāśī*, the *mūṣa*, sand, a conch shell, a lotus root, powdered *śamī* leaves of all fragrant species, a boat made from a tree that has been pacified,
and a tripod— one should make two earthen vessels, one with a hundred holes and the second with a thousand holes; they should be easy to pour from.
Sikatāḥ (sand);
śaṅkhaḥ (conch shell) is well known;
śālūkāni (lotus roots) are well known.
The powder of all fragrant medicinal herbs, the powder of *śamī* leaves,
and a boat made from a *śānta* tree.
The three-footed [syllable] is Śivaya.

Two threads being unwound—one blue and one red; a cord for the left side; four stakes of the *śānta* tree and four enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *vāraṇa*, *śāmīla*, *audumbara*, and *pālāśa*; herbs for the *śānti* rite;
two worn-out garments being unwound;
and the blue and red threads are well known.
A rope twisted counter-clockwise;
four stakes of a tree with auspicious characteristics;
and four enclosing sticks.
The stakes and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are made from these trees: the *vāraṇa*, *śāmīla*, *audumbara*, or *pālāśa*;
or they may be from a tree that has been pacified.
There are two small leaf-cups from a pacified tree.
These materials are to be gathered;
such are the materials for the ancestral deposit.
Now, the time for depositing the ancestral offerings is stated:
"One should deposit them in the month of Māgha, thinking, 'May there be no sin (māgha) in the family. May there be no evil in the lineage.
One should deposit it on the new moon day of the month of Māgha.
"In autumn one should deposit it, thinking: 'May sin be pacified.'"
In the summer heat, one should place [the object], thinking, "May evil be consumed. *Kauśikasūtra* 11.4.7.
"One should deposit [the fire] on the new moon day, for on that day the ancestors truly come to be present. Alternatively, one may deposit it in autumn or during the summer heat;
thus the times for the depositing have been stated.
[Now follows the conclusion. That which is called the "bone-holding" is said to be that location.
[That which is] level, with its roots intact, not burnt, firmly established, and sloping toward the northeast. // KauśS_11,4{83}.10 //
Where the trees and medicinal herbs are free from thorns;
where the trees and medicinal herbs are peaceful—one should perform [the rite] there. One should prepare such a place as a site for the conclusion.
Thus ends the section on the place of cessation.
[For one desiring heaven, it should be elevated.
One should perform the piling of the altar so that it is elevated for one who desires heaven.
Now, this rite for the fourteenth day will be explained: "On the morrow, which is the new moon day, one causes a cow to be prepared.
On the morning of the new moon day on the morrow, one should perform the rite.
On the fourteenth day, one slaughters a cow; [in this case], there is no agent.
Having placed its left shoulder and its cooked portion [into the vessel].
He causes alms to be given.

Having set aside the flesh of her left thigh, the buttocks, the blood, the bile, the belly, and the internal organs, he should place the remaining flesh according to the prescribed rule for the *vaśā*;
its application will come first [at the beginning].
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is identical to the [Darśa-]Pūrṇamāsa sacrifice.
[Having performed the Yāmasārasvata oblations in the village (KauśS 11.4.16):
Having constructed a pavilion in the middle of the village and having performed the Yāmasārasvata oblations there with a single fire, one should churn the fire from the two kindling woods (*araṇī*).
Some omit the rite of slaughtering a cow, or the ritual procedure (*tantra*) itself.
Having performed the circumambulation of the site of the dwelling with the two sprinkling-vessels and a branch of the *kāmpīla* tree,
and having purified the site of the dwelling with the two sprinkling-vessels and the *kāmpīla* branch, [he recites]: "Go away, depart" (ŚB 18.1.55) and "I give this to him" (ŚB 18.2.37).
Having thus prepared the water for pacification with two [verses], he sprinkles the dwelling.
Having pierced the southeastern branch, then having ploughed around it with a plough and having surrounded it by encircling it with branches.
Having pierced the southeastern branch,
then, having ploughed around it with a plough and having surrounded it by encircling it with branches.
The action of the place of cessation.
Now the rite concerning the bones is described:
with the verse, "Give back again, O Lord of the Forest" (*punardehi vanaspate*), he takes [the bone] from the root of a tree.
*Kauśikasūtra* 11.4.19. "Give back again, O Lord of the Forest"—with this ṛc, he takes it from the root of a tree.

[If they say, "That which Kṛṣṇa... (18.3.55), having gathered from the earth into a garment, having scattered all kinds of fragrant powders over it, and having raised it with the *utthāpanī* verses, they should carry it away with *hariṇī* verses.
If he takes [the soil] from the earth with the verse "yatte kṛṣṇaḥ," he takes it from the earth.

Having placed the bones in a cloth, having bound it, having sprinkled it with all kinds of fragrant powders, and then having tied a knot, one should raise it up with the *utthāpanī* mantras and carry it away with the *hariṇī* mantras;
thereafter, one should perform the rite that is about to be described.
Now, the rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the event of the loss of bones is described:
"Not knowing [the location], [they take] dust from the place.
Upon the loss of the bones, having taken dust from that spot and having placed it in a garment, they should raise it up with the *utthāpanī* verses and carry it away with the *hariṇī* verses.
"Arise, go forth" (18.3.8), "Move forward" (18.3.9),
"The watery one" (18.2.48).
"ita ete" (Pāṇini 18.1.61), "agnīṣomā" (18.2.53),
"idaṃ pūrvam" (18.4.44).
Thus are the *utthāpanī* verses.
With the eight verses beginning with "ati drava" (18.2.11–18), [one offers] the *hariṇī* verses.
Alternatively, having spread out a garment at the edge of the water, he should call out, "O so-and-so! or he should shave [the hair] while saying, "O so-and-so!"
In that case, whichever creature should fall therein, they shall raise it up with the *utthāpanī* mantras and carry it away with the *hariṇī* mantras.
"Or else, three hundred and sixty palāśa twigs:
having fashioned a man with three hundred and sixty palāśa twigs, and having raised him up with the *utthāpanī* verses, they should carry him away with the *hariṇī* verses.
This is the expiation when the body has been burnt and the bones destroyed."
This concludes [the section on] the destruction of bones when one has died in a foreign land.
[In the village, he causes a measured pavilion with doors facing south and north to be spread with *darbha* grass.
One should provide both a northern door and a southern door for that pavilion which was previously constructed in the center of the village;
then, one spreads the pavilion with *darbha* grass.
"The north is the path of the living; the south is the path of the ancestors.
By the north humans travel;
by the south the bones of the ancestors.
"One should cause [the sun] to come while it has not yet set" (KauśS 18.4.62); thus,
one should perform this rite in that pavilion before the sun has set.
With the verse "Come hither, O fathers," he causes the bones to enter the pavilion through the southern door.
With the verse "ācyā jānu" (KauśS 18.1.52), he causes the bone-effigy to sit upon a three-legged stool.
With the verse, "May they settle down" (RV 10.85.29), he causes them to lie down.
He causes them to lie down with the ṛc, "May they settle down."
"‘This is your vessel, O Fathers’— with this mantra, he pours out three bronze vessels filled with water while facing the bones;
the mantra is repeated three times."
In that pavilion.
He causes three Brahmins who have bathed and anointed themselves to drink honey-mixture (*madhumantha*).
He causes the honey-mixture (madhuparka) to be brought for the Brahman priest.
They cause the cow to be known.
"Perform [it]," he said. KauśS 11.4.34.

He feeds the Brāhmaṇas with the southern half of that [cow], and the ancestors with the northern half. The performer first causes the *madhuparka* to be brought for the Brahman priest, optionally including a cow;
if he provides a cow, he feeds the Brāhmaṇas with its southern half.
The left [hand] should be employed for the oblation to the ancestors;
according to the rule for the barren cow, the primary mantra is "Svadhā to the ancestors."
In the eleventh [chapter], the fourth section (kaṇḍikā).
"Carry the omentum, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors where you know them to be placed in the distance;
let streams of fat flow toward them; may their blessings be true and their desires fulfilled—svāhā, svadhā! With these words, he offers the omentum three times.
"Carry the omentum"—with this verse, he offers the omentum three times.
[With the verse beginning "imaṃ yama" (18.1.60), one offers the fourth oblation to Yama.
With the ṛc "imaṃ yama," the fourth [oblation] is offered to Yama.
The section concerning the killing of a cow, dedicated to the ancestors, is completed.
[With twenty-one barley grains, he cooks *kṛśara*, along with another dish that is already cooked.
Thereupon, the performer cooks two types of *caru*: one containing barley and one without barley;
he causes the *kṛśara* to be cooked with twenty-one barley grains.
He cooks a sacrificial pap of barley.
[The living beings eat the barley-gruel.
Those born of his own lineage partake of the meal of the barley-gruel.
[Then he offers a ball of food for the other.
According to their ability, they offer the ball of food near the bones with cooked rice and the like, mixed with barley and meat broth.
The one who performed the bone-rite eats the remainder of the ball.
He pours out the stirred barley meal, as prescribed by the mantra beginning "yaṃ te mantham," into the measured space.
The slaves who remove the heat arising from that [fire] enjoy [the fruit].
"Let the lutes speak," he says;
and likewise his own slaves.
Then the performer gives the command to the kinsmen.
One should play the lute;
one should play musical instruments.
"Having placed an empty pitcher in the middle of the pavilion with the words, 'Make the ancestors great,' they strike it with worn-out sandals.
One should have an empty pitcher placed at the edge of the bones in the middle of the pavilion; everyone, including the performer of the rite, runs toward it and strikes it with two worn-out sandals.
With the verse, "Whose head are you cleansing? (KauśS 18.3.17), they walk around three times counter-clockwise with disheveled hair, striking their right thighs;
at this point, the performer should recite the mantra.
"Trirapasavyam" means with hair disheveled, that is to say, with hair loose;
"pariyanti" means they wander about;
"all the kinsmen" (gotriṇaḥ) [do so] while striking their right thighs.
The repetition of the three mantras.
In this same manner, it is performed at midnight and during the latter part of the night.
[Before the departure, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is with meat.
"Before the departure" means before dawn;
therefore, the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) should be performed with meat.
The procedure for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is performed with worldly-prepared meat;
this rite is to be performed in a pavilion in the middle of the village on the night of the fourteenth day.
Now, the ritual for the new moon day at dawn is described:
"Having raised them up with the *utthāpanī* verses, they should carry them away with the *hariṇī* verses.
Having raised those bones from the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with the *utthāpanī* verses, they should carry them away with the *hariṇī* verses.
Then, having placed [it] upon the tripod.
Now the conclusion is stated:

"Then the conclusion" means that after the previously performed [rites], the piling [of the fire-altar] for the ancestors should be performed first; and after those, the [piling] for the younger ones.
That is to say, the piling for the ancestors who were previously honored should be performed first.
The former [are] earlier;
the latter [are] subsequent, being younger in their effects.
[They stand facing the southeast, the north,
and the west. The cremation grounds are to be commenced facing the southeast and are to be completed in the northern direction.
They should also be constructed to the south of the village.
[Just as with the funeral pyre, so too the cemetery should slope toward the south-western direction.
Just as with the funeral pyre, so too are the ritual rules (*dharma*) in the cemetery:
beginning with "May they rise up" (*udīratām*), and so forth.
It has been stated: "with the two sprinkling-vessels" (KauśS 80.42).
It has been stated: "crossing over the desert-tracts with a pause" (KauśS 43.3). Cemeteries are to be established on ground sloping toward the south.
The fifth section (kaṇḍikā) in the eleventh [chapter].
Now, the measures are being stated:
[Now, the measures]. (KauśS 11.6)
The *diṣṭi*, *kudiṣṭi*, *vitasti*, *muṣṭi*, *aratni*, *pada*, and *prakrama* [are the measures]. KauśS_11,6{85}.2 //
"With a span and with a bow, we measure this measure" (KauśS 11.6.38–44).

Regarding the excavated [pit]: the *diṣṭi*, *kudiṣṭi*, *vitasti*, *nimuṣṭi*, *aratni*, *pada*, and *prakrama* are to be measured by means of these standards, using either a span (*prādeśa*) or a bow (*dhanus*).
With the seven verses beginning with "imāṃ mātrāṃ mimīmahe," he consecrates the ground as it is being measured out in each direction.
He measures seven [steps] to the south, seven to the north, five in front, and three behind.
He measures out a pavilion of this kind; or alternatively, he measures nine [steps] to the south, nine to the north, seven in front, and five behind.
Alternatively,
he measures eleven [steps] to the south, eleven to the north, nine in front, and seven behind.
These are the options for the construction of the funeral mound in the cremation ground.
[With eleven [verses] for those who have seen the gods.
This is one section of the Atharva branches.
[The cremation grounds for those who follow the *śaunaka* tradition are of uneven measurements, circular, or square.
One should make them of uneven measurements; the cremation grounds for those who follow the *śaunaka* tradition should be made either circular or square as an option.
For it is thus that they are seen. (KauśS 11.6)
As tall as a man with his arms raised is the piled fire-altar. [KauśS 11.6.10] As tall as a man with his arms raised is the piled fire-altar; it is to be piled upwards.
Or one may make it two men high with the arms raised.
The leftward paths are those leading from the southern doors, consisting of an odd number of stones and an odd number of bricks;
the piling should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder. The gathering of the ritual materials is done from the south.
The gates should be made facing south;
the funeral pyre should be built with an odd number of stones, or the cemetery itself should be constructed with an odd number of bricks.
Having measured the left cord on the south side with the verse, "We measure this measure" (RV 10.71.9), [he proceeds].
With the words, "May they ward off evil," he places the obstructing enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) and drives in the peg (*śaṅku*).
Upon that ground, having measured seven [units] to the south with the left cord using the mantra, "We measure this measure," he places the obstructing enclosing-stick with the mantra,
"May they ward off evil," and drives in the peg.
The mantra is to be repeated for each direction.
Having measured out [the space] in front, he places a fence of *śamī* wood around it with the words, "May the sin go to the *śamī* plants," and he drives in a wooden peg.
Having measured toward the north with the words, "May sin be appeased," he places an Audumbara enclosing-stick and drives in a peg.
Having measured [the distance] from behind with the formula, "The sin has been pacified," he places a palāśa enclosing-stick and drives in a peg.
Then from the front;
then from the north.
Thereafter, pegs and enclosing sticks (paridhis) should be placed in each direction. To the east, a piece of *śamī* wood should be placed with the mantra: "From the peaceful ones, [I take] the evil."
"To the north, [he places a branch] with the words, 'May sin be pacified.
To the west, he places a Palāśa branch with the words, 'Sin is pacified.'"
[He recites the mantra] "amāsi" (KauśS 18.2.45–47). Then, with the three verses beginning "amāsi mātrām," he consecrates the cremation ground.
Having tied it crosswise with a red thread.

Having dug a pit in the middle [of the ground] with the words "Praise the famous one" (*stuhi śrutam*), he pours into it earth from a cemetery, sand, water, *udumbara* wood, *śaṅkha* shell, *śālūka* lotus-root, all fragrant substances, and powdered *śamī* wood. Then,
having bound that [pit] diagonally with a red thread in that cremation ground, he digs the pit with the verse "Praise the famous one."
Into that pit, he scatters the powders of rope, sand, a rat, a conch shell, lotus root, Udumbara wood, all fragrant substances, and Śamī wood.
With the mantra "May sin be cast out" (*niḥśīyatām agham*), he spreads out a worn-out garment that is being discarded into the pit.
It is not blameworthy. KauśS_11,6{85}.21.
With the mantra "May misfortune be dispersed," he holds the second outer garment outside at that very place. Having held it there, the subsequent ritual action shall be performed with that cloth.
The human sacrifice has been described, as well as the strewing of grass from the south.
One should offer clarified butter into the pit with these [verses]: "Indro mā marutvān" (18.3.25–37),
and "Idaṃ pitṛbhyaḥ" (18.1.46).
With this verse, he strews darbha grass upon the pit.
With the two verses, "Etad ā roha" (18.3.73) and "Dadāmy asmai" (18.2.37), the youngest son pours down— that is, deposits— the bones into that pit.
The performer should recite the mantra.
With the verse "edaṃ barhiḥ" (KauśS 18.4.52), the eldest son of the family collects the bones according to their joints.
Like the limbs of a person.
[May your mind not [be distracted] (18.2.24); whatever limb of yours [is injured] (18.2.26);
may Indra [protect me] (18.3.25);
[may he] draw me up from the water (18.3.37).
Thus, from this point, he consecrates [the water] with these [verses]:
"May thy mind," "Whatever limb of thine," "Indra accompanied by the Maruts," and "The water-carrier"; with these, he consecrates it from this point onward.
[He pours in the parched grains with the verses containing the word *liṅga*.
(KauśS 11.6)] "Those parched grains of yours" (18.3.69; 18.4.26)—these two [verses]; and "The parched grain became a cow" (18.4.32).
One [verse] is: "etāste asau dhenavaḥ" (18.4.33); one is: "enīrdhānāḥ" (18.4.34); and one is:
"yāste dhānā anu" (18.4.43).
This is one [verse]; with these, he places sesame-mixed parched grains upon those bones.
The sixth section (kaṇḍikā). // KKp_85 //
[With the words] "This is the bitter water" (KauśS 11.7),
all those of the same lineage look at those bones situated in the pit. They look with the verse beginning, "This is the bitter water."
The performer should recite the mantra.

Having filled a sacrificial pot (*caru*) with clarified butter and honey while reciting the two verses, "And those who are living" (*ye ca jīvāḥ*, 18.4.57) and "Those who have passed away before" (*ye te pūrve parāgatāḥ*, 18.3.72), he places it at the head of the deceased.
"And those who are living" is one verse.

With the two verses beginning with "Those who have passed away before," he fills two pots with clarified butter and honey, consecrates them with mantras, and places them near the head, close to the bones.
They place the items mentioned in the mantra beginning with "apūpavān" in the eight directions.
[He places the one] cooking in the middle.
With the nine verses beginning with "apūpavān," he places eight cooked rice offerings (*caru*) starting from the western direction,
setting them down in each cardinal direction.
Having placed one in the middle, he then consecrates them.
For each mantra, all the cakes mentioned in the mantras—filled with milk and so forth and covered with flour-cakes—must be prepared;
they should be offered in a counter-clockwise direction.
Having sprinkled with water [using the formulas] "thousand-streamed" (18.4.36) and "hundred-streamed" (18.4.29–30). KauśS 11.7.5.

With the verse "sahasradhāram" as one and "śatadhāram" as two, having placed these over the middle of the sacrificial vessel (caru-pātra) which has a hundred holes and a thousand holes, he consecrates the water above them and douses the bones with that water.

With the verse "The king is the Parṇa tree" (18.4.53), he covers [the vessel] with middle palāśa leaves; with this ṛc, the performer recites the mantra while they cover everything, including the hundred-holed and thousand-holed [vessels] and the sacrificial porridges, using middle palāśa leaves.
[With the verse "ūrjo bhāgaḥ" (18.4.54), he covers [it] with stones.
With the ṛc "ūrjo bhāgaḥ," he covers it with stones, pebbles, or bricks.
And the chariots are to be piled like a house.
With the verse, "I prop them up" (KauśS 18.3.52), he fills the hollows between the joints with clods of earth, the sacrificial porridge, and bones, following the order of their placement.
With the mantra "May sin flow away" (*niḥśīyatām agham*), he covers [the bones] with a worn-out cloth.
Having strewn *darbha* grass over the cemetery, he spreads a second cloth upon the bones.
[idamidvā u nā (18.2.50–52), upa sarpa (18.3.49–51),
Thus they collect [the earth]:
three verses beginning with "This very one," and three verses beginning with "Crawl near."

With the two verses beginning "Asau hā iha te," they construct the cremation ground—the dwelling of the ancestors—by piling up uneven stones or bricks in a counter-clockwise direction. They also make the southern door in the temple of the gods. The performer recites the consecratory formulas over these acts.
[As it is said, "Just as for Yama" (KauśS 11.7.11): With the verse beginning "Just as for Yama," they strike and break up the cremation ground.
In all cases, the mantra is the agent;
having made the father's house high, [it is said]:
"It should be elevated for one desiring heaven."
The sacred revelation.
With the mantra "May he destroy the evil," he places a stalk of *śara* grass upon the cremation ground;
it should be moist and with its roots so that it may grow.
Some [teachers] prohibit it. KauśS 11.7.13.
[With the words, "May sin be hidden," he raises up an eight-finger-long splinter from unspotted reeds from the vicinity of the village.
Likewise, there is an option regarding a clump of *śara* grass.
Having consecrated an eight-finger-long wedge of spotted wood with the mantra "May sin be hidden," he effects the concealment between the village and the cremation ground.
Having sprinkled around counter-clockwise, they break the jars. Having sprinkled around the jars three times counter-clockwise with *kuśa* grass,
they burst them open in the western direction.

With the verse, "Come together, O all" (*sameta viśve*), all the kinsmen fasten the *dhuvana* (shaking-instruments) at the western end of the cemetery row. "Three times they walk around counter-clockwise, with disheveled hair, striking their right thighs"— thus all the kinsmen perform the *dhuvana*.
[To the northwest of the fire: "With splendor, may Vivasvān [bestow] upon me... (18.3.10–11); "O Indra, [grant] wisdom... (18.3.67).
Thus [ends the section].

Then, standing behind, the performer and the members of his lineage perform worship with these [verses]: the two beginning with "May I [be endowed] with splendor" (*varcasā mām*), followed by those beginning with "Vivasvān" and ending with "O Indra, grant us wisdom" (*indra kratuṃ naḥ*).

With the two verses beginning "They kindle the immortal" (*samindhate amartyam*), he brings the pavilion that was constructed in the middle of the village and, having placed it in the area behind the cremation ground, he ignites and burns it, saying, "[They kindle] the immortal" (*samindhate amartyam*)— thus, subsequently, he inflames the *saṅkasuka* fire. (KauśS 11.7.18)
Having offered oblations with the *saṅkasuka* verses to the *yāmasārasvatas*, that which is to the north of the *jīvaśarada* and to the south of the *yajjuna* is called by the term *saṅkasuka*;
he kindles it.
The rite of the cremation mound at the cemetery is completed.
By this procedure, one should perform the piling of the bones;
either a son or a kinsman performs this rite for one desiring heaven.
"whatever offense," (12.2.40);
"be gracious upon our heads," (12.2.19).
Thus he causes [the guest] to sip water,
[reciting] "In this [we]," and "Whatever offense."
The mantra beginning with "sīse mṛḍḍhvam" has been explained by way of the pacification of the flesh-eating spirits (kravyād).
Having wiped the hands and feet with black wool.
All [these] belong to the same lineage.
"These living beings" (12.2.22) and "with those directed northward" (12.2.29) are as stated in the mantra. KauśS 11.7.21.
Having covered twenty-one steps from the cremation ground with pebbles, [he performs the rite]. KauśS 11.7.22.
The cremation ground is also called *dahana*.
The phrase "the station of death" (*mṛtyoḥ padam*) [is used] with the accusative case to denote the boat. KauśS_11,7{86}.23.
Having driven the wooden pin toward the southeast with the mantra, "Beyond death" (RV 10.18.1).
Having caused seven forms of rivers to be made and having filled them with water.
"Ascend this ship of Savitṛ" (12.2.48);
"The good protector" (7.6.3);
"The great earth" (7.6.2).
Thus he causes [the bride] to board the boat, which contains gold and barley.
With the verses, "The stony river flows" (12.2.26) and "Arise,
cross over to happiness" (12.2.27), he causes him to cross while facing northward.
[The offering] beginning with sugar is performed by means of placing fuel sticks [into the fire]. (KauśS 11.7)
The ritual from the [offering] to Vaivasvata onwards is the same.
Having dug a pit to the north and performed the pacification of the flesh-eating spirits (*kravyād*),

then the rites beginning with those that do not involve barley are performed by those facing east, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*), and moving clockwise (*dakṣiṇāvṛt*).
Then he should perform everything beginning with "He pours seven pebbles into their hands," and so forth;
he offers the *śāmyākī* plants,
and they consume their smoke (KauśS 82.19–20).
The kinsmen perform everything up to this point, beginning with the injunction:
"Having cooked the *sthālīpāka* for Yama Vaivasvata" (*KauśS* 82.36). The teacher’s fee consists of two bulls and at least ten cows.
The performer [performs] for twelve nights; everything up to the conclusion of the Yama-vow occurs.
[Upon reaching the house, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is common.

Having reached the house, the single Piṇḍapitṛyajña is to be performed according to the rule for all members of the lineage. Then, on the new moon day, one should perform the placement; on the new moon day, one should perform the pacification of the flesh-eating fire.
Some perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña even in the worldly state.
The Pitṛmedha is concluded.
Both those who maintain a single fire and those who maintain the consecrated fires (Āhitāgni) are entitled to perform the Pitṛmedha.
The funeral rites, the piling of the vessels, the provisions for when one has died in a foreign land, and the Pitṛmedha sacrifice.
The seventh section (kaṇḍikā) in the eleventh [chapter].
Now follows the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
[On the new moon day, it is known that [the rite is performed] in the evening on the same day.
On the new moon day, one should perform [it] in the afternoon.
With the verse, "May Mitra and Varuṇa encompass me" (18.3.12), he washes his hands.
Having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite, he recites "And the woolly ones" (19.68).
Having recited this, he washes his hands with the verse: "May Mitra and Varuṇa encompass me."
[With the verse beginning "With luster, me" (18.3.10), he sips water.
He causes him to sip water with the ṛc verse, "With luster, me."
[Then, having performed the sipping of water with the left hand and having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya), he gives the instruction to the one who performs the summons.
Thereafter, he silently performs the sipping of water again with the left hand;
then, having become one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (pitryupavītī), he performs the rite that is about to be described.
He gives an order to the attendant.
"Having washed the mortar, the pestle, the winnowing basket, the cooking pot, and the bronze vessel, bring the sacrificial grass, the water-pot, and so forth.
[KauśS 11.8] "Bring the mortar and pestle, the winnowing basket, the cooking pot, the bronze vessel, the water-pot, the *darbha* grass, rice, fuel-sticks, the stirring-spoon, and other such items."

Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, facing the intermediate direction between the south and the east, he pours out the sacrificial materials fit for oblation into a winnowing basket upon which a single strainer has been placed.
With the formulas, "This for Agni Kavyavāhana; Svadhā to the Fathers dwelling on earth," "This for Soma accompanied by the Fathers;
Svadhā to the Fathers dwelling in the intermediate space who are accompanied by Soma," and "This for Yama accompanied by the Fathers;
Svadhā to the Fathers dwelling in heaven," he offers three oblations while facing downwards.

Then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), facing the intermediate direction between the south and the east, he places a winnowing basket containing a single strainer; from that, he pours out a handful of rice.
With the mantras beginning "This for Agni Kavyavāhana," he pours out three handfuls with the palm turned downward.
Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (pitryupavītī), he performs the sprinkling three times with the mantra "This for Agni Kavyavāhana."
Having poured [the grain] into the mortar, he threshes it three times with the mantra: "This is your oblation, O ancestors. (KauśS 11.8)
He attends upon [the deity] in the same manner as the sacrificial oblation.
For the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) consists of the oblation (havis) itself.
Then, having poured [the grain] into the mortar, he threshes it three times with the mantra: "This is your oblation, O ancestors.
Thereafter follows the winnowing with a winnowing basket.

[He gives instructions regarding the performance of the *praiṣa*: "Wash the *caru*, place it on the fire, pour water into it, and having thrown in the rice grains, stir it with the stirring-ladle; do not let it burn.
Then follows the washing of the rice grains.
"Wash the *caru*, place it on the fire"—this is the *praiṣa* (direction).
"Placing the porridge on the fire";
"having poured water," the sprinkling of water upon the porridge;
"pour in the rice grains," the pouring in of the rice grains.
With the verse, "Around thee, O Agni" (7.71.1), he performs the circumambulation with fire; with a stirring-ladle, he stirs the sacrificial porridge three times clockwise.
One should act in such a way that it becomes thoroughly purified.
[They declare that it is the seizing of the head.
One should not perform the seizing of the head.

Having gone outside the fire-hall, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, and facing the intermediate direction between the south and the east, he digs a trench one span deep and one finger-breadth wide with the verse, "May they rise up" (RV 10.57.44). Having gone outside the fire-hall, having become one who wears the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, and facing the intermediate direction between the south and the east, he digs a trench one span deep and one finger-breadth wide with the verse, "May they rise up."
Some say it should be as long as the finger up to the first joint.
With the Yajus formula, "Struck away are the Asuras and Rakṣasas who sit among the Pitṛs," he scatters dust toward the southeast.

Having washed both the trench and his hands, and having filled the trench with water while reciting the mantra, "This, O Fathers, is your vessel" (KauśS 11.8.17), he then takes the sacrificial offering and the strainer, prepares a bronze water-vessel, and pours it into the middle of the trench with the mantra, "This, O Fathers, is your vessel. Having poured it out, he covers it with whey or fresh butter from within, and then carries it away toward the south. (KauśS 11.8.18)
Then, having entered the middle [of the fire] and having moistened [the oblation] with whey or fresh butter, he should cast it into the cooked rice;
he removes it from the fire toward the south.
Taking two pieces of wood, he kindles them with the two verses beginning with "uśantaḥ.
Taking two pieces of wood, he kindles them with the two ṛg-verses beginning with "uśantaḥ."
[He replaces one of the two that have been set ablaze. // KauśS_11,8{87}.20 //
Having taken one [piece], with the verse "Be right here, a winner of wealth" (RV 18.4.38),
he takes one glowing piece of wood and places it upon the dust with that same ṛc.
Having placed them in the dust, he adds fuel with the verses:
"Those which were buried" (18.2.34–35), "They kindle" (18.4.41), and "Those which have thirsted, those which are true" (18.3.47–48). (KauśS 11.8.22)

With the five verses— "Those who are buried," "Two [verses] beginning with 'They kindle,'" "One beginning with 'Those who have thirsted,'" and "One beginning with 'Those who are truthful'"— he places five fuel-sticks. Then:
He brings together the necessary provisions. // KauśS_11,8{87}.23 //
The water for sprinkling, sacrificial grass, a water-jar, a bronze vessel, a ladle, clarified butter, a vessel for the āyavana, the *caru* oblation, garments, collyrium, and ointment.
[KauśS 11.8.24] The water for sprinkling, the sacrificial grass, the water-jar, the bronze vessel, and the ladle.
Clarified butter;
the stirring; the sacrificial porridge.
Garments, collyrium,
and ointment.
Having set aside all these vessels.
Whatever is to be brought together here, having brought that together—// KauśS_11,8{87}.25 //

Therefore, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), wearing the ancestral cord over the right shoulder (pitryupavītī), and having taken up the sacrificial grass (barhis) and untied the binding-cord, he should cast it down toward the southwest, the eighth direction.
Then, wearing the ancestral cord over the right shoulder, having taken up the once-cut sacrificial grass and untied the binding-cord, he silently discards it in the south-western region.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass with water, [he recites]: "The fathers who sit upon the sacrificial grass" (18.1.51),
"Our fathers are invited" (18.3.45),
and "The Agniṣvātta fathers" (18.3.44).
He spreads [the grass] with the verses: "Those who are our fathers' fathers" (18.3.46) and "Those who are ours" (18.4.68). [KauśS 11.8.27]
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with water, [he recites] the verse "The fathers who sit on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣadaḥ pitaraḥ*),
the verse "Our fathers have been invited" (*upahūtā naḥ pitaraḥ*), the single verse "The Agniṣvātta fathers," and the single verse "Those who are our father's fathers."
With the half-verse beginning "Our fathers who... he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*);
upon the sacrificial grass, he performs the invocation.
[The three beginning with the invitation:
With the verse "Come, O fathers" (RV 10.15.4), and [the formula] "Bending the knee" (ŚGS 4.3.1).
Having scattered sesame seeds with these two verses, "May they settle" (18.2.29) and "May they enter" (18.2.29).
With the three verses beginning "udīratām" (KauśS 18.1.44–46), he should pour out water-vessels one by one according to each verse.
With the three verses beginning "udīratām," he pours the water-vessels onto the sacrificial grass, verse by verse.

Therefore, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the ancestors (*pitryupavītī*), he circumambulates the fire-brand, which is blazing at both ends, three times from right to left with the mantra "Those Dasyus... (KauśS 18.2.28), and then casts it away.
Having sprinkled water around [the fire],
he then, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, carries a firebrand blazing at both ends around [the site] with the verse, "Those who are Dasyus," and casts it away.
Having sprinkled water around [it again].
The eighth section (kaṇḍikā) of the eleventh [chapter].
"Those who, assuming various forms, being *asuras*, move about by means of the *svadhā* offering—drive them far away, O Agni! May the blessings of our ancestors be true! *Svāhā! Svadhā!*";
having offered the clarified butter with the *sruva*-ladle while reciting this verse beginning with "ye rūpāṇi," he pours it over the *kumbhīpāka* vessel.
Then he silently pours the Kumbhīpāka over it.
[He offers with the words, "To Agni Kavyavāhana... (KauśS 11.9).
Thereafter, he offers the cooked rice-oblation (caru) with the formula: "To Agni Kavyavāhana, svadhā to the ancestors!"
The second [offering] is according to how it was poured out. KauśS 11.9.3.
"Yamāya pitṛmate svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ"— with these words, he offers the third oblation.
With the verse, "yad vo agniḥ" (VS 18.4.64), he offers the evening parched rice grains.
With the verse "saṃ barhiḥ" (7.98.1),
he offers rice grains together with *darbha* grass;
then follows the sprinkling around (*paryukṣaṇa*).
[Therefore, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), and wearing it over the right shoulder for the ancestors (pitryupavītī), he draws up the food with the ladle.
Then, wearing the cord over the right shoulder for the ancestors, he draws up the food from the vessel with the ladle.

"The sky is an unguarded, immeasurable, inexhaustible ladle; as the sky is an unguarded, immeasurable, inexhaustible ladle, so is this ladle of my great-grandfather unguarded, immeasurable, and inexhaustible.

The intermediate space is an unguarded, immeasurable, inexhaustible ladle; as the intermediate space is an unguarded, immeasurable, inexhaustible ladle, so is this ladle of my great-great-grandfather unguarded, immeasurable, and inexhaustible."
"The earth is an unguarded, unlimited, unfailing ladle; as this earth is an unguarded, unlimited, unfailing ladle, so may this ladle here be an unguarded, unlimited, unfailing one.
With the three [verses], "The sky is an unguarded, unlimited ladle," he draws [the water] out with each mantra.
Having taken up [the portions] and mixed them with clarified butter, he places three combined balls [of food], saying: "This for you, O great-grandfather" (KauśS 18.4.75–77).

Then, having taken up [the portions] and mixed them with clarified butter, he places three combined balls upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) with the three verses beginning, "This for you, O great-grandfather."
To the south, for the wives: "This for you, O wives. KauśS 11.9.12.

With the words, "May this be inexhaustible, accompanied by *svadhā*, for all those— both women and men, scattered and dispersed— who desire this, who hope for this, to whom we are givers, and who depend upon us, together with their wives," he scatters rice three times in a counter-clockwise direction. "May this be inexhaustible, accompanied by *svadhā*, for all those— both women and men, scattered and dispersed— who desire this, who hope for this, to whom we are givers, and who depend upon us, together with their wives"— with these words, he scatters rice three times in a counter-clockwise direction.

Having smeared the *piñjūlī* wicks with collyrium and anointed them with clarified butter, he places them upon the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) while reciting the mantra: "Anoint yourselves, O Fathers" (*aṅdhvaṃ pitaraḥ*).

Thus it is stated in the *Kauśikasūtra* 11.9.14. Having prepared the *piñjūlī* wicks and the collyrium by anointing them with ghee, he deposits them upon the *piṇḍas* using the mantra "Anoint yourselves, O Fathers."
"Grow, O fathers; do not separate yourselves from us further, O fathers"—with these words, he lays down the cords.
"Grow, O fathers"—with this verse, he places the cord.
Regarding the phrase "they anoint, they anoint thoroughly" (*añjate vyañjate*), this refers to the act of anointing;
with the verse "they anoint, they anoint thoroughly," he sprinkles [the offering] with clarified butter.
"With ghee he continuously pours over the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) with the verses, 'And those who are living' (18.4.57) and 'Those who have gone before' (18.3.72).
With the verse 'And those who are living,' he pours ghee over the rice-balls."
With the verse, "Those who have departed before," he pours a stream of water over the funeral cakes.
"O Pitṛs, rejoice here; according to your portions, according to your worlds, be refreshed.
With these words, "O Pitṛs," he mutters over each individual piṇḍa.
"Here, O wives, rejoice; according to your shares, according to your worlds, be satisfied.
With these words, he murmurs over the *piṇḍa* for the wives.
Having circumambulated that internal fire which is there from left to right,
he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having turned around, [he says]: "The fathers have rejoiced; according to their portion, according to their world, they have been satisfied."
"The wives have rejoiced; according to their portion, according to their world, they have been sprinkled.
Thus he worships the funeral cakes with the words "they have rejoiced" once again.
Having sprinkled water over the fire with the verse "āpo agnim" (18.4.40),
[he recites: "āpo agnim" (18.4.39), [the verse] "satisfying sons and grandsons."

Having sprinkled water around [the offerings] from left to right (prasavyam) with the verse "Drink, O my great-grandfathers, grandfathers, and fathers, together with your wives; may they be satisfied; drink," and having washed the vessel with the verse "A son, a grandson... and the formula "Drink, O my great-grandfathers, grandfathers, and fathers, together with your wives; may they be satisfied; drink," he sprinkles water around the top of the *piṇḍas* from left to right with that same vessel, saying:
"O my great-grandfathers, grant me heroes; O my grandfathers, grant me heroes; O my fathers, grant me heroes; the fathers ask for heroes."
With the words, "May my great-grandfathers be heroes," he worships the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
He stands in attendance with the words, "Homage to you, O fathers" (18.4.81).

Setting aside the *uttara-sīca* with the rule *akṣan* (Pāṇini 18.4.61), one should pour out the *uttara-sīca* with the verse beginning *akṣann amīmadanta*. One causes [them] to go away with the verse beginning *parā yāta* (Pāṇini 18.4.63).
One should dismiss the ancestors with the verse beginning, "Go forth."

[Therefore, wearing the ancestral cord (pitryupavītī), that is, the sacrificial cord (yajñopavītī), he invokes the mind with the words: "That which here has become one with the mind along with the ancestors—that I summon hither. Thus he invokes the mind.
Then, he wears the sacrificial cord.
The ninth section (kaṇḍikā) in the eleventh [chapter].
We now invoke the mind with a hymn of praise consisting of the Nārāśaṃsa verses,
and with the prayers of the ancestors.
May our mind return to us again for the sake of will, for skill, and for life, so that we may long behold the sun.
May the Fathers and the divine folk grant us back our mind;
may we be united with the company of the living.
O Soma, bearing our minds within our bodies according to your law, may we, possessing progeny, abide together in harmony.
"May the prosperity of those living beings who are born together with me, who are well-disposed, and who belong to my own kin,
be established in me in this cow-pen for a hundred years.
[KauśS 11.10] Having touched his heart, he should mutter the hymn beginning with "yanna idam" and "mano nvā hvāmahe."
Having consumed the warm remnant of the boiled rice that remains in the *caru* pot, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa.
If a Brāhmaṇa cannot be found, he should consume it in water.
"‘To his own servant,’ say some. (KauśS 11.10)
He gives the middle portion of the rice-ball to his wife who desires a son.
O Fathers, bestow the embryo, a boy adorned with a lotus-wreath,
so that there may be a man here.
"The speckled bull has mounted you; the wise fathers have placed you as an embryo.
May this man come to you, a man from among men;
may he be born for your preeminence, and may he sing the *sāman* at the *soma* sacrifice. [KauśS 11.10]
With the hymn beginning "ā dhatta pitaraḥ," he gives the middle rice-ball to his wife who desires a son, for her to consume.
If there is another second wife,
he offers a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for her father to that second wife with that same mantra.
[First of all, to the one learned in the Vedas // KauśS 11.10(89).8 //] He gives the first rice-ball to the one learned in the Vedas.
Now, if one's wife or female slave has run away, he gives those rice grains which have been scattered counter-clockwise to her.
With the verse, "Come hither at my approach; do not stay away," he gives the husked rice from the west to the female slave, saying: "Food is the bond of the vital breath; with that I bind you to me.
(KauśS 11.10) With the verse beginning "Come hither at my approach," he hands over the western rice grains to the female slave.

Having taken the water for sprinkling and the fuel-sticks, and having returned with the verse "May we not go astray" (13.1.59–60), he stands worshipping his home with the verse "Bearing strength" (7.60.1–6).

Having taken up the water for sprinkling and the fuel-sticks, and having murmured the two verses beginning with "May we not go astray," he goes home. Then, with the six verses beginning with "Bearing strength," he worships the house.
Rejoice, do not fear; O dwellers of this stall rich in dried cow-dung! Milking out strength, pure and observers of pure vows, may we, as living beings, sit down near you, our homes.
The gods have given me strength, and men have given me strength;
from the ancestors I have brought strength. Full of strength be my home.
The gods have given me milk, and men have given me milk;
from the ancestors I have brought milk. Full of milk are my homes.
"The gods have granted me vigor, and men have granted me vigor;
from the ancestors I have brought vigor; my home is full of heroes.
With the hymn beginning "Rejoice, do not fear," he worships.
Having stepped inside, he places the fuel-sticks upon the fire with the verse:
"This Agni is our overseer; this one is our best finder of wealth. By sitting near him, may we not suffer harm; may he protect our progeny."
In this house of our own, may a thousand prospering fires flourish;
may we kindle this fire, long-lived and full of splendor.
O Agni, you who are praised...
[18.3.42] "May we kindle thee, O Agni" [18.4.88].

Then, having entered the *agnihotra* hall, he places fuel-sticks (*samidh*) upon the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire, verse by verse: two with "This is our Agni," one with "Thou, O Agni," and one with "Come to thee, O Agni"; with these he places the fuel-sticks.
With the verse "He has become the messenger" (*abhūd dūtaḥ*), he brings back the fire.
With the ṛg-verse "He has become the messenger," he brings back the fire.
If everything were to be offered on the *praṇītā* vessel, then this [offering] for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) would be made in the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
[In the domestic rites for one who has not established the sacred fires:
In the domestic rites, there is an oblation for one who has not established the sacred fires.
"This much has been done by me; this much I am able to do; may the ancestors indeed know me. (KauśS 11.10)
The gods know him who sacrifices; men know him who gives; the ancestors know him who performs *śrāddha* rites—the ancestors indeed know him.
With the mantra, "This very thing has been done by me," he worships the fire with [the verse], "From whatever treasury... (19.72).
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is completed.
In the eleventh [book], the rule for the rite of the Pitṛmedha, which is performed for the sake of the body's final disposal, is proclaimed together with that of the Pitṛyajña.
The tenth section (kaṇḍikā) in the eleventh [chapter].
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Kauśikapaddhati.
Now begins the twelfth chapter:
[The Madhuparka]. Now, the madhuparka is described.
When the teacher has arrived at the house, he performs this rite.
[When about to offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka), he brings darbha grass.
The giver says:
"I am about to offer the honey-mixture."
Then the teacher says,
"Bring darbha grass," and the giver speaks again.
[Then he causes the mats to be made.
"Now, make the mats. Thereupon, the teacher makes the mats with the mantra.
"He indeed prepares a single-stemmed [blade of grass] for the water for the feet, a two-stemmed one for the seat, and a three-stemmed one for the honey-mixture;
thus he makes a triple set of spreading-grass."
Having taken as much as he deems necessary, having separated and prepared it—both the roots and the tips—so that it may be as wide as required, he draws it upward and binds it together in the middle.
"With *ṛta* thee, with *satya* thee, with austerity thee, with action thee"—with these words he girds himself.
Then he releases [the cord]: "Released, let the hater go—him who hates us and whom we hate.
With the words, "Thee by Truth," he performs the binding;
he makes a knot in the middle part.
He prepares the seats with the mantra, "atisṛṣṭo dveṣṭā";
the mantra is repeated for each seat.
Having prepared the seats, he looks at the giver with the words, "And of this giver. He looks at the giver with the words, "And of this giver."

The radiant Brahman has risen up, [filling] the intermediate space and the sky; with the immortal, the Brahman has shaken off death.
The Brahman is the direct witness of good deeds; may the Brahman strike away from us blemish and darkness.
"An excellent ox"— the rest is the same.

Having prepared the *śāntyudaka* (water for pacification) with the *ātatana* and the names of the Mothers appended, and having performed the rites from the sipping of water (*ācamana*) up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, [he recites] the two verses beginning with "ārādarāti" and the verse beginning with "ayāścāgne."
One should offer clarified butter with the two verses beginning "ārād agnim" and with the hymn beginning "apeta etu";
thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra).

In a family feud, in a battle between royal houses or villages, in a conflict among castes such as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and so forth, in a battle or quarrel among women, in a battle or quarrel among men, and in a battle or quarrel with another within one’s own family—
the pacification of quarrels and portents [is prescribed].

Now, the pacification of an earthquake is described:
"Then, wherever this earthquake occurs, there one should offer oblations. (KauśS 13.6)
Unshakable is the sky, unshakable the atmosphere, unshakable the earth, and these quarters are unshakable.
This unshakable one, firm from his confinement and obstruction, shall stand victorious, established in the kingdom.
As the sun shines in the sky, as Mātariśvan clothes the atmosphere.
Just as fire has entered the earth, so may this [pillar] be firm, unshakable, and victorious;
just as the god, thundering in heaven, shines forth, and just as rain falls for one who desires rain;
just as the waters have entered the earth, so may this [pillar] be firm, unshakable, and victorious.
Just as the rivers flow day and night without ceasing toward the ocean with their sediment,
so may all the subjects, being of one mind, come here without fail to my call.
May the goddess Earth, together with the deities, be firm, stable, and unshakable for me.
"Having driven away all evil from me, may it pierce my enemies and those who hate me;
Svāhā to the Earth! Having thus offered the oblation.
I have brought you hither; the sky is firm; the Great Truth.
With this Anuvāka, one should perform the oblation. *Kauśika Sūtra* 13.6.3.
That is the expiation there.

Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water of pacification) up to the *ājyabhāga* (oblation of clarified butter) portions, one should offer clarified butter with the hymn beginning "The heaven is unshakable" (*acyutā dyauḥ*),
and [with the verse] "I have brought thee hither" (*ā tvāhārṣam*).
One should offer oblations with this Anuvāka beginning with "The sky is firm" and "The Great Truth," followed by the subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra) starting from the Pārvaṇa.
The peace regarding the earthquake is concluded.
The sixth section. KKp_98.
Now, the pacification ritual for an eclipse of the sun is described:
"Then, when the darkness seizes the sun, one should offer oblations there. (KauśS 13.7)
The divine one, arranging the seasons with wondrous skill, rises up, causing the first of the seasons to revolve.
May that Āditya, crossing over, lead us from all sides; these waters move throughout these worlds.
In harmony with the plants, may Indra and Agni protect you.
By that which is the Law, by that which is the speaker of truth—by that, destroy all darkness!
Having offered with the words, "To Āditya, svāhā! // KauśS 13.7.2 //
One should offer oblations with this hymn, *viṣāsahiṃ sahamānam* (17.1).
He worships with the *rohit* verses.

That is the expiation there. Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water for pacification) up to the *ājyabhāga* (libations of clarified butter), one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the two verses beginning "The celestial, variegated... or with the section beginning "The subduer of poison... (*viṣāsahi*).
He worships with red deer-skins;
thereafter follows the subsequent ritual procedure beginning with the *pārvaṇa*.
With the mention of "and so forth" (*ityādi*), the *śānti* is concluded.
The seventh section. 99.
Now, the pacification rite for the seizing of the moon is stated:
"Then, wherever this moon is eclipsed, there one should offer oblations. (KauśS 13.8)
Rāhu stalks King Svaran; here he strikes him first.
A thousand of his bodies must perish here; let a hundred of his bodies be destroyed.
Having offered the oblation with the words, "To Candra, svāhā! // KauśS_13,8{100}.2 //
One should offer oblations with this hymn: "The smoke of dung, the stars... (RV 6.128).
That is the expiation there.

Having prepared the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*), and having performed the rites up to the portion of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the verse "Arā rājānam" and with the hymn "Śakadhūmam."
Or he worships with the Rohita verses from the hymn beginning, "viṣāsahiṃ sahamānam.
The subsequent ritual procedure (uttaratantra) is the same as for the Pārvaṇa and other rites.
Thus concludes the propitiatory rite (śānti) regarding the lunar eclipse.
The Eighth Section. 100.
Now, if the dawn does not break there, the pacification rite is prescribed:
"Then, wherever this dawn does not arise, one should offer the oblation there. (KauśS 13.9)
May the Dawn arise, fashioning prosperity; having made the offerings ready, let the wandering thief go away with his gray hair.
Bearing the seasons in their many varied forms, may she, the wise one, ordain what is auspicious for me.
Having offered the oblation with the words, "To the Dawn, svāhā! (KauśS 13.9).
With the words "The divine Gandharva" (2.2), he should offer oblations using the names of the mother.
That is the expiation there.

[KauśS 13.9] Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water for peace) up to the *ājyabhāga* (butter-portions), one should offer clarified butter with the verse "May Fortune rise at dawn" (*udetu śrīruṣasaḥ*) and with the *mātṛnāmagaṇa* (group of names of the Mothers). The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) is that of the *pārvaṇa* and other such offerings.
When the radiance of dawn is no longer seen, then this is peace.
The Ninth Section. 101.
Now, regarding the pacification during a terrible year, it is said: "Then, wherever such a terrible year occurs, there one should offer oblations. (KauśS 13.10)
She who, being uniform, goes forth with her brilliance, shaking off the offspring of Prajāpati—
her, whom the deities know as satisfaction, you we fashion together.
We fashion you, O doe with a golden womb, the mother of the hunter.
We fashion you, such as you are.
"Whatever is terrible in you, whatever is your poison—that we deposit among your enemies; [name], so he should say. (KauśS 13.10)
Having offered the oblation with the mantra: "May it be auspicious for us; [may it be] equal in peace and equal in long life; svāhā to the equal one! // KauśS_13,10{102}.3 //
One should offer oblations with this hymn, "samāstvāgne" (2.6).
That is the expiation there.

Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water for peace) up to the *ājyabhāga* (oblation of clarified butter), one should offer clarified butter with the three verses beginning "The year that is white... When the fierce year has arrived in the sign of Capricorn, or when disease has arisen, or during fear of a foreign kingdom, or during the terrible fear of thieves and robbers—in such a year, the rite for peace is completed.

The ritual procedure for the Pārvaṇa and subsequent rites follows.
When there is no rain, or when there is an eclipse of the planets or constellations, or when [such phenomena] appear in the field, the rite for pacification (śānti) is completed.
The eleventh section. // KKp_103 //
Regarding the taking up of weapons by Brāhmaṇas, the pacification rite is prescribed:

"May Indra be our leader; may he protect us from all sides.

That is the expiation there.

Having prepared the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*) and having performed the invocation by the names of the Mothers, one should then perform the rites from the altar (*vedī*) up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, and offer clarified butter (*ājya*) with the two verses beginning "Those who belong to the Asuras," and with the two verses "May they not find us" and "Homage to the slayers of gods."
The subsequent ritual procedure for the Pārvaṇa and other rites follows.
The rite for pacification regarding the Brāhmaṇas' taking up of weapons is completed.
The twelfth section. 104.
The pacification of portents caused by deities is now described:
"Now, wherever these deities dance, weep, laugh, sing, or assume other forms— whether they be asuras or humans— the mantra 'mā no vidan' (1.19) and 'namo devavadhebhyaḥ' (6.13) [are to be recited]."
Thus one should offer oblations with the *abhaya* mantras.
That is the expiation there.

Having performed the *śāntyudaka* (water for pacification), the *cātanādi* (rites beginning with the driving away of evil), and so forth, up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* (butter-portions) offerings, one should sacrifice clarified butter (*ājya*) with the mantras: "Those who are Asuras," "May they not find us," and "Homage to the slayers of gods."
The ritual procedure for the Pārvaṇa and other rites follows.

The deities dance, exude moisture, laugh, sing, move forward, emit fragrant smoke, open their eyes, flow with blood, manifest, and perform movements within all divine images— whether made of stone or the like, or silver, gold, crystal, and so forth— including the Liṅga, Vāsudeva, Śaṅkara, Sarasvatī, and others.
Or they may assume many other various forms, such as those of deities and so forth.
The *Devatādbhutaśānti* is completed.
The thirteenth section. // KKp_105 //
Now, the pacification rite (śānti) regarding contact with a ploughshare is described: "Then, when they have come into contact with the ploughshare, having cooked a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)..."
Having gone halfway into the forest.
Having established the furrow facing the east.
Having placed the fuel-stick upright in the middle of the *sītā*, he adds it to the fire.

Then he offers the oblation: "Thou art gain, thou art prosperity, thou art fortune; belonging to the descendants of Prajāpati, thee, desiring prosperity for myself, I offer with svāhā! KauśS 13.14 (106).6.
The lotus-lake Kumudvatī, the Sītā river beautiful in all her limbs,
and agriculture of a thousand varieties— this Fortune has been established within me.
Men call you the wide earth; they know you as the glory of the mind.
Place within us a store of food that is free from disease and full of vigor.
O wife of Parjanya, you who are golden-hued and victorious, speak for us;
O Kālanetrī, enjoy our oblation and grant nourishment to our bipeds and quadrupeds.

With those [powers] by which the gods fashioned the Asuras, the Yātus, the Manus, the Gandharvas, and the Rākṣasas— with those, O auspicious one, come to us today with a gracious mind, bestowing thousandfold prosperity.
Wearing a golden garland, lotus-eyed, dark-complexioned, and beautiful in every limb—
may this Śrī, who is agriculture, gold, and the earth itself, be established within me.

O Goddess, being in harmony with the two Aśvins, together with Indra and prosperity, come to us. May all the quarters of space grant you favor; may days and nights, half-months, months, and the seasonal periods, together with the seasons, be favorable to you.
The supporter of gods and mortals alike, the supporter of progeny and of men;
together with elephants, foot-soldiers, field-folk, and charioteers—
with gold, horses, and cattle— may this Śrī be established within me.
In this case, one should employ the *śunāsīra* formulas.
"A choice bull" and so forth is the same [as before].

Having gone to the forest and established there a furrow running eastward, having performed the rites from the water for peace (*śāntyudaka*) up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings in the middle of the furrow, and then having made yoke-pins serve as the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he then offers the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Taking portions repeatedly, the offering of the cake is performed with four portions (*caturavatta*).
With the hymn beginning, "Thou art wealth, thou art nourishment," he should then prepare the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*) everywhere and apply the *cātanā* mantras everywhere;
in all instances, he should employ the names of the Mothers.

There is a specific distinction regarding the application of the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*): the hymn "They harness the ploughs" (*sīrā yuñjanti*, 3.17) and the hymn "He whose this region...
(*yasyedam ā rajaḥ*, 6.33).
Thus, one should append this hymn— the section beginning with "Truth is Great" (12.1)— to the water for peace;
and with that water for peace, one should perform the sipping of water and the sprinkling for the one who causes the rite to be performed.
One should sprinkle the plow with water,
and the field with a Ṛgvedic verse; the subsequent ritual procedure is that of the Pārvaṇa and other rites.
In that field, there is the application of ritual action:
when the plough touches the middle of the furrow or touches the tail, there is the "Miraculous Pacification of the Plough."
The fourteenth section.
Regarding the cutting of the cord, peace is prescribed:
"Now, when two women are spinning or cutting, and they join various threads together, one should offer oblations with this hymn beginning with *manāyai tantum prathamam*. (KauśS 13.15)
One woman shall first behold the thread; others shall weave it out. Regarding this, O women, I speak to you: may you be virtuous and may you be fortunate.
May the weaver be successful; may the chosen chariot proceed successfully.
Therefore, O swift horses, run forth in the morning to draw you.
Like swift screech-owls, like a fierce descent into the waters, let them fall like swift ones; let the fertile lands fall by the straight path.
Those two who are beyond words are being pricked, as if by the piercing of two mules; I have praised the hymn of the fertile lands that lie extended.
The woman makes the fifth ray into a garment, like a thread, for wealth. Unharmed is its wearer; O Indra, clothe him and drive away [evil].
One should give a garment to the performer.
That is the expiation there.

Having prepared the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*) and the clarified butter (*ājya*) in the fire-chamber, one should offer the *ājya* with this hymn, "To the ill-disposed one, the thread" (*amanāyai tantum*).

May you two be of one mind with us, dwelling in one home, and free from blemish.

The seventeenth section.

Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] in this manner.

Some perform the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*) beforehand; others perform the water for pacification afterwards.

Having placed the newborn child upon his lap.

The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) is that of the *pārvaṇa* and other [standard offerings].
The cow suckles the cow; peace is completed.
