May there be milk among the gods, milk in the plants, milk in the quarters, and milk in the intermediate space.
May Dhātṛ and Savitṛ bestow that upon me; may all the gods grant their approval to it.
The milk that is in the waters, the milk in the cows, the milk in the wells and in the mountains—may Dhātṛ and Savitṛ bestow that upon me; may all the gods grant their approval to that.
Whatever milk is present in wild animals, whatever moves and flies among winged birds—may Dhātṛ and Savitṛ bestow that upon me; may all the gods grant their approval for it.

With this hymn— "The waters that have been bestowed from heaven, those many and manifold ones that are in the intermediate space— may the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, being ungrudging and submissive, grant us today their mastery over them"— one should perform the oblation.
That is the expiation there.

[KauśS 13.23] Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water for peace) up to the *ājyabhāga* (butter-portions), one should offer clarified butter with the hymn beginning "In the gods is milk" (*apayo deveṣu*).
The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) is that of the *pārvaṇa* and other such offerings.
Whether it be a cow, a horse, a mule, or a human, etc., [if] one eats foam, in that case the *adbhutaśānti* (rite for pacifying portents) is completed.
The twenty-third section.
Now, regarding that place where ants of improper appearance are seen, the pacification rite is prescribed there:
"Then, wherever these ants of improper appearance are seen, one should offer oblations there. (KauśS 13.24.1)
Svāhā to the earth! Svāhā to the world! Svāhā to the lord of the world! Svāhā to the lord of the worlds! Svāhā to the wide one! Svāhā to the expansive one!
To Śatāruṇa, svāhā!
To him who is the king of the white ants in the eastern direction, Svāhā!
To him who is the king of the black ants in the southern direction, svāhā!
To him who is the king of the silver ants in the western direction, svāhā!
To him who is the king of the red ants in the northern direction, svāhā!
To him who is the king of the brown ants in the fixed quarter, svāhā!
To him who is the king of green ants in the intermediate direction, svāhā!
"To him who is the king of the reddish ants in the upward direction, svāhā! [KauśS 13.24.116.3].
Having performed the rites from the water for pacification up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one should offer clarified butter with the hymn beginning "To Bhū, svāhā.
The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) is that of the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice and so forth.
If many ants there are red, black, or yellow, there [should be] a ritual for pacification.
Now the exorcism against ants is described:
if they are not appeased by this much, then one should subsequently prepare a fire.
Having strewn sacrificial grass made of reeds, cut off at both ends, around [the fire] from right to left.
He offers clarified butter that has been destroyed by poison, purified with a leaf of the *śākapalāśa* tree, using a *bādhaka* dipping-spoon.
Arise and run away; let there be no more lingering for you here! Indra shall shatter the embryos and the eggs of you all at once.
"The ants are falling away," [he says]. KauśS 13.24(116).7.
"Indra is yours, Yama is yours, Varuṇa is yours, Agni is yours, Vāyu is yours, Sūrya is yours, Candra is yours, Prajāpati is yours, and Īśāna is yours.

Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water for pacification) up to the *ājyabhāga* (butter-portions), one prepares sacrificial grass (*barhis*) made of *śara* reeds, cut on both ends, and spreads it around counter-clockwise (*prasavya*). There is clarified butter (*ājya*) that has been strained and purified; the purification of the butter is done with a leaf of *śāka-palāśa*, and the oblation is offered with a *sruva* ladle used for warding off obstacles (*bādhaka*).
With the hymn "uttiṣṭhata nirdravatam," he offers the iṅguda fruit;
he should apply the concluding verses (udarka) according to the specific purpose.
The definition of a repeated verse (*punarukta*) is stated in the fifth chapter (*pañcapaṭalikā*) as "that which has been spoken or not yet spoken."
In Mīmāṃsā, it is stated that "the connection [of a word] continues until the completion of the sentence":
"Yama is the restrainer of you all together," and "Varuṇa is the restrainer of you all."
"May Agni be yours all," "May Vāyu be yours all," "May Sūrya be yours all."
"Candra for all of you," "Prajāpati for all of you," "Īśāna for all of you."
"Together with the embryos, he will break the eggs;
the ants shall be crushed!
Thus he utters the mantra for each [action].
The subsequent ritual procedure for the *pārvaṇa* and other rites follows.
The *pipīlikā-abhicāra-śānti* (the pacification of the calamity caused by ants) is completed.
Furthermore, if one observes ants that produce disease—various kinds of ants, red, black, white, yellow, and blue—appearing in the house;
They appear frequently in fire-sanctuaries, fields, cities, or villages;
they are seen within food, within liquids, or in ghee, and there the rite of sorcery (abhicāra) is performed.
The twenty-fourth section.
Now, the pacification of flies is described: "Then, wherever these blue flies of improper appearance are seen, there one should offer oblations. (KauśS 13.25)

Those terrible messengers of Death who go forth with mortals in their chariot, becoming flesh-eaters—may the eye of the auspicious ones and their cry be auspicious; may there be well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.
"Peaceful is the eye of the female crows, as is their terrible mental impulse.

O Lord of the Mind, protect me with your body from that which is terrible; do not harm me in my body, nor in my offspring, nor in my cattle—svāhā to Vāyu! Having thus offered the oblation. KauśS 13.25(117).2.
One should offer oblations with this hymn, beginning with "May Vāta breathe forth the remedy. (KauśS 13.25)
May Vāta breathe forth healing for us, bringing bliss and joy to our heart;
may he prolong our lives.
And you, O Vāta, are our father, and you are our brother and our friend;
as such, grant us life.
"O Vāta, that medicine which was placed by you in your house in secret—that, grant to us for our living. With this hymn, one should offer oblations. (KauśS 13.25)
That is the expiation there.

[KauśS 13.25] Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water for pacification) up to the *ājyabhāga* (oblation of clarified butter), he offers clarified butter with two hymns: the hymn beginning with "The one who with mortals shares the same chariot" (*ayā matyaiḥ saratham*) and the hymn beginning with "May the wind blow healing medicine" (*vāta ā vātu bheṣajam*).
The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) follows that of the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice and others.
A blue fly falls into the house, or flies of other colors appear; thus ends the ritual for the pacification of flies.
The twenty-fifth section.
Now, the pacification rite for when a honeycomb has become attached to a house is described:
where these honey-bees appear in a manner that is improper to the customs, one should offer oblations with this hymn, "The winds bring forth honey" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*). 1. *Kauśika Sūtra* 13.26.1.
That is the expiation there.

Having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings with the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*), one should offer clarified butter with this hymn, "The winds blow sweetly for the one who follows the cosmic order" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*).
The subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) is that of the *pārvaṇa* and other such rites.
If a honeycomb has become attached to a house, whether inside or outside, or if it is seen in a place where one has settled, the ritual for its pacification is completed there.
The twenty-sixth section.
Now, the pacification for all portents is stated:
"Then, wherever such an unknown portent is seen, there one should offer oblations. (KauśS 13.27)
Whatever of our purpose or ritual action has been misunderstood or left unrecited, O Agni, protect us from that; for you indeed know each thing as it truly is.
To Agni, svāhā! KauśS_13,27{119}.2
And [the deities] Vāyu, Sūrya, and Candra. KauśS 13.27 (119.3).
The purpose of ritual action is commensurate with man;
therefore, may Vāyu protect me from that, for he knows each thing as it truly is.
To Vāyu, svāhā! KauśS_13,27{119}.4

Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water for pacification) up to the *ājyabhāga* (oblation of clarified butter), one should offer clarified butter with the two hymns beginning with "ayadājñātam" and "puruṣasammitaḥ," accompanied by the formulas: "May Agni protect me," "May Sūrya protect me," and "May Candra protect me."
It has been stated in that very context [of KauśS 8.22]: "One should apply [the supplements] according to the sense," and "The *anuṣaṅga* is the completion of the sentence" (Jaiminisūtra 2.1.48).
Thus, in the Mīmāṃsā;
"of what has been stated and what has not been stated" is said in the Pañcapaṭalika;
the Pārvaṇa and so forth constitute the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*).
Regarding that which is "unknown" (*anājñāta*) and "wondrous" (*adbhuta*): whatever is not recited in the *Grantha* is called entirely "unknown.

Furthermore, regarding what is recited in the *Pariśiṣṭas*: when everyone has entered the house, seeing everything as very small; or [in the case of] being equal to all, [during] agitation, the appearance of water, and movements; [or] a bow, twilight, meteors, halos, lightning, thunderbolts, *paripra*, and *parigha*—[all these are included].
In the case of a thunderclap, there is rain of dust, rain of stones, rain of eyes, honey, and ghee, and rain of marrow and blood;

the two paths have their rays diminished; lightning occurs during the waning of wealth and the waning of the moon; there is illumination during the fullness and the filling; there is immediate darkness at night and so forth;

there is the burning of the quarters, fuming, planetary irregularity, ascending, and invasion; and there are cities of the Gandharvas, the fury of the winds, and anomalies in the lunar days (*tithi*), divisions of the day (*karana*), auspicious moments (*muhurta*), asterisms (*nakshatra*), conjunctions (*yoga*), and fixed stars (*dhruvaka*).
The conjunctions and separations of the planets and so forth; rivers flowing against the current; and springs.
Crows flocking together upon palaces, gateways, watchtowers, banners, and parasols; the mounting of wolves onto carts;
being struck by a wildcat and sinking [into water];
and the hooting of owls being easily heard—these are omens of misfortune.
Hawks and other birds such as vultures alight upon the banners;
deformed humans or human beings born of men—whether women, children, the elderly, youths, or the very young—utter incoherent cries.
Or, when the staffs and feet of those with inflamed senses break, objects appear with double shadows or lack shadows altogether, being blurred, indistinct, or mixed.
Beyond this, [one should predict calamity] from the sudden falling of a shrine, a tree, or a pillar; from the upward growth of a tree, or from the regrowth of its trunk;

from the appearance of blisters, the shedding of leaves, or the withering of a tree or its branches; from the appearance of smoke, silver, or water on trees and forest plants; or from the breaking of an arm or a weapon, or from [the collapse of] sapphire-blue gate-towers, watchtowers, banners, umbrellas, and the like.

Or, in cases of breakage—whether it be the breaking of what is appropriate, the promotion of what is inappropriate, or a firm breakage; or in the case of dry growth, an anthill in the house, or the site of a bed; or upon the birth of a child, or in the reverse of friendship and the worship of deities;
or in the cutting down of these two, and wherever the king is present, or in [the occurrence of] *prasṛti* and so forth—[these results] come to pass.
And there are verses on this subject:
When the moon-like *prakṛti* appears distorted,
and a hole is seen in its center, death is within the king’s domain.
But when the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight becomes naturally deformed—
whether by being eclipsed or torn asunder— one should predict the death of the king.
Clouds may have the forms of weapons, possess hundreds of colors and shapes, be five-colored, or resemble staffs.
When the orb of the sun or the moon becomes dark in the center,
that planet should be known as Śaṅku, which is extremely terrible.
In that situation, the king would incur execution, which brings fear to all living beings;
therefore, he should perform a great pacification ritual using the immortal, universal medicine.

Now, one should know that in whatever region others than [the aforementioned] engage in the occupations of cowherds, Brahmins, charioteers, astrologers, physicians, wandering mendicants, bards, forest-dwellers, celibate students, or women— that is a calamity. That results in a confusion of occupations, as well as a confusion of sacrifices, legal proceedings, and ritual offerings.
And where Dharma is oppressed by Adharma, one should know that Dharma is then in a state of wonder amidst those acts of unrighteousness.

When Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and others cause mutual harm, if one does not establish peace among them, then great portents occur. These occur when deities manifest or depart, when falsehood prevails, and when disease breaks out among cattle.
In times of famine, during the destruction of districts and the like, when solar eclipses occur, when rats have proliferated, when insects, locusts, bedbugs, lice, nits, and birds have swarmed,

or during legal disputes within the royal family— one should burn with fire the horses, weapons, or armaments, as well as the house, all elephants, horses, clothing, ornaments, couches, and cosmetics. Furthermore, upon seeing an ill omen, one should perform various rites of pacification (*śānti*).
This is the peace upon the earth, in the atmosphere, and in heaven.

It is practiced by kings, horses, birds, wild beasts, and six-faced beings; likewise, where there are distorted forms in the forest or on the road, or where there are kings, ladles, those with three eyes, or among village families, or even in regions honored by royalty.
Likewise, the disposition toward the twice-born among animals is of a distorted form, and it is likewise among humans.

Now, if one's own birth-star (nakṣatra) is struck by an eclipse, hit by a meteor, eclipsed, cast down, or scorched; or if his birth-star, action-star, consecration-star, or country-star is in the eighth position from the moon when the thunderbolt is released; [then there is danger].
When a pillar or a shoulder [of a house] collapses; when there are various forms or many forms; when a horned animal bleats with the sound "kilava";

when thunderbolts strike and the conch-shell sounds "kambu," "dhuvati," "ṣavati," laughs, smiles, shines, roars, or makes a noise; when the Vaiśvānara fire blazes up and ashes, bones, and embers fall upon the house or the head; and when a rainbow appears at night—[these are inauspicious omens].

In a cloudless sky, the moon, sun, constellations, planets, and stars appear; at night, crows, pigeons, vultures, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and wild beasts cry out, sing, or play musical instruments; when the wind arises or one travels, there are wheels, banners, houses, pavilions, and upper stories; wells overflow and roar, lightning flashes, and chariots, mechanical devices, carriages, and musical instruments emerge as the utterances of sacred hymns and the like.

If smoke or flames appear as omens, or if the limbs of the king's body show signs of affliction; or if a queen or a king appears [in an inauspicious manner]; or if the royal parasol is struck down by the nesting of crows, owls, lizards, or house-lizards; or if the banner is broken, or the semen is discharged; or if the king’s staff is broken, or an elephant goes mad, or a village woman gives birth [to twins or deformed offspring]; or if the royal chariot, with the king mounted upon it, has its axle broken—these portend the death of the king within seven nights.

In the event of the destruction of a domestic priest, a commander-in-chief, an elephant, a queen, or a prince; or in the case of a deformity in cattle or humans—such as having two heads, a head on the back, feet like those of an elephant, or likewise two noses—as well as having too few or too many fingers, these [omens] arise through them. Similarly, in the case of the destruction of the feet or shanks, or the ears and nose, a decapitation occurs.
If a seed should sprout within a fruit due to negligence—whether in honey, clarified butter, curd, or milk; while eating or when applying ointments;
or in mechanical vehicles, palaces, houses, or weapons.
There may be the sight of crows, owls, and pigeons;
or other questions regarding the arrival of wild animals and birds;
or the sight of black pairs within the house of one of immeasurable splendor.
The sight of snakes or of swarms of reptiles,
or where abnormalities are seen in milk, boiled rice, or sacrificial offerings—
these portend the end of the lifespan of people and the exhaustion of a man's allotted life-span.

Vehicles travel unyoked and without horses or men, or conversely, even when yoked, they do not move; this portends great danger for kings. Furthermore, kettledrums, clay drums, and war-drums may sound even without being struck.
Struck instruments do not sound, and mountains move;
if the sound of musical instruments were heard in the forest from the sky,
or if a cow-pen should ever dance with a ladle in its hand.
Where, while the pestle is being struck especially hard against the potatoes,
the mortar or the winnowing basket shakes by itself;
or where a stone rolls down into a well or climbs up the mountain peak.
In the company of monkeys, there is a transformation of the moon and the sun;
a woman suckles another woman, and danger arises for the rice. Trees, stones, and plants spread out as if drawing back [in retreat].
Likewise, when there is the crying out of birds, as well as of beasts and winged creatures;
when there is the speech of non-human beings, the movement of stationary objects,
a confusion of genders, or a rain of flesh and blood.
Likewise, when there is no blazing of fire, nor the raining of clouds;
when weapons blaze forth, and when the painted images on shrines wither and fall;
and when the sacred emblems and temples weep or thunder.
When there is the overflowing of tanks, or fire and thunder,
or the appearance of fish, snakes, and birds, or the raining down of liquids; and where the sounds of singing and musical instruments occur without any apparent cause.
And whatever other portents of a distorted nature arise—
for all those portents, this pacification is prescribed:
during the lunar first-day [omens], planetary conflicts, planetary conjunctions, the movement of Rāhu, the movement of Ketu, the characteristics of Rāhu and Ketu, and the division of the tortoise.

In the case of fires in the cardinal directions, the falling of meteors, the falling of lightning, the appearance of lightning, the falling of thunderbolts, halos around the moon and sun, the signs of portents involving constellations and planets, the signs of calamities, the signs of immediate rain, the recitation of rites for pacifying wonders,
the recitation of chapters on dreams, and regarding all bad dreams— whenever such pacification is required, it is prescribed.

When the *Atharvahaṛdaya* texts have been recited, when the wonderful *Bhārgavīya* texts have been recited, when the wonderful texts recited by Gārgya have been recited, when the *Bārhaspatya* treatises have been recited, when the *Uśanasa* treatises have been recited, when the great wonders (*mahādbhuta*) have been recited,
and when the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, *Jyotiḥśāstra*, *Aśvavaidya*, and *Naravaidya* have been recited— this is the pacification (*śānti*) for all wonders.

Alternatively, the commentator states that among all portents not mentioned by Kauśika, this *śānti*—or the *mahāśānti*, or the *amṛtā*, the *ghṛtakambala*, or the *koṭihoma*—may be performed according to one's choice.
The twenty-seventh section.
The pacification for when [a sacrificial vessel] breaks in a fire-sanctuary, in an assembly hall, or in a forest is stated as follows:

"Now, if this should break in a village, in a settlement, in a fire-sanctuary, or in an assembly hall, four cows are prepared: a white one, a black one, a ruddy one, and a fourth that is well-formed."
He places this butter, milked from them over these twelve nights, [in its proper place].
On the morning of the twelfth day, having kindled the fire to the north of the very spot where the [earthen vessel] was previously split, he proceeds.
Having swept around [the fire], having sprinkled water around it, having strewn sacrificial grass (barhis) around it, and having mixed the white [milk] with clarified butter.
Having consecrated [the earth] with the three verses beginning "Agni is in the earth" (RV 12.1.19–21), he should touch it.
Then he should offer the oblation. (KauśS 13.28)
Likewise in the southern half.
Likewise in the latter half. KauśS 13.28.8.
Having placed [the vessel] in the northern half, one should offer oblations with the Vāstoṣpati mantras.
Having brought the portions from the split [vessel] and having established them, he performs the oblations.
Having sprinkled the cracked [vessel] with water for pacification.
A Brāhmaṇa should give those very same [offerings]. KauśS 13.28.12.
The Vaiśya [should give] a plough, the local ruler a horse, and the king an excellent village.
That is the expiation there.
Four cows are prepared: a white one, a black one, a ruddy one, and a fourth that is well-formed.
One sets aside the fresh butter from their milk, which has been milked for twelve nights.

On the morning of the twelfth day, at the very spot where the ground has been split open, one should perform the rites beginning with the *śāntyudaka* (water for peace) and ending with the *ājyabhāga* (oblation of clarified butter). Then,

having mixed rice with the clarified butter of a white cow, one touches it while reciting the three verses beginning with "Agni on the earth," and subsequently offers the oblation to the east of that spot.

Likewise, having mixed boiled rice with clarified butter in that same fire on the southern half of Kṛṣṇā, likewise on the southern half of Rohiṇī, and likewise on the southern half of Surūpā, he then offers the clarified butter with the Vāstoṣpati group of mantras and brings the remnants (sampāta) to a spot that has not been cracked.
The subsequent ritual procedure (uttara-tantra) begins with the Pārvaṇa offerings.
Then, having sprinkled the collapsed site with water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*), one gives a cow;
and in all cases, cows and other such gifts are given.

Whether a house has fallen, or a village, or a cremation ground, or a fire-sanctuary; or upon the collapse of a field or land, when a fissure in the earth is seen, or during an earthquake, the collapse of a house, or the collapse of a village and so forth—this is the rite of pacification.
Alternatively, one offers the four tantras respectively in the four directions;
one offers [oblations] in each direction, starting with white, black, and so forth,
and offers them in the eastern half.
In the Pūrvatanttra, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is a cow in all cases; [there is] the tantra for sitting in the ritual enclosure (tantra-upaveśana),
and the tantra for the altar and the secondary altar (vedy-uttaravedi-tantra).
Then follow the *sampāta* offerings beginning with the conch (*śaṅkha*). According to the view of Dāriila, this occurs throughout the entire ritual manual (*tantra*):
having first completed the manual [in the east], one then proceeds from the south, then the west, and finally the north.
Having completed the ritual manual and sprinkled those cows with water for pacification, the Brāhmaṇa should give them away;
the Vaiśya should give a plow, the local ruler a horse, and the king an excellent village.
In all cases, one should give a choice gift such as a cow and so forth.
Peace has been restored to the house, the village, and the countryside.
This concludes the twenty-eighth section. (KKp 120)
Now, regarding the case where there is an excess of water in a place that is not naturally watery, the rite for pacification is stated:

"Then, wherever this occurs in a non-watery place and there is an overflow of water, one should offer oblations with the hymns addressed to the waters (*apsu-sūkta*), beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ* (1.33). (KauśS 13.29.1)
That is the expiation there.
Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers clarified butter with all the hymns addressed to the waters, namely *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ* and *yad adaḥ* (3.13).
The subsequent ritual procedure begins with the *pārvaṇa* offerings.
If an abundance of water is observed in a place that is not naturally watery,
the *udakonmīlana-śānti* (the rite for the manifestation of water) is concluded.
The twenty-ninth section. // KKp_121 //
Now, when the sesame seeds become level with their oil, therein the rite for pacification is prescribed:
"Then, wherever these sesame seeds become level with their oil, there one should offer oblations. (KauśS 13.30)
Hail to the undiminished! Hail to the imperishable! Hail to the immeasurable!
To the Perfect One, svāhā! KauśS_13,30{122}.2
Facing south, he should pour blood [onto the ground], saying: "I pour this blood upon the hope of him whom I hate.

Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water for peace) up to the *ājyabhāga* (portions of clarified butter), he offers the clarified butter with these four [mantras], beginning with "To the non-deficient, svāhā!
With the mantra "He whom I hate," facing south, he should sprinkle sesame seeds with the water for peace (*śāntyudaka*).
The ritual procedure for the Pārvaṇa and other rites follows.
When oil is unavailable, then the propitiatory rite (śānti) is performed.
When sesame seeds produce equal oil, the propitiatory rite is concluded.
The thirtieth section. // KKp_122 //
Now, if they should touch the omentum or the sacrificial oblations, or birds, or bipeds and quadrupeds, and then depart, the pacification for that occasion is stated:
"Now, where they should touch the omentum or the sacrificial oblations, or birds, or bipeds and quadrupeds, and then depart: 'The fires...
(3.21), "'Homage to those who slay gods... (6.13).
With these two hymns, one should perform the oblation.
That is the expiation there.

Having performed the rites from the *śāntyudaka* (water of pacification) up to the *ājyabhāga* (butter-portions), one should offer oblations of clarified butter with these two hymns: "ye agnayaḥ" and "namo devavadhebhyaḥ."
The ritual procedure for the Pārvaṇa and subsequent rites follows;
the omentum and other parts should proceed, and there shall be peace.
The thirty-first section.
Now, if a boy or a girl has two whorls on the head—one turning to the left and one a local whorl—it is called *śānti* (pacification).
[Now, where this occurs for a boy or a girl, with two whorls on the head—one turning to the left and one a local whorl—there he should offer oblations. KauśS 13,32(124).1.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, who transforms forms in many ways and brings forth progeny of manifold and universal aspects,
fashion us here in this very place, making us free from error and arranging us in due order.
To Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā!
Within the wombs he extends himself in many ways, generating offspring of manifold forms;
may he bring us about that which is not contrary [to our purpose], fashioning us here in due order.
To Tvaṣṭṛ, Svāhā!
Whether it be rubbed away or rubbed toward, or whether they wipe away the crosswise misfortune—
the god Savitṛ, being in harmony with Prajāpati and all creatures, shall make that auspicious.
To Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā!

O God, may those forms of yours which turn to the right, those of universal form, and those which turn inward within your joints— may they be manifold, many, pleasant, efficacious, and auspicious for him.
Having offered with the words, "To Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā! // KauśS_13,32{124}.5 //

In all extraordinary portents—such as thunderclaps, earthquakes, meteors, the appearance of comets, the falling of stars, the burning of the quarters, rain of blood, rainbows, mock suns, and quarrels among jackals and owls—one should not study for three nights.

One should not study when a corpse has fallen into the house, nor when four-footed or two-footed creatures have fallen; one should not study while traveling on a road; one should not study in the middle of a village or in the middle of a city.

[The Concordance of Ritual Action: Now, the authorities (*pramāṇa*) of Kauśika should be applied according to the method of Mīmāṃsā. Just as the authority of the Veda was stated in the first chapter of the Mīmāṃsā, so too, at the beginning of the *Saṃhitā-vidhi*, the authority is stated by the initial sūtras.
Next is the exposition of ritual action (*karmavidhāna*).
In this treatise, the twelve-fold Mīmāṃsā must be applied:
in the first chapter is the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*).
In the second chapter, the definition of difference and non-difference;
in the third chapter, the definition of the primary and the secondary;
and in the fourth chapter, the definition of that which subserves the purpose of the sacrifice and that which subserves the purpose of the person.
In the fifth chapter is the definition of sequence (krama);
in the sixth chapter is the definition of modification (vikāra);
in the seventh chapter is the definition of location (deśa).
In the eighth chapter is the definition of specific extension (viśeṣātideśa);
in the ninth chapter is the definition of modification (ūha);
and in the tenth chapter is the definition of annulment and addition (bādhābhyuccaya).
In the eleventh chapter, the definition of *tantra* (contextual connection) is presented;
in the twelfth chapter, the definition of *prasaṅga* (incidental application).
And so it has been said:
One should apply the twelve-limbed Mīmāṃsā to all principles of logic found within the *mantras*, *brāhmaṇas*, ritual manuals (*kalpas*), supplements (*pariśiṣṭas*), and commentaries (*bhāṣyas*).

Likewise, it is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "What, then, are the purposes of the instruction on words? Preservation, modification, addition, economy, and the removal of doubt are the purposes of grammar. Through grammar, the meaning is determined.

In all the Mantras, Brāhmaṇas, and Kalpas, the meaning is determined by means of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). Furthermore, in the worlds, there is neither word (*śabda*) nor non-word apart from Vedic grammar;
therefore, through both Mīmāṃsā and grammar, the sacred tradition (*sampradāya*) is distinguished.
Whatever meaning is established by tradition, that is so and not otherwise. Now, the connection with the subject matter is set forth; first, the aphorisms on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[The Greatness of the Atharvaveda] In the Atharvaveda, dharma exists; dharma protects the one who protects it.
Thus it was said in the Pūrvabrāhmaṇa: "Having created the subjects, Prajāpati said, 'Protect them! Thereupon, he became the Atharvan."
Kauśika, Vatsaśarman, and his son Dārila—
indeed, the knowledge of the scriptures does not belong to a fourth among them.
For it is indeed improper to say that there are many who understand [this].
Likewise, Kauśika knew this in their lineage:
that because he was born from Vāha, he is Keśava; and because he arose from Keśava, he is called Ananta.
From Ananta was born Someśvara, and from Someśvara likewise Keśava;
all of them were knowers of the Atharvaveda and likewise performers of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
All of them performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma according to the rules,
and all of them performed Sava-sacrifices with the prescribed sacrificial fees.
They were caused to perform many and manifold great propitiatory rites;
all were learned in the Vedas and most righteous, and all were devoted to asceticism.
All were capable of both cursing and bestowing grace; all were peaceful and friendly.
Furthermore, the office of the Brahman priest was performed by them according to the injunctions of their own respective Vedic branches.
Even among the four Vedas, including those prescribed by the Atharva,
it is impossible to recount all the virtues within this lineage, which possesses so many qualities.
Keśava extracted the essence of all three commentaries;
by that [work], he composed the *Kauśikapaddhati* for the benefit of his disciples.
All were masters of grammar; all were followers of Bhaṭṭa and Prabhākara; all were knowers of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and all were devoted to the Smṛtis.
Dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā in their youth, they lived according to the conduct of sages;
all were completely free from egoism and were experts in dharma. They all refused gifts and were devoted to the practice of japa and homa.
In the illustrious city of Bhojapura, there was a learned Brahmin named Someśvara;
by his son Keśava, this *Kauśikapaddhati* was composed.
Indeed, this [work] was composed by the ancient teachers after they had perceived it through their vision;
having understood it according to the commentaries and with the approval of Atharvāṅgirasa, a person [should follow it].
Yet those who teach the philosophy of words do not understand that he stated the meaning of the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya based on his own imagination, rather than the true Kauśika [tradition].
Fools of little intelligence do not understand this instruction;
it was told to Atharvan only with great difficulty and even out of fear.
Having performed the initiation (upanayana) in that manner, the wise man should arrange it for the sake of welfare;
all the practices of the Atharvaveda, as well as the four castes and those belonging to the same lineage (gotra).
And so it has been said by those who know the systems of Bhaṭṭa and Prabhākara:
"Having understood even his [the latter's] hundred [verses], this manual was then composed."

May there be well-being for all those of the Ātharvaṇa [Veda], whose lineage is Pippalāda, known as the descendant of such-and-such (āmuyāyaṇa), and designated by the three *pravara* names of Kaśyapa, Asita, and Devala. These pure Brahmins reside in the city of Ānandapura.
All those known as inhabitants of Ānandapura, renowned throughout Ānandapura, and others who call it Kalpagrāma, proclaim it to be the boundary [of their domain].
Others, however, call it the city of Oṃkāra;
it is like an island in the midst of the ocean for humans, O King,
and like heaven for the gods, so is this city upon the earth.
Through righteousness and truthful speech, they were always devoted to the duties of their respective castes and stages of life;
even among the fourth caste, no falsehood was ever seen.
Every year there is purification through marriage after a fall from grace;
with effort, the protection of the Brāhmaṇas is maintained according to right conduct and the laws of the Smṛtis.
I am unable to describe anywhere the virtues proclaimed in Ānandapura.
In whose view, however, mutual benevolence is seen—
those Brāhmaṇas who prioritize the Sūtras and are masters of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas—
for the sake of preserving proper conduct, a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) is performed on the full moon day of Pauṣa.
The Atharvaṇa [tradition] has long been established among the Bhojas;
however, having reflected upon the Kauśika [lineage], this manual (paddhati) was likewise composed.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Kauśikapaddhati.

The rites of pacification (śāntika), nourishment (pauṣṛtika), and likewise those of sorcery (abhicāraka);
the office of the domestic priest (paurohitya), the role of the Brahman priest (brahmatva), and likewise the science of kingship (rājavidyā).
And likewise, in the Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda, it is said: "It leads to the destruction of the priests, the king, and the realm;
that sacrifice in which the ritual is impaired results in a year of calamity."
The passage beginning with "the sacrifice is complete with four feet" demonstrates the prohibition [of other priests].
Furthermore, among the four Vedas, the office of the Brahman priest and likewise the office of the domestic chaplain (paurohitya) are prescribed in the Atharvaveda.
Thus, it is stated in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa:
A Bahvṛca indeed destroys the kingdom, while an Adhvaryu would ruin the Soma-pressings;
a Chandoga leads to the loss of wealth; therefore, an Atharvan is the [proper] teacher.
And so Yājñavalkya says:
"He should perform the duties of a domestic priest, being one who knows the omens of the gods and is renowned for his learning;
likewise, he should be skilled in the science of government (daṇḍanīti) as well as in the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda]."
Likewise, in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "A king should have the duties of the domestic priest, rites for peace and prosperity, and the office of the Brahman priest performed by means of the Atharvaveda."
And likewise, in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "The *Atharvāṅgirasa* Brāhmaṇa is employed for the royal priest;
he should also cause rites such as those for pacification (*śānti*) to be performed."
And likewise in the Matsya Purāṇa: "A Brahmin who recites the Atharva-mantras, who is endowed with a complete and perfect body, [should be appointed] as the domestic priest (purohita)."
And likewise, in the Vārāha Purāṇa, regarding the characteristics of a domestic priest (purohita): "One who recites the Atharva-mantras and Brāhmaṇas..."
And likewise Paiṭhīnasi says:
"But he who feeds another at a śrāddha while an Atharvavedin is present—
the deities, together with the ancestors, depart from him disappointed."
And so says Kāmandaki: "Furthermore,
the domestic priest should be skilled in the science of government (daṇḍanīti) and should perform the rites prescribed by the Atharvaveda for pacification and prosperity."

And so it is said in the *Cāṇakya*: "The duties of the domestic priest consist of rites for pacification (*śāntika*), prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), malevolent magic (*abhicārika*), the pacification of portents (*adbhuta-śānti*), and so forth;
the four Vedas are employed in the performance of sacrifice."
Likewise, in the *Mahābhārata*: "The grandson [of the priest], being an expert in the Atharva-vidyā, should perform rites for peace.
Indra heard from Bṛhaspati, the seer of the Atharvāṅgirasas: "My heaven has been seized by the Asuras.
Having performed propitiatory rites and rites for victory, he regained his heaven once more.

Likewise, in the Mahābhārata: Drupada had two brothers, Yāja and Upayāja, who were practitioners of the Atharva-Angirasa [mantras]. For the purpose of destroying the entire lineage, he caused a *kṛtyā* (magical spell) to be performed by one of them.
And so it is stated in the *Atharvaparīśiṣṭa*:
"The deities, the ancestors, and the twice-born do not accept the sacrificial offering (havis) of that lord of the earth in whose house there is no preceptor learned in the *Atharva*."

Likewise, in the *Raghuvamśa*, there is the praise of Vasiṣṭha: "Then, having conquered his foremost enemies, the lord of wealth (Rāma), the best among speakers, took up meaningful speech from that treasure-house of the Atharva-veda."
And so Manu says: "The Atharva-Angirasa Veda shall perform rites of malevolent magic."

Likewise, Paiṭhīnasi states: "A gift given to one who knows the Ṛgveda has a single merit; it has double the merit for one who knows the Yajurveda; it is said to have triple the merit for one who knows the Sāmaveda; and it shall be infinite for one who knows the Atharvaveda."
And so it is stated in the Vārāha-jyotiṣa: "The pacification of portents occurs through the Atharva-Āṅgirasa rites, the Mahāśāntis, and the Koṭihoma."
Likewise, in the *Ariṣṭaka*, the *Vāyulakṣaṇa*, and the *Khaṇḍakhādya*, the *Atharvamahāśānti* mantras are recited for the purpose of pacification.
Similarly, there are meritorious consecrations (*puṇyābhiṣeka*) and royal rites (*rājakarma*) as taught by the experts of the *Atharva-veda*.
Likewise, in the medical treatise of Caraka (*Carakavaidyaka*), diseases are classified into two types.
These are the signs of food and the signs of impurity.
Regarding the signs of impurity, pacification occurs through the rites of peace (*śānti*) in the *Atharvaveda*.

Likewise, it is stated in the *Purāṇas*: "In the case of ten thousand, hundred thousand, or ten million oblations (*homādi*), the establishment of the fire, the establishment of the hearth, the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*), and so forth, are found in the *Atharvaveda*."
And so says Gautama: "One should cause rites such as those for pacification (*śāntika*), nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) to be performed.
Likewise, Bhaṭṭa states in the Mīmāṃsā: "Rites for pacification, nourishment, and malevolent magic, which rely upon a single Brahmin priest, are performed in the Atharvaveda."
Likewise, in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "One who has been consecrated with the mantras of the Atharva Veda enjoys the earth together with its oceans."
And so it is stated in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"In whatever king's realm an Atharvan priest who has mastered the rites of pacification (*śānti*) resides, that kingdom flourishes, free from affliction."
Therefore, a king should especially and constantly honor an Atharvan priest who has mastered his senses with gifts, marks of respect, and ceremonial rites.
One should constantly perform rites for peace and worship the planets and constellations.
Likewise, in the Mīmāṃsā, in the sixth chapter on the section concerning the domestic priest (*purohita*), the singular number is heard in the Atharvaveda:
"one domestic priest" (*ekaṃ purohitam*).
Likewise, in the Purāṇa: "One should cause Brahmins to perform the rites of giving prescribed by the Atharvaveda."

By these and many other statements, the Atharvaveda rite for pacification (*śāntika*) has been prescribed. This is according to the consensus of all authorities across all the major scriptures (*samastaka-śāstra*), as well as in the *Gṛhyatīkā*: "Through the Great Pacification (*mahāśānti*), the prosperity of the entire kingdom occurs; and there is growth."
Likewise, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "The four Vedas were divided by Vyāsa into the offices of the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Brahman;
and both the Śānti and the Brahmatva rites are prescribed in the Atharvaveda.
Similarly, among the eighteen Purāṇas: "The Śānti and the Brahmatva [rites] are in the Atharvaveda."
Likewise, according to the eighteen Purāṇas, a king should have all rites performed by means of the Atharvaveda;
through the pacifying rites of the Atharvaveda, victory accrues to the king and the prosperity of the kingdom ensues.
Likewise, in the *Brāhmaṇa*: "Now, the Atharvans and the Āṅgirasas... and so forth, regarding sacrifices, ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and other rituals.
Therein is the injunction of praise for the *Atharvaveda*: "When his speech is satisfied, Agni is satisfied; when his breath is satisfied, Vāyu is satisfied," and so on.
Likewise, in the *Bhārata*: King Viśvāmitra was made a Brahmin by Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras.
Likewise, in the *Bhārata*: King Pratardana was made a Brahmin by Bhṛgu.
Likewise, Aṅgiras, having performed a rite for the peace of the son of the King of Kāśī whose kingdom had been lost, [he] enjoys the earth.

In the narrative concerning Indra accompanied by the Maruts, having made Marutta his domestic priest (*purohita*), you became equal to Indra in battle; however, Indra hurled his thunderbolt at him, which was then warded off by Atharvan-Aṅgiras. Likewise, by the curse of the Bhṛgus, King Nahuṣa became a serpent, a python.

Likewise, after Bhārgava Ṛcīka had performed the marriage of Sukanyā, he restored youth to the two Aśvinīkumāras through the study of the Vedas; consequently, they were established among the gods and made recipients of their sacrificial shares.
Similarly, the Bhārgava Śaunaka, acting as the domestic priest for King Janamejaya, commenced the snake sacrifice (*sarpasattra*), wherein the Bhārgava served as the *hotṛ* priest.
The primary agent was the serpent;
thus, by means of the weapon of a *rākṣasa*, the *rākṣasas* were struck down by Bhārgava, the grandson of Vasiṣṭha and descendant of Parāśara.
The others were protected by the words of Bhṛgu and Pulastya.
Likewise, in the *Pūrvabrāhmaṇa*: "Therefore, whoever may be all-knowing, him one should make the Brahman;
for he indeed is the learned, all-knowing Brahman who knows the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases."

"These indeed are the pacifiers and protectors of this entire [universe]. Likewise, in the *Saṃhitā-vidhi*: "In that regard, the king, the lord of the earth, should desire a learned Brāhmaṇa; for he who knows the *Bhṛgvaṅgiras* is indeed learned. These—the *Bhṛgvaṅgiras*—are indeed the pacifiers and protectors of his entire [universe]" (*KauśS* 94.2–4).
Likewise, in rites for well-being (*svastyayana*), he asks, "O Śakadhūma, what day is it today?
and receives the reply, "It is auspicious, most propitious.
This is because of the departure.
And so it is stated in the *Nakṣatrakalpa*: "A Kṣatriya about to engage in battle should seek an Atharvāṅgirasa as his domestic priest—one who is learned and most proficient in the scriptures.
Likewise, an Atharvāṅgirasa Brāhmaṇa should ask [the king] at the beginning of the day and night:
"By whom has he not been conquered?"
If he should say, "It must be done," one should do so accordingly;
it becomes an auspicious day, and indeed on an auspicious day one performs the departure.
Elsewhere, Vyāsa is of the Bhṛgu lineage, as are Mārkaṇḍeya, Durvāsas, Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras.

Likewise, in the Yajurveda, there is a supplementary section (pariśiṣṭa) named *Pratijñā*, which states: "The science of elephant-archery (*hastiśalyā*), the characteristics of horses (*aśvalakṣaṇa*), the sciences of weaponry and medicine (*āyurveda*), the pacification of portents occurring in the atmosphere and on earth, rites for peace, prosperity, and auspiciousness, and those intended for malevolent magic, eradication, subjugation, and delusion must be imparted."
All of them, as many as they may be, are the Upavedas of the Atharvaveda. (35.1)
Now, it is heard in the first pāda of the Mahābhāṣya: "The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda—these are the four Vedas.
The Ṛgveda has twenty-one branches.
Likewise, [the verse] 'four are the horns' is explained as referring to the four Vedas."
Likewise, in the Mahābhāṣya, in the second quarter (pāda) under the rule *vibhāṣā chandasi*, [the forms] *aśaṃ no devīḥ*, *agnim īḷe*, *iṣe tvā*, and *agna ā yāhi* are cited.
First comes the Atharvaveda, and then the other Vedas.
Likewise, in the *Nirukta*, the verse beginning with "four horns" has been explained [as referring to the Vedas].

Similarly, in the *Brāhmaṇa* of the *Atharvaveda*, by means of the same verse beginning with "four horns," it is explained that there are four Vedas. Furthermore, in the first section (*pāda*) of the *Mīmāṃsā* concerning the authority of the Vedas (*vedādhikaraṇa*), two branches of the *Atharvaveda* have been cited: the *Paippalāda* and the *Maudaka*.
It has been established that the Vedas, being uncreated and eternal, are a valid means of knowledge.

Likewise, in the Mīmāṃsā, in the second chapter, in the section concerning all the recensions (*sarva-śākhā-adhikaraṇa*), two branches of the Atharvaveda—the Paippalāda and the Maudaka—are cited and established as being recognized by all recensions. Similarly, in the third chapter, in the section concerning the Pravargya rite (*pravargya-adhikaraṇa*), it is stated that there is no sacrifice called the "first sacrifice" (*prathama-yajña*) in any of the four Vedas; thus, the mention of the four Vedas is made, and it is declared that the four Vedas are for the purpose of sacrifice.
The author of the Bhāṣya likewise explained the verse "four horns" (*catvāri śṛṅgā*) in the section on the Atharvaveda as referring to the four *hotr̥* priests for each Veda.
Similarly, in the Nyāyamañjarī, it is stated: "There are four Vedas;
the first is the Atharvaveda."
In the *Pūrvabrāhmaṇa*: "By means of the Atharvaveda, the three Vedas were created;

likewise the worlds, the Vedas, and so forth. Furthermore, in the Atharvaveda Brāhmaṇa: "Now, Prajāpati, being about to sacrifice with Soma, said: 'Whom shall I choose as my Hotṛ priest—one who knows the Vedas?'"
"Who shall be the Adhvaryu? Who the Udgātṛ? Who the Brāhmaṇa? They replied:
"Choose one who knows the Ṛgveda as the Hotṛ; one who knows the Yajurveda as the Adhvaryu; one who knows the Sāmaveda as the Udgātṛ; and one who knows the Atharvāṅgirasa as the Brāhmaṇa.

For in this way, his sacrifice becomes firmly established in the four worlds, among the four classes of gods, in the four Vedas, and in the four offices of the Hotṛ-priests—the four-footed sacrifice."
He who knows thus becomes established in offspring and cattle;
likewise, his followers also become knowers of that in all four Vedas.
Likewise, in the subsequent Brāhmaṇa:
"The sacrifice is complete with its four parts, fashioned by the fourfold *hautra* ritual;
it is established by means of the four kinds of mantras and by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have mastered the Vedas."
In the *Sabhāparvan* of the *Mahābhārata*, it is said that four [beings] indeed stand in embodied form by the side of Brahmā in the assembly hall of Brahmā.
In the previous Brāhmaṇa, it was said: "By means of this triple knowledge, [one attains] Triviṣṭapa, Tridiva, the highest Nāka.
Beyond that are the great worlds of Brahman belonging to the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases; that is the goal of the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the Kauśikapaddhati.
